#### 78.41 THE QUESTION SHEET: QUESTIONS IN A FIXED FIRST ORDER, DEPTH BY STAKE AND FACT (2026-11-12; Kaveh: "we're asking a bunch of questions. First set of questions is between us and the chess board ... The next set of questions includes the opponent response. The order of the questions is the most important thing, because it decides whether we have time to see the real threats/opportunities or not"; "we need to break them down logically"; "The order initially is my king first, then their king, then their queen, my queen, etc. But how deep on each question depends on the stakes and the facts ... Maybe we go a bit deep here, then a bit there, then if there's more time a bit deeper here")

A PROBE FIRST (scratch script, a general chess library and textbook unit worths, NOT engine code; the 4156 positions of 78.37's fresh games, seeds 11 12 13 at 0.2 s; a "bad move" is a MISSED surprise where the judge's reading fell):

READING: where a unit is in contact the short search already sees it and errs about half as often; where NO question says yes the mover errs most (the last line), and those positions hold four in ten of the bad moves; a confined king (either side's) is the one sign that raises the rate. The engine has no question for a quiet position and none for an attack that is not yet a contact.

DESIGN (generic: a TARGET is a unit, its STAKE comes from the goal clause for the goal unit and from the judge's worth for the rest; nothing names a game):
  QUESTION   one target and one side asking: "can this target be taken or confined, and by what". The first order is by stake, sides alternating: mine at the top stake, theirs at the top stake, theirs at the next, mine at the next, and so on down.
  BREAKDOWN  each question is a tree of smaller ones, and a NO closes everything under it.
             level 0, the board as it stands: where is the target, what strikes it now, what guards it, which of its exits are open (78.39's HOLES and COVERED).
             level 1, one side's moves alone: which units could come to strike or cover, in how many moves (78.39's SUPPLY and SCENARIOS). No supplier closes the question: the target is SAFE from that side, and the sheet says why.
             level 2 and on, with the other side's reply: can the plan be stopped (cover, exchange, a counter at a higher stake); an exact search over the moves the question names, one ply deeper each time it is asked again.
             the quiet question, when every question above is closed or idle: which unit of mine does least (fewest strikes, fewest places to go), and where would it do more.
  SCHEDULE   anytime. Every open question holds its stake, its level, what it has cost and what its last step found. The next step goes to the question with the most at stake per unit of cost among those still open; a step that finds nothing new lowers its question's urgency, a step that finds a live plan raises it. So the clock goes a little here, a little there, and deeper where the facts keep it open. The sheet's answer at any moment is the list of open questions with their best lines; the move search starts from those lines.
  MEASURES   (a) the share of bad-move positions in which no question is open should fall against the probe's last line; (b) the level-1 SAFE verdicts should be right (the judge agrees no loss follows); (c) cost per step, and the order of steps printed in plain words; (d) later, the surprise rate of 78.37 with the sheet's lines as the search's first moves.
  STAGE 1    the sheet and the schedule as a training-side tool over the existing engine calls (facts, 78.39's scenario for any target, the ledger search for the reply levels); measures (a) to (c). Not yet in the wake.

(2) WHAT THEY ARE: in seven of ten the judge preferred a quiet move to our quiet move, in one of ten a check; a missed capture is rare (1.4%). (3) THE DIFFERENCE THE SHEET DOES SEE IS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE BOARD: after the judge's move the stake of THEIR units live at level 0 is 5.26 against 2.06 after ours and 1.93 after a random other move; the questions on MY units read the same after both (0.72 and 0.85 live, 39.19 and 39.09 open). Our move keeps our units as safe as the judge's does and makes no more threats than a random move. The engine answers "is anything of mine about to be lost" and does not ask "what can I attack". (4) The search step is dear as built (89.20 ms a step at depth 2, 343.79 ms at depth 3) and leaves 4740 ways not settled because a quiet first move takes nothing and threatens nothing at once: its value is in the question it opens, which is the next thing to count.
OPEN: the value of a way is a formula over the reason chain's answers, not a full exchange; a quiet move's worth to a question is unread; the run with search takes 1720.7 s for 400 positions.

OCTOBER'S FRAMES LOOKED AT AGAIN (Kaveh: "check out the frame methods from october, we were pretty good at solving puzzles there"; a read of JOURNAL 2026-10-07 to 10-24 and the code): a frame was a small game with its own moves and EXITS, searched to its own size and not to a fixed ply (the exchange on one place, the forcing line, the cornered unit whose top case is the goal unit, the promotion, the double threat, and WAITING frames with what they wait on and what breaks them); questions by stake; a memory keyed by what each result read. Its proofs were right (67 of 69 at 15 s a puzzle) and its unproved picks were not (5 of 21); quiet moves 24 to 27 of 100; skipping the replies outside the frame was wrong in 10.9% and was switched off. Game-free and still in the tree: catspace/incubator/analyst/frame_search.py (the Frame protocol, exits, retractable records) and rust/analyst_core/src/agenda.rs; the frames themselves are bound to a chess library.

#### 78.42 THE QUESTION GRAPH: THE CHECKER IN TWO LAYERS, OBSTACLES BY COUNTERFACTUAL, STAKES AS BOUNDS, THE CLOCK BY EXPECTED STAKE (2026-11-13; Kaveh, in order: "the cheap check ... should basically say that to ... the one that's doing the slow calculation ... like a scout giving a location ... take a right and then take a left ... it should always go for the entire flow"; "the waiting frame needs to come in"; "go back to the October code and port over everything that is useful ... assume that it already exists"; "the fact that it's considering pieces as fixed is a big blind spot ... given the medium of movement and the rules of movement, how many hops is it going to take ... that's layer one of the checker. And then layer two of the checker would be the pieces ... the only way it wasn't here is either you capture it or it moves"; "I think of reasoning as a starting point and a chain of claims ... a graph structure ... every question inspires the next question"; "there's always going to be counterfactuals"; "there might be other obstacles, not just these three"; "maybe my knight is pinned, or maybe my knight is protecting something else"; "what's going to change if this piece goes on to join the attack? ... what obstacles is it going to face along its way? And what is my opponent going to do likely ... I'm going to spend as many milliseconds on this question as I estimate the worth of the stake ... every question should carry some sort of a bound or a probability distribution for a stake ... the worst case ... or the expected value should guide the decision, or our tolerance for risk")

WHAT THE CODE DID BEFORE THIS (78.41, read in the source): level 1 read reach from tables of the board as it stands (a blocker fixed, the other side never moving) and kept only the count of moves, the unit and the arrival place; the frame then played the FIRST move of a two-move way to an in-between place taken first in sorted order, found no new striker, and CLOSED the question as refuted; nothing was carried to the next position.

DESIGN
  LAYER ONE, THE MEDIUM  hops of a kind from place to place on the empty medium, from the movement rule alone (a concept file, the injected game layer; a table made once a game). A unit farther than the attack allows is closed with the count said.
  LAYER TWO, THE UNITS   for each geometric route, what stands against it as the board is. Not a list of shapes: AN OBSTACLE IS ANYTHING WHOSE ABSENCE WOULD LET THE STEP HAPPEN OR SUCCEED, found by asking the kernel the same question on the board without one unit, each unit in turn; and for a step that is legal but answered, the unit that made the answer, tested the same way; and time (the other side's faster way on as much). A finding read on a board without a unit is marked so.
  THE COST OF LEAVING    before a unit's route is read: what of its own side is newly lost once it has left its place (the cheap verdicts rerun after its first step). The route's worth is what it wins less the most it drops.
  THE ORDER PER UNIT     what changes if it leaves; what stands in its way; what the other side is likely to do. The third opens its own questions and is where the clock must be rationed.
  THE GRAPH              nodes are questions and claims with a verdict (confirmed, refuted, WAITING, not read); edges typed: needs, blocked_by, if_removed, holds, stopped_by, waits_on, breaks. A chain prints as "because ... ; if ... were gone then ...".
  WAITING ACROSS MOVES   October's waiting frame (what it waits on, what breaks it) kept from position to position with its read set; re-read only when a move touches the set.
  STAKES AS BOUNDS       every node holds a low and a high stake, tightened as answers come; and a CHANCE.
  THE CLOCK (next stage) the chance of a node from the measured base rates of its verdict kind in our own games (78.41 already printed them: lost where it stands 11 of 13 for theirs and 7 of 22 for mine; confirmed after an arrival 14 of 71 and 7 of 79; closed by reach 0 of 161), refit at sleep, no outside judge needed; a question's next step gets time in proportion to chance times stake over the cost of the step; for my own units the worst case (the high bound) leads, for theirs the expected value, the weight between the two a named parameter (the tolerance for risk). What the other side is likely to do is read from the same sheet from their side: their confirmed and waiting ways, by expected stake, are their likely moves, and those order the answers tried against my routes.
  REUSE                  October's frame search is in use; its fact store (read sets, stale flags) and waiting frames are to be used as they are where they fit, the game-bound parts behind the codec.
BEING BUILT (one builder, amendments in the order above): routes and whole-route following, the three verdicts, the pool, layers one and two, the removal test, the cost of leaving, the graph, bounds on nodes. Measures H (two-move ways, by verdict and by kind of route) and I (how many plies before a taking the unit was first under watch).

READ. The verdicts on my units did not move; one of theirs went from refuted to waiting. Moving aside explains few of the rejected removals: the steps with "no single unit" are mostly steps with two or more units in the way, which layer one already lists one by one as standing on a place passed over (see the printed chains: the corner unit's step along its own back row names three units and then says none). So the word "none" is wrong there: it is "several, each of which must go", and the follow-up should be asked of each in turn, cheapest first. The time per position fell, not to the earlier form's level. What remains is one thing: the goal sign after a leaving builds a whole reading of the child position. The narrow reading misses a small share of duties, all of the kind "goal unit newly under the sign", reported in the audit line.

STILL WRONG: (a2) the goal sign after a leaving needs to be computed from the changed places, not a whole reading; (c2) a step blocked by several units is called "none" and its follow-ups are not asked; (b), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h), (i) of the list above stand.

(c2): where no single removal frees a step and layer one names two or more units on it, the set is removed together (Params.joint, max_joint 3) and each member gets its follow-up, cheapest first, stopped at the first dead one. The chance: question_key (whose unit, verdict kind, moves the way needs, route group) with coarser prefixes as fallback; fit_chances counts, per key, whether the exact unit was taken within 4 and 8 plies in our own games (moves only; the judge's files are not opened, a test holds this); Chances smooths toward the next coarser key; Params.chances loads it and every question and node gets a chance. The clock: Params.clock present / chance / plain, Params.risk the dial (own units: risk times the upper bound plus the rest times the midpoint; the other side's: the midpoint), run with budget_seconds, budget_cost or max_steps. READ. (1) Several units together account for most of the former "none" steps; most such sets hold a member that cannot go, so the route stays refuted, now with the unit named. (2) The chance separates: "lost where it stands" and "live at level 0" are high, "waiting" sits at the base rate, "closed by no gain" is far under it; on unseen games the bands hold. (3) The clock by chance times stake is NOT better than the present order. With the dial at the worst case it spends its first steps on the asker's own units and reaches the other side's late; with the dial at the expected value most of that comes back, not all. The plain order, each question to its end in turn, is the worst under any small budget. Without a budget all three end alike, as they must. (4) The ceiling is the trouble, not the order: without a budget the sheet had raised danger on about one in five of my units that were then taken and about two in five of theirs; of the danger verdicts raised, about one in six of mine and two in five of theirs were followed by a taking. (5) Budgets under the cost of reading a position mean nothing: the reading and the goal unit's first step cost more than the budget.

STILL WRONG: the takings no danger verdict foresaw have not been looked at one by one (which kind they are decides what comes next); the reading of a position is the floor of the cost; the chance of a way node borrows the question's table; the other side's answers are not yet ranked by the same sheet from their side; (a2), (b), (d), (e), (g), (h), (i) stand.

NEXT: read the missed takings by kind (was the unit never flagged, flagged and refuted, or waiting) before more machinery; then the sheet on October's event kernel.

READ. Two things, and both are about the measure before they are about the reasoner. (1) "Taken" is not "lost". Of the other side's missed units most went in an exchange that was taken back at once: the sheet had read that exchange and called it worth nothing, and the game played it anyway; that verdict was right. Of my missed units most had MOVED before they were taken, many of them by taking something themselves, which the count calls a plain loss. (2) A question is asked about the place a unit stands on. A unit that walks to another place and is taken there is outside every question asked so far. That is the question of the move, not of the unit: "if this unit goes there, is it lost there", which the cornering frame already answers for one unit and nothing asks for the move about to be played.

NEXT, replacing the NEXT above: (i) measure J with LOSS in place of taking: the balance of worth over the exchange on that place, by the mined worths, so that an even exchange is not a miss and a unit that took more than it cost is not a loss; (ii) the question of the move: for the move about to be played (and the best few), the frame on the place it lands on and on what it leaves, which is the cost of leaving read for my own move; (iii) then the event kernel.


78.42 FOURTH FORM: LOSS IN PLACE OF TAKING; THE QUESTION OF THE MOVE (2026-11-13; question_sheet.py, the codec's `events`; tests 116). unit_loss: a unit is LOST when it is taken and the balance of worth over the run of takings on that place, its own arriving capture counted, is against its side; EVEN and GAINED otherwise. Measure J gained columns by LOSS; fit_chances takes outcome=loss (flag only, the table was not refitted). move_question(env, reading, move, params): (a) what the move leaves (cost_of_leaving, narrow), (b) where it lands (the exchange frame on the position after the move, what it took counted), (c) what the other side then has (units on changed places, the goal sign); verdict SAFE / LOSES / NOT SETTLED, explain_move, move_sheet over the legal moves under a budget; Params.move_question, off by default. READ. (1) With LOSS as the outcome the sheet foresees three in four of the other side's real losses; of my own, under one in three. The asymmetry is the finding: against their units the mover acts next, so what stands is what happens; against mine, the other side moves first and I move again before most losses land. (2) The question of the move is nearly always right when it says LOSES of the move played, and it says so rarely, because the search that played these games already avoids such moves. It calls about one legal move in five LOSES, and the move played is almost never one of them: as a screen it agrees with the search, it adds little to it on these games. (3) Of the 52 units that moved and were then taken, most were no loss at all by the balance; a few remain, and in the examples the loss came from a LATER own move or after the other side's next move, not from the move asked about. (4) Losses of my units within four plies are charged to the move played now, though a second own move lies in between: the measure must charge a loss to the last own move before it. (5) The cost of a move question is the reading of the position after the move; the frames cost nearly nothing.

STILL WRONG: K charges later moves' losses to this move; part (c) never fires because (a) reads the same units; units of the least worth are not asked about; the chance table is still fitted on taking; the reading of a position is the cost of everything (the kernel's facts call and the rows built from it).

NEXT: (i) K with each loss charged to the last own move before it; (ii) the mover's own losses need the other side's next move: the sheet asked from their side for their best open question, which is also "what is the opponent likely to do"; (iii) a cheaper reading of a child position (from the changed places, not anew); (iv) the event kernel.

Classes: A the unit already stood lost before the charged move (the sheet said so) and a move that kept it existed; B the charged move took the unit itself to where it was lost; C the charged move took away a guard or a shield; D neither: the other side's next move took another unit at once and this one went in the same exchange.

READ. At the move a loss is charged to, the sheet or the question of the move had SEEN the loss in most cases (A, B and C against D), and a move that the question of the move calls SAFE and that keeps the unit existed in nearly all. The games played the losing move anyway: they were played by the plain search, which never asked. So for losses of this kind the reasoner's sight is no longer the limit; what it sees is not yet USED. The unseen class D is small and mostly a second unit going in an exchange on a place the sheet had already marked. The count is small (one set of games), and this says nothing yet on what the SAFE moves cost elsewhere: the question of the move calls about one legal move in five LOSES, and a standing "lost" on my units is followed by a loss less than one time in three.

NEXT: USE. A player that takes the search's move, asks the sheet on standing losses and the question of the move on that move, and where the answer is LOSES or a standing loss is left without a keeper, asks the search's next choices in order until one is SAFE; played against the plain search at the same clock, measured by weighty units lost a game (unit_loss), by the result, and by 78.37's surprise rate. The reading of a position is the cost to cut for this.

    OBS (control) judge on overridden moves 0 (tolerance 0.02 expected result): override better 0, equal 0, worse 0; mean expected result played minus search's choice +nan, mean centipawns +nan

READ. (1) The guided player loses fewer weighty units than the plain search across the board from it, and the question of the move alone does most of that; the standing check alone does harm. (2) The result and the judge's mean loss barely move, and the judge calls the overrides about as often worse as better. (3) The guided player spends about four times the clock. The plain search GIVEN that same time beats the plain search by far more than the guided player does, on the result, on the balance of worth and on the judge's mean loss. So, as wired, the sheet is worth less than the time it costs: the same milliseconds are better spent searching. (4) The cost is the reading of positions in Python (the position, then the position after the move), not the frames. (5) Known wrong: a promotion is called a loss of the promoting unit; the next choices are not the search's own; games at the ply cap are left out of the scores.

NEXT: the sheet is not to stand beside the search as a veto in Python; what it knows has to cost near nothing and go INTO the search: (i) the reading of a child from the changed places and the sheet's cheap levels in Rust beside the kernel's facts, so that a move question costs what a frame costs; (ii) the verdicts as the search's ordering and as its quiet-move extension (a move the sheet calls LOSES searched last, a standing loss a reason to look one move deeper there), measured at EQUAL time against the plain search; (iii) fix promotion in unit_loss and the question of the move. The event kernel after that.

READ. (1) The cost is gone: the question of the move went from the cost of a whole search move to a small part of one, with the same verdicts except where the full form said NOT SETTLED for the goal sign. (2) At equal time the guided player does NOT beat the plain search: every guided score is under the control's, the judge calls the overrides worse about three times as often as better, and the guided player's lost units are a little under the control's, not clearly outside noise. (3) So the finding of the first form stands with the cost removed: replacing the search's move, on the word of a one-move reading of losses, by a move the search rated lower, does not help. What the sheet sees at one move the search at this clock mostly sees too, and where they differ the search is more often right.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE PLAN. The reasoner is not to second-guess the search on what the search can already see. Its use is where the search does not reach: the order in which things are looked at when the clock is short, and the things more than a few plies away (a way of two or three preparing moves, a waiting record that comes true). Both are 78.42's own subject (routes followed whole, waiting, the clock), and both were too slow to try in play before the light reading.

NEXT: (i) the whole sheet on the light reading (levels 0 to 2, the routes), with the audit against the full form, so that a position's sheet costs milliseconds; (ii) then the routes and the waiting records measured for what the search at its clock does NOT see: of the ways the sheet confirms at two or three moves, how many the search's own line at that clock contains or avoids; (iii) the sheet kept across the moves of a game on October's event kernel (what a move changes is re-asked, the rest served), which the light reading and the changed places make cheap; (iv) the goal sign in the light reading.

READ. (1) The light sheet gives the same verdict kinds as the full one on every question read, and the question of the move now agrees wholly since the goal sign is read. (2) A whole sheet is several times cheaper, not yet milliseconds: what remains is level 1's geometry in Python and the kernel's reason and census on the goal questions. (3) THE FINDING. Where no unit stands lost already, the ways of two or more moves the sheet confirms are few a game, the search at its clock already plays, answers or values most of them, and those it does not see come true about as often as not at all: the cell "the sheet confirms, the search does not see, the unit is lost" holds a handful of targets in all 16 games. The waiting records are many, the search sees almost none by these flags, and they come true at the base rate whether or not their condition came true. (4) In positions with the mover in check the sheet confirms many ways read from the board as it stands; they come true at the base rate: an artifact, in the full sheet too.

So on these games, at these clocks, the route reasoning does not see what the search misses often enough to count. The games are the search's own, which stops the comparison from being independent: a search that never walks into a prepared attack leaves none in its games to be found. The sheet's value against a stronger or a different opponent is unmeasured.

OPEN, for Kaveh: where the reasoner is to earn its place. The measured facts: it explains (chains with because and if-gone), it is right about standing losses, it agrees with the search at one move and adds nothing over it there, and its multi-move ways are rare and mostly seen by the search. Candidates not yet tried: the puzzle sets October was measured on (a prepared attack exists by construction, so the cell is not empty); games against a stronger opponent; the reasoner as the source of the search's ORDER inside the search rather than beside it.

STILL OWED: the sheet kept across the moves of a game on October's event kernel; a position in check read by the answers to the check, not as it stands.

READ. (1) CORRECT NOW. The first form served wrong verdicts because its read sets missed the units that bear on the route and the asker's context; with them, no served verdict differed from a fresh sheet on these games, nothing stale is served, waiting records wake on their condition and die by their break, and the store holds about a hundred live facts a game. (2) NO TIME SAVED. The kept sheet costs what a fresh one costs. Few verdicts survive a move untouched, and refuted ways are woken constantly; what a position costs is the reading of obstacles and reach, which is not what the memory holds. A recheck can almost never be settled cheaply. A cache of single frames would cost more in bookkeeping than it saves. (3) ONE AGENDA BY STAKE. At the two shortest budgets it holds a little more of the danger verdicts by stake than a fresh sheet, and fewer of them by count; from the middle budgets up it holds less, and its own bookkeeping runs over the budget. Kaveh's claim is not borne out as built: mostly refuted, by one run on a few games. (4) A waiting record woken by its condition is followed by a loss about three times as often as the base rate: the one new signal here; it has no cell in the fitted table yet. (5) October's Rust agenda is already game-free and could carry only the small Agenda class; the listeners, read sets and rechecks would stay where they are; the agenda is not where the time goes.

WHY THE MEMORY DOES NOT PAY, as far as these numbers show: the unit of memory is the verdict of a whole way, and a way reads many places, so most moves touch it. What would survive a move is smaller: the reach of one unit, the obstacle on one step, one exchange on one place. Those are what the time goes on, and they are not what is filed.

NEXT, not started: file the PARTS (a unit's reach, a step's obstacle, a place's exchange) with their own small read sets, so that a move wakes only the parts it touches and a way is re-put-together from parts still good; the agenda's bookkeeping inside the budget; the woken-waiting kind fitted into the chance table.

### 78.42: the event memory on by default (2026-11-14)

Kaveh's rule: cache when caching is not slower. The measure of the last section showed the same time kept as fresh and no wrong serve, so `run` and `read_position` now drain the pool's agenda by
default whenever a pool is carried (`refresh` defaults to `math.inf`; `refresh=None` is the old form, where a question asks for what a move touched). With no pool nothing changes, so the
match player, which carries none, plays as before. The one test of the old form is pinned to `refresh=None`. The four test files of the sheet: 212 passed.


### The high-level spec (2026-11-14)

Kaveh restated the target system: one graph of units, frames, facts and claims; tactical reasoning; frames from the bottom up; a policy toward tactical opportunity that talks in subgoals; sleep as an agent with tools whose step goal is to explain a surprise; Rust in the hot paths. It is written in docs/SYSTEM_SPEC.md. Every plan from here names the piece of that spec it serves.


## 78.43 THE QUESTION SHEET IN THE RUST ENGINE (Kaveh 2026-11-14: "go autonomous, while staying on path to the high level spec"; Rust first in the hot paths)

Serves docs/SYSTEM_SPEC.md sections 3 (tactical reasoning), 2 (the claims the graph waits for) and 8 (Rust in the hot paths).

WHY. A profile of the light sheet on 18 positions of the saved games (one run, directional): `OBS positions 18 seconds under profile 9.1`,
35957184 function calls. No single primitive holds the time: the route geometry (`geometric_routes`), the counterfactual obstacles, the board
edits of the codec and the interpreter's own calls share it; the one Rust call in it (`cs_engine.reason`) is about a ninth. So the speed is
not won by moving one function down; the sheet's core has to live in the engine, with the Python sheet kept as the readable mirror and as the
ORACLE the Rust form is checked against (the 72.7 precedent of Python twins).

WHAT, in stages, one commit each. No Cargo.toml is changed and no new crate is made: new modules go inside the existing layer crates (the
tactics crate), exposed through rust/engine/py/src/lib.rs. Never touched: rust/engine/gdl/src/lib.rs, rust/engine/game/src/gdl_game.rs,
rust/engine/Cargo.lock, any Cargo.toml. The layer modules name no object of any game (the source test of tests/test_plan78.py applies).

 A. THE READING AND THE ROUTES. The light reading in Rust (units with their places and worths, the strike and move tables, the distances
    between places, what bears on what as the board stands) and levels 0 and 1 by geometry (`level0`, `geometric_routes`, `_level1_geometry`
    and what they call). Whatever the Python codec supplies as the one game-specific place is supplied to the Rust form through one small
    trait or one data table, never by naming a game in the layer. ACCEPTANCE: on every position of the saved games where the Python light sheet
    reads, the Rust reading gives the same units, the same level 0 verdict per target and the same set of level 1 routes per target; every
    difference is listed with its position and cause. One timing line for each side.
 B. THE OBSTACLES AND THE FRAMES. Counterfactual removal (one unit, a goal unit moved aside, several jointly), the exchange and cornering frames
    (a Rust frame search equal to `frame_search.FrameSearch` on the frames the sheet builds), `settle_way`, the cost of leaving, the verdict of
    a way. ACCEPTANCE: the same verdict kind for every way of every target on the same positions.
 C. THE WHOLE SHEET AND THE MOVE QUESTION. The schedule (`run` with its clocks and budgets), `finish_levels`, `settle_flagged`, `unit_loss`,
    `move_question`. ACCEPTANCE: the same sheet (targets, verdict kinds, stakes) and the same move answers; the time per position printed.
 D. THE MEMORY. Read sets, listeners, waking and the drain in Rust, checked by the audit of 78.42 (served against fresh).

Then the uses that waited on speed: the opportunity number logged along every self-play game (SYSTEM_SPEC section 5), and the claims filed
as nodes of the engine's graph (section 2).

## 78.44 THE OPPORTUNITY NUMBER ALONG A GAME: is it a target worth steering by? (SYSTEM_SPEC section 5)

The policy of section 5 is to be trained toward "abundance of high-value tactical opportunity". Before any policy, the number itself is tested.
 - THE NUMBER. At a position, for the side to move: the sum over the other side's units of chance x worth for the open claims against them,
   minus the same sum for the claims against its own units. The chance is the fitted table's (data/derived/question_chances/fit1112.json, fitted
   on earlier games, so every game here is unseen by it); the claims are the Rust sheet's (`SheetModel.game`, clock present).
 - THE QUESTION. Does the number at a ply foretell the change of material over the next plies, beyond what the simplest count foretells?
   Outcome: the mover's balance of worth at 4, 8 and 16 plies ahead minus now. Baselines printed beside it: the same sum from the first level
   only (what can be taken at once), a count of claims with no chances, and the number with the positions shuffled within a game.
 - THE READING. A table by bands of the number (mean later change, count), and the rank correlation, for each horizon; by phase of the game;
   for the parts mine / theirs separately. On about 500 new self-play games of the control player. Nothing is fitted in this plan.
 - NEXT, only if the number foretells: log it for every legal move's child (which moves raise it), and fit the sparse subgoal statements.

DEFINITION AS BUILT. An open claim against a unit: the top verdict of its question is live0, live1, lost, confirmed, waiting or unsettled (closed1..3, refuted, idle0, idle1, unread are not open). Baselines: net0 = the same sum over the units level 0 read as live (chance of the table's cell (owner, live0)); count = open claims against theirs minus against mine; shuffled = net permuted among the plies of a game (seed fixed). READ (directional, one run on 500 games of one player). The number rises with the later change of material at all three horizons, and the shuffled control is near zero, so the rise is not an artefact of the ranking. It stands well above the plain count of claims (count: about 0.1). It does NOT stand much above the first-level baseline: net0 is within about 0.01 to 0.02 of net at each horizon, and the intervals of the two nearly overlap at 4 plies. Beyond the first level the reading is small: net - net0 has a correlation of about 0.2 and the partial rank correlation of net with net0 held out is about 0.19 / 0.18 / 0.15 at 4 / 8 / 16 plies; among the plies where net0 is zero (about 62 percent of them) net foretells almost nothing (about 0.05). The bands are not monotone: the mean outcome is about the same over the four lower bands and the whole rise is in the top band. net_d (danger kinds only) correlates better than net at every horizon, which says the waiting and level-1 claims add noise to the number as built. Gain predicts worth won and risk predicts worth lost, each about 0.3 to 0.4 at 4 plies; the correlation falls with the horizon. Caveats: the outcome is the material of the games of one player (a plain search at 0.2 s a move), including captures the first move of the horizon makes; a high net0 is probably often a capture on the board that the mover then makes (not separated here). Nothing here says the number steers a game.

construction; games against a weaker answerer are the other half and come after.

## 78.45 THE SHEET ON PUZZLES: does the route reasoning see a prepared attack that is there? (SYSTEM_SPEC section 3)

A puzzle is a position where a winning line of a few moves exists by construction. Sets: data/derived/ledger_puzzles_dev_300.json (to study
the misses) and ledger_puzzles_fresh_300.json (held out, read once at the end). Fields used: the position, the answer (first move), the
solution line, the themes, the rating. Measure only: nothing of the puzzles reaches the wake or any fit.
 - SEES: the sheet holds a claim for the side to move, in danger (lost or confirmed) against a unit of the other side or against their goal
   unit, whose way begins with the answer. PICKS: a plain chooser (the first move of the top such claim by stake) names the answer.
 - BASELINE beside it: the engine's plain search on the same position at the time the sheet took, and at 0.2 s.
 - THE MISSES, each put in one class by cause, by theme and by length of the solution: the target not on the sheet; the way not among the
   routes; the way read and refuted (with the stop that refuted it); not settled or not reached under the budget (the same sheet with a
   budget five times larger tells these apart); seen but outranked.
 - The four-way table: sheet sees / search finds.
The classes of misses are the work list for the reasoner; nothing is fixed in this plan.

## 78.46 THE FORCING READ: a move, the claims it makes, every reply, the claims that stand (SYSTEM_SPEC section 3; Rust first, section 8)

Kaveh's design of 78.41 already names it: per move, what changes, and the opponent's reply; a double threat is a move whose claims no one
reply answers. October measured the same idea as lambda frames (catspace/incubator/analyst/lambda_frames.py); the literature calls it a
threat-space search. It is built in the Rust sheet first; the Python mirror is owed afterwards.
 - A THREAT MOVE of the side to move: a legal move after which, the board read as if that side moved again, a unit of the other side or
   their goal stands in danger that did not before, or a move that itself takes a unit.
 - THE READ. After a threat move EVERY legal reply is read (soundness: no reply is left out). For each reply: what the reply took, the claims
   of the move that still stand and what carrying out the best of them wins by the exchange on its place, and, where none stands, the mover's
   next threat moves, one level deeper, while the budget lasts. The goal is read by the engine's own forced-win clause (`force`). The value
   of the move is the least over the replies. A cut is NOT SETTLED, never a refutation and never a confirmation.
 - THE ANSWER, as claims: the move, the claims it makes, and for every reply which claim stands (the explanation of why the reply fails), the
   units won, the nodes read.
 - ACCEPTANCE. (1) Puzzles (78.45's measure, a second column): SEES and PICKS with the forcing read beside the sheet alone and the plain
   search, on dev_300 while building and fresh_300 once at the end; the misses left, by class. (2) SOUNDNESS, on ordinary positions of the
   held games: every claim the forcing read confirms is checked against the engine's ledger search at a depth that covers the line; the
   share it contradicts is printed, and each contradiction is read. A confirmation the search contradicts is a bug or a named limit, never
   a tolerated rate. (3) The sheet's existing answers do not change: the 78.43 measures still print zero differences.

Rust: rust/engine/tactics/src/sheet/forcing.rs (`Forcing::read`, `ledger_check`), `cs_engine.SheetModel.forcing` / `forcing_check`, wrappers `sheet_rust.forcing` / `forcing_check`; measures forcing_soundness_measure.py and the second column of puzzle_sheet_measure.py; tests/test_plan78_46_forcing_read.py. `sheet`, `move_question`, `game` are not changed. THE PYTHON MIRROR OF THIS READ IS OWED (SYSTEM_SPEC section 8); until it is written the read has no oracle, only the ledger search as the judge of its claims.
AS BUILT. A THREAT MOVE of the side to move: a legal move that takes a unit, or ends the game in its favour, or after which -- `Game::pass` on the child -- a unit of the other side stands lost to the sheet's exchange frame (the real frame, from the position) where it did not stand before the move, or the goal is forced in one (`wins_in`, n = 1); where the game gives no pass for the child (the other side is under the goal's sign) the move is a threat by that alone and what stands is read on the replies. Ordered for the budget by what it takes plus its claims (a priority, never a verdict). EVERY legal reply is read. A reply line's value for the mover = what the move took - what the reply took + the best of: a claim that stands after the reply (the exchange frame from the position after the reply, credited only as far as it exceeds what stood on that place before the move, less what the other side then keeps after the claim is carried out), the goal forced in one (the goal, `BIG`, is above every worth), or holding (less what the other side keeps if we passed). Where that is not above zero the mover's own threat moves after the reply are read one level deeper, the same read. The value of the move is the least over the replies. WHAT THE OTHER SIDE KEEPS (`their_gain`): its best single exchange or its goal in one, and its moves that put our goal under the sign followed by the best of what it then takes; with us to move, read on the position after our pass. CONFIRMED: every reply above zero. NO CLAIM: some reply closes at or below zero with nothing further of ours to read (its reply is kept in the answer). NOT SETTLED: the budget stopped it with no reply closing it. UNREAD: the fuse stopped before it was read. A cut at one of OUR options (a deeper threat move not read) only leaves a lower bound lower and matters only to a line not already above zero; a cut at a reply is a cut of the whole move; a cut is never a confirmation and never a refutation. THE FUSE: `FUSE_POSITIONS` = 20000 positions read (one `wins_in` call has 4000 nodes of its own, one frame 20000); the deepening is by levels (0, 1, 2, ...) over the moves not yet settled, so no depth is a tuned count; the fuse stopped the read in about four positions of five (it is large because NOT SETTLED lines go on until it is spent). THE ANSWER as plain data per threat move: move, verdict, value, took, claims (target, kind: takes | exchange | goal | sign | ends, value, line), per reply: reply, took, the claim that stands or the deeper move, line, value, open, whether the reply ends the game; nodes, fuse, cut, level.
CHOICES MADE WHILE BUILDING, each from a measured contradiction (held_games, 2 games, then 32): (1) the first build counted what the line wins and left the other side no move after it: 33 of 99 confirmed claims contradicted in 2 games (one run, directional); the other side's move after a claim is carried out or after a line that only holds is now read (`their_gain`), and 2 of 23 then contradicted. (2) A parry read as the least over OUR moves of what the other side then keeps was built and measured (13 of 844 on held_games) and taken out again: it confirms more and is less sound; the pass-based hold stays. A threat move whose line was not confirmed is never made confirmed by a looser reading.

READ OF THE CONTRADICTIONS. By hand: game 1 ply 50 (the read takes a bishop with a rook; the other side then takes a second rook with a knight: two of our units hang and one move saves one), game 1 ply 58 (the exchange on a place is read as one run of takings; the other side plays a taking WITH CHECK in between before the recapture: the exchange frame's known blindness), game 26 ply 25 (the escaping unit goes with a check and the taking that follows leaves a second claim of the other side). The others show in their search lines the same kind of thing and were not each taken apart: a second step of the OTHER side after a taking or after a quiet reply (a fork, a promotion run in game 10 of held3, a skewer). THE NAMED LIMIT: the other side's gain is read as one exchange, its goal in one, or one check followed by a taking; a gain of theirs that needs a step of their own after that (a taking that strikes a second unit, a move in between before a recapture, a quiet fork, a promotion) is not seen, and the exchange frame reads takings on one place only. These are limits of the reading, not a rate to accept: a read of the other side's threats as deep as ours (their forcing read, with ours below it) would close them and costs a second read inside the first.
READ. Directional, one run each. On both puzzle sets the forcing read added about a quarter to a third of the puzzles to what the sheet sees (SEES 38 to 66 on dev, 39 to 69 on fresh, in percent) and the chooser that takes the highest confirmed value names the answer in about two puzzles of three; the plain search at the same seconds still names it in more than eight of ten. The forcing read costs about one second a puzzle, ten times the sheet. Of the misses left, the large class is F: the answer is read as a threat move and the budget stopped it before every reply was settled (NOT SETTLED), mostly with the first reply of the plain search's own line as the reply that was left open; the old classes R and X nearly vanish (the forcing read reads the quiet and the double-claim answers the ways could not list). Soundness: about one confirmed claim in a hundred is contradicted by the search, each by a gain of the other side that needs a step of its own. Nothing is said here about use in play.

## 78.47 THE FORCING READ, SPENT WHERE IT MATTERS: replies by what they touch, and the search as the last word (SYSTEM_SPEC sections 2 and 3)

Serves: tactical reasoning (section 3), using the dependency idea of section 2: a change wakes only the claims that
read it. Rust first. No game object named.

A. WHERE THE POSITIONS GO (measure first, short). For the read as built, count the positions spent per kind of work
   (standing claims of a child, the other side's gain, the goal read, deeper threat moves) and per reply kind, on
   dev_300. Print as OBS. The rest of the plan is ordered by what this shows; if the cost sits elsewhere than assumed
   below, say so and follow the cost.

B. REPLIES BY WHAT THEY TOUCH. A claim made by a threat move has a read set: the places and units its exchange frame or
   goal read looked at (the Reading already records what a frame read; plan 78.42). A reply is RELEVANT to the claim if
   it moves a unit of the read set, ends on or passes over a place of it, takes something, or is itself a threat move
   of the other side (its own gain or sign). A reply that is none of these leaves the claim exactly as the read after
   our move found it, so it is answered by carrying the claim out, from the stored result, with no new frame read.
   This must change NO verdict where the fuse does not bind: acceptance is zero differences in verdict and value
   against the read as built, on positions where neither read is cut (run both with a large fuse on a few hundred
   positions). Any difference is a hole in the read set and is fixed there, not waved through.

C. A MEMORY OVER POSITIONS inside one read: the same position reached by two orders of moves is read once.

D. ORDER. Among the unsettled threat moves, deepen first the one with the fewest holding replies, and inside it the
   holding reply first. This is the proof-number idea in its plainest form; no tuned number.

E. THE SEARCH AS THE LAST WORD. A verdict CONFIRMED is given only after the ledger search, from the position after the
   move, to the depth that covers the read's longest line, does not contradict it. A claim the search contradicts is
   printed as NOT BORNE OUT with both lines, and counted. The soundness measure is then run with a DEEPER check than
   the verdict's own (two plies more), so the measure is not the verdict checking itself.

Acceptance:
1. B alone: zero verdict differences against the read as built where neither is cut.
2. dev_300: SEES2 / PICKS2 and class F at the same fuse, before and after; fresh_300 once at the end.
3. Soundness on held_games, with the deeper check; every contradiction printed.
4. The 78.43 measures still at zero differences; the 78.46 tests pass.

Not in this plan: the read as a level of the sheet's schedule, the Python mirror, use in play. They follow once the
read settles more of what it starts.

B. REPLIES BY WHAT THEY TOUCH. Built as the plan states it, from the game's own data: a reply is answered from the stored result of an earlier reply of the same move when it takes nothing, ends no game, is one plain move of one unit that no exchange or goal read involves, changes no other unit's lines (no line opened or blocked, no guard lost or gained), neither leaves nor lands on a place of ours, bears (and could, after one more move of its own, bear) on no hot place (the places of our units and of the units the read is about, the places any move of ours ends on where we move again, the places the goal units may step to). Only where the stored reply was read no deeper than the claims that stand (the reading of our next threat moves belongs to that position alone). `forcing(..., shortcut=False)` keeps the old path (every reply read in full); forcing_shortcut_measure.py reads every position both ways at one large fuse and compares verdict, value and every reply, where neither read is cut.
HOLES FOUND by the first comparison (held_games every third position, fuse 100000, 220 compared positions; 4 threat moves in 3 positions differed) and how each was closed: (1) a unit that guarded a place one of our moves lands on (the goal read, mate in one: the guard of the landing place was gone) -- the places our moves end on are now hot, and the place a unit leaves counts as well as the place it lands on; (2) a unit whose NEXT move would be a threat of its own (a check, or a taking after one more step) -- the places a unit could bear on after one more move are now tested; The set of units the read is about (`involved`) was tried first as the full contact closure (every unit that bears on a place of one of them, again and again: the first run answered about 1 pct of the replies from a stored result), then as the exchange's own sources (the units that bear on a target's place, the units of the same side behind them, the units that could pin one: about 5 pct on the first sample, 0.0 pct on the last). C. A MEMORY over the positions of one read: `their_gain` (what the other side keeps at a position) is read once per position however many orders reach it; the position memory of the stands, the threat moves and the move reads was there already. Hits are in the cost lines ('the other side's gain, answered from the memory of positions').
D. ORDER. Per level of deepening the threat moves go by their number of holding replies, fewest first (equal numbers keep the order of the priorities); inside a move the reply that held at the level before is read first, then the one that closed it, then by what the reply takes. Two exact steps on the other side's sign moves: our replies to one are tried in the order of what they take (the one that leaves them least ends the loop soonest), and a sign move is read only as far as it can raise what a direct exchange already gives them (`floor`). The second step was compared with the build before it on 859 positions at fuse 30000: threat answers that differ 0 on the 194 positions uncut in both; positions asked on those 194: 429901 before, 378286 after (a script-printed line of the session, scratchpad s7847/dumpboth).
E. THE SEARCH AS THE LAST WORD. A confirmed move is given as CONFIRMED only if the ledger search from the position after it, to the depth that covers the read's longest line (the reply first, two plies per level, one more; cap 14, fuse 5000000 nodes, both named), does not contradict what the read claims from there; otherwise the verdict is NOT BORNE OUT, the answer keeps both lines. A cut search or a depth over the cap is no check (the claim stays CONFIRMED, marked unchecked in `search`).

## 78.48 THE OPPORTUNITY NUMBER WITH THE FORCING READ: do its claims foretell what is won, beyond the next move (SYSTEM_SPEC sections 3, 5, 10)

Serves: the opportunity policy (section 5) and the chances as currency (section 3). Plan 78.44 found the sheet's number
is mostly its first level. The forcing read now holds the prepared attacks the sheet missed. This plan asks whether its
verdicts, with fitted chances, foretell later material where the first level says nothing. A measurement; nothing is
used in play.

A. THE TERMS, per position of a game, for the side to move and (by the game's pass where it gives one, else from the
   next position) for the other side: the threat moves by verdict (CONFIRMED, NOT BORNE OUT, NOT SETTLED, NO CLAIM), each
   with its value or floor, its level, and the kind of its claim (takes, exchange, goal sign). The fuse is a parameter;
   take the cost per position at two fuses on a short run first and say which the long run uses and why.
B. THE CHANCES. For each (verdict, kind of claim, level) cell: how often the side gained at least the claimed worth
   within 4, 8, 16 plies. Fitted on one half of the games (split by game), with the plain base rate beside it.
C. THE NUMBER. Ours minus theirs of chance times stake, by the fitted table, on the other half of the games.
D. THE TEST, on the held half, with bootstrap bands by game as in 78.44: rank correlation with material won 4, 8, 16
   plies later, for (1) the 78.44 number, (2) the forcing number, (3) both; and the same on the positions where the
   78.44 first level is zero and no threat move is CONFIRMED, which is where a policy would need it. Controls: the
   count alone; the number shuffled within a game.
E. OPPONENT (section 10), only if A to D are done: the same table fitted on games where the answering side is a weaker
   player (the control player at a smaller budget), printed beside the first. The question is only whether the cells
   move with the opponent.

Games: artifacts/experiments/opportunity_78_44/games_s5016_n500 for A to D (a subset if the cost demands; say how many).
No oracle, no human game, no puzzle enters. Rust for the read; the fit and the test in Python beside
opportunity_measure.py, game-free.

A measurement: nothing is wired into play, nothing reads its output.
DEFINITIONS AS BUILT. Per threat move: verdict (CONFIRMED, NOT BORNE OUT, NOT SETTLED, NO CLAIM; a move the fuse left unread is counted NOT SETTLED), level, kind of claim (the first present of ends, goal, exchange, takes, sign), claimed worth (CONFIRMED: its value, the goal at the goal's stake; the others: the best claim it makes). Cell = (verdict, kind, level); the cell's chance is the sheet's `Chances` (counts smoothed by the chance of the coarser key: (verdict, kind, level) -> (verdict, kind) -> (verdict) -> all), so a thin cell falls back by the same smoothing as the 78.41 table, no count limit. 'Gained at least the claimed worth within h plies' = the mover's worth WON (78.44's outcome code, the balance at t+h) is at least the claimed worth and above zero, for the mover's threats; the mover's worth LOST for the other side's. The number at horizon h: FORCING = max over the mover's threat moves of chance x claimed worth, minus the same for the other side (the sum form is printed as a labelled second form; both forms and the choice of the max as primary were fixed before the long run). BOTH = the 78.44 number plus FORCING. Split by game: even game ids fit, odd ids are the test. Where the game gives no pass the other side's terms are empty (counted). The subset: net0 = 0 and the mover has no CONFIRMED threat. FUSE: probe on 10 games at the default 20000 and at a quarter of it (5000); the long run used 5000 on all 500 games because 20000 would have cost about 0.2 s of wall per position (about 150 minutes for 45179 positions) against 0.054 s (the run took 2299 s for the reads); at both fuses most reads were stopped by the fuse (1466 and 1519 of 1912) and the threat moves differ in 1401 of 1912 reads, so the numbers below are of a read that is mostly unsettled (see the verdict counts). Games: the 500 of 78.44 (artifacts/experiments/opportunity_78_44/games_s5016_n500), all of them. Stage E: 200 new games (seeds 5516 to 5715) of the control player in which one colour (alternating by seed pairs) searches 0.02 s a move against the control 0.2 s, cases split by whether the side that ANSWERS the threat is the weaker colour or the control colour, same games, fitted on the even half.

READ (directional, one run on 500 games of one player, the test half 250 games; nothing here is a verdict). (1) The forcing number rises with the later material change much less than the 78.44 number on all test positions (about 0.09 / 0.07 / 0.04 against about 0.35 / 0.32 / 0.27 at 4 / 8 / 16 plies), and adding it to the 78.44 number LOWERS the correlation (both below the 78.44 number alone at every horizon). The shuffled control is near zero. (2) On the positions where the 78.44 first level is zero and no threat move is CONFIRMED (the part a policy would need), the 78.44 number is itself near zero at 4 plies (about 0.01, interval reaching zero) and the forcing number is also small (about 0.02 / 0.02 / 0.03, intervals above zero but only just); the partial rank correlation of the forcing number with the 78.44 number held out is about 0.02 there with the lower end of the interval near zero. At 8 and 16 plies the CONTROL, the plain count of threat moves (mover's less the other side's), is as high or higher than the forcing number (about 0.08 and 0.11 on the subset) and the sum form is higher than the max form (about 0.07 / 0.08 at 8 / 16); so at longer horizons what the forcing number picks up in the subset looks like how many threat moves there are, not the fitted chances. (3) The fitted chances barely separate the cells that matter: almost all threat moves (492282 of 571400) are NOT SETTLED because the fuse stopped the read (68692 of 86967 reads were stopped), the cell NOT SETTLED/exchange/0 alone holds 149863 of the 275656 cases at 4 plies, and CONFIRMED cells are rare (18087 threat moves; 1863 test positions had one). CONFIRMED cells have a chance of about 0.6 of gaining the claimed worth at 4 plies against 0.31 for the exchange cell of a not settled move and 0.33 for the base rate, so the verdict does carry information, but it is on few positions. (4) A flaw of the measure, named: the goal and ends claims are judged by MATERIAL; a goal claim cannot be paid in material, so the cells of kind goal show a rate of zero (NOT SETTLED/goal/0 gained 0 of 3401), and the goal terms contribute nothing to the number; the measure says nothing about goal claims. The claimed worth of a NO CLAIM or NOT SETTLED move is the best claim it makes at the move, not what a reply leaves, so its cell is a weak statement. (5) Stage E: with a weaker answerer (one colour at a tenth of the clock) the base rate of gaining the claimed worth is higher at all three horizons (about 0.31 to 0.37 at 4 plies, 0.52 to 0.61 at 8, 0.76 to 0.84 at 16, same games, cases split by who answers) and most cells with many cases move up in the same direction (the exchange cell of a not settled move from about 0.29 to 0.32, CONFIRMED/exchange/1 from about 0.51 to 0.63 on few control cases); a few cells go the other way and cells with tens of cases move by amounts that are not distinguishable from noise here. So the cells do move with the opponent in direction and in the base rate; how much per cell is not read from one run of 200 games. What would change the reading: a read that settles more of the moves (the fuse stopped 79 percent of the reads at 5000; the probe says the verdicts at 20000 differ in 1401 of 1912 reads, so the number is fuse-bound), games where prepared attacks come true more often than a search against itself allows, and an outcome that can pay a goal claim. Not done: the longer fuse on the long run (cost), the Python mirror of the read (still owed), goal-aware outcome. The shared editable install of cs_engine now points at the worktree agent-a55465c1599922796; the parent rebuilds main after the merge.


### 78.48 READ BY THE PARENT (2026-11-15)

Merged to main (fast-forward), the extension rebuilt, the 78.47 and 78.48 test files pass on main. The stage D and E
numbers above are the builder's run; I did not rerun them. Reading, directional (one run, and at the smaller fuse, where
most reads are cut):
- Two measurements now agree (78.44 and this one): chance times stake over the OPEN claims, credited by material some
  plies later, foretells little beyond the next move in games between two equal searchers. Where the first level is
  silent and nothing is confirmed, the forcing number is near the shuffle, and the plain count of threat moves does as
  well or better at the longer horizons.
- A CONFIRMED claim does carry information (its cells sit well above the base rate), and such claims are few.
- The cells move with the opponent (stage E): against the weaker answerer most large cells and the base rate are higher.
  So section 10's table key is real in direction; its size is not read from this run.
- Consequence for section 5: the policy's target, as a number credited by later material, is not supported yet. A
  nearer target is tried next: does a CONFIRMED claim ARRIVE.

## 78.49 GO TOWARD THE TACTICS: what, read in a quiet position, foretells a confirmed claim arriving (SYSTEM_SPEC section 5)

Serves: the opportunity policy, its first half ("go toward the tactics"). A measurement; nothing is used in play.

A. BUILT BY THE PARENT: catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/forcing_arrival_measure.py, on the reads kept by 78.48
   (fuse 5000, the odd games). A position is quiet when neither side holds a CONFIRMED threat move. Target: a CONFIRMED
   threat move arrives for the mover within h plies, less the same for the other side. Output kept as
   artifacts/experiments/forcing_opportunity_78_48/arrival_obs.txt. Lines (the full file has the rest):

   Reading, directional: the difference of the two sides' counts of threat moves foretells the arrival weakly, clear of
   the shuffle, and about as well at 16 plies as at 4. Weak, but it is the first term seen to carry past the next move.

B. STATEMENTS. A set of game-free statements over the position, counted for each side, from the `Placed` trait and the
   reads only: for example the moves a side has; its units that bear on a unit of the other side; its units borne on by
   its own (guarded); pairs of its units that bear on each other along a line with nothing between; places beside the
   other side's goal unit that it bears on; the free steps of its own goal unit; its units that have not yet moved; the
   reach of its long-range units; its units of least worth by their distance to the far edge; its threat moves by
   verdict. Each statement is one line of text and one number. In Rust, a batch entry over games.
C. THE SPARSE FIT. On the even games: a sparse linear fit (L1, scikit-learn, the penalty chosen by cross-validation over
   games) of the arrival target at 4, 8, 16 plies on the differences of the statements, ours less theirs. On the odd
   games: the rank correlation of the fit with the target with bands by game, beside the count difference of stage A and
   the shuffle; then the same against material won, which is what finally counts. Print each kept statement with its
   weight: these are the candidate subgoals, each with its own evidence.
D. ONE STEP OF CONTROL, only if C is clear of stage A's line: for each quiet test position, does the move the game's
   player chose raise the fitted number more than the average legal move does. This says whether a searcher already
   follows it without knowing.

Acceptance: tests for the statements (each on small hand-made positions of two variants), the fit and the split; the
78.43 measures at zero differences if the sheet's files are touched. No oracle, no human game, no puzzle.

STATUS: stage A done by the parent; B to D given to a builder agent on 2026-11-15.


78.49 BUILT (branch worktree-agent-af54c0b4e6a72a8bb, 2026-11-15; stages B, C and D by the builder agent). A measurement; nothing is wired into play, no subgoal enters any value.
B. rust/engine/tactics/src/sheet/subgoal.rs: 26 game-free statements, each one line of text and one number per side, from the `Placed` trait through the light `Reading` (units, kinds, places, bearing, reach,
   the goal unit of each side, the worth of each kind) and nothing else; batch entries `SheetModel.subgoal_names`, `subgoal_games` and `subgoal_children` in rust/engine/py/src/sheet_py.rs (std threads over games).
   LEFT OUT because the trait does not give them: which units have not yet moved (no history is asked of a game) and a unit's distance to the far edge (a place is a number and a name, no geometry); the
   "long-range" reach has no game-free definition either (the bearing of a unit stands for it: widest_bearing, bearing_total). The forcing terms are the counts of threat moves by verdict from the kept 78.48
   reads (fuse 5000), not rerun. Where a statement counts "the other side's units borne on" it is made once from each side, so ours less theirs of a statement and of its mirror would be the same number; the mirrors are not listed.
C. catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/subgoal_fit_measure.py (stage A's functions `counts_of_game`, `quiet_indices`, `arrival_targets` were cut out of `rows_of_game` so that the fit imports them; its output
   is byte-identical on the kept reads). Fit half: the even game ids; L1 linear (scikit-learn LassoCV), the penalty chosen by 5-fold cross-validation grouped by game on the even games only; the test half: the odd
   games only; bands: 300 draws over games. Two feature sets: P (the statements) and P+F (with the three counts of threat moves by verdict that a quiet position can have). Targets: the arrival target at 4, 8, 16
   plies, and material won less lost (the 78.44 outcome, read at the quiet positions only: not the test of 78.48, which took every position). D: run only at a horizon where the lower end of the P fit's band is
   above the upper end of the count difference's band (arrival target); one step of control, the sign convention in the module docstring (the number of a child is read from the side that moved) and tested with a
   weight on the material statement alone.
Output kept as artifacts/experiments/subgoal_fit_78_49/full/obs.txt (all lines, the kept statements at every horizon for every fit) and result.json; never staged. The OBS lines (the kept statements of the P fit on the

Reading, directional (one run; no verdict): the sparse fit of the statements foretells the arrival target better than the count difference of stage A at 4 plies, clear of it on the band, and at 8 and 16 plies
its band overlaps the count's; with the counts of threat moves by verdict added (P+F) its point value is higher at all three horizons (the bands overlap). Against material won less lost the statement fit reads a good deal higher than the count
difference, which has almost none, but it carries the statements that say a unit is loose or overloaded, which is the next move's material, so this is not evidence that it goes beyond the first level. The fit
keeps most of the 26 statements (the cross-validated penalty is small); the weights of collinear statements (controlled_empty against only_controlled in the material fit) are large with opposite signs and
should not be read one by one. The single-statement correlations on the test half are all small (the largest of the P statements on the arrival target about 0.10). Stage D ran at 4 plies only: the mean of the number after the move the game's
player chose less the mean over the legal moves is a tiny positive number with its band above zero, but the played move is above that mean in fewer positions than not and beats a little under half of the
listed moves, against the control of a random move: mixed and small, no sign that the player follows the number. Not built: the unmoved-units, edge-distance and long-range statements (above); the fit on any set but the 500 games of 78.48; any use of the fitted number in play.


### 78.49 READ BY THE PARENT (2026-11-15)

Merged to main (fast-forward), the extension rebuilt, the 78.48 and 78.49 test files pass on main. I reran the fit with
stage D on main; the lines for the fit P, the fit P+F, the count difference and the shuffles on the arrival target, and
the first material lines, came out the same as in the builder's note above. Reading, directional (one set of games):
- The fit over the statements foretells the arrival of a confirmed claim better than the count of threat moves, clearly
  at 4 plies, with overlapping bands at 8 and 16. It is still a weak signal.
- The weights are not yet a vocabulary of subgoals. Many statements are kept, pairs of near-equal statements take
  opposite signs, and the leading ones (material, the sum of bearings) are the plainest. No single statement stands out.
- The moves the player chose do not follow the number (stage D). So if the number is worth anything, the player is
  leaving it unused, and the only way to learn whether it is worth anything is to play with it.

## 78.50 PLAY WITH IT: the fitted number as the choice among moves the search holds equal (SYSTEM_SPEC sections 5 and 7; AGENTS rule 7)

Serves: the wake's second half ("where no tactic is confirmed, follow the policy"). A measurement by matches; the wake
itself is not changed.

A. HOW THE CONTROL PLAYER CHOOSES AMONG EQUALS. Read the control player of the 78.4x measures and say how it picks when
   several root moves have the best value. Print, on the 500 games, how often that happens and how many moves are tied.
B. THE CANDIDATE. The same search at the same time. Among the root moves whose value EQUALS the best (no margin), it
   plays the one whose child has the highest fitted number (the fit P of 78.49 on the arrival target; weights fitted on
   the even games and kept in a file under artifacts, passed by path; no forcing read at play time). The number enters
   only as this choice among equals: the value is untouched (rule 7).
C. THE MATCHES, same openings played with both colours, a few hundred games each, results with a band by paired
   openings: candidate against control; control against control with a different seed as the noise floor; and a
   candidate that picks among the equals at random, to separate "any change of the pick" from "this number".
D. Printed beside the results: how often the candidate's pick differed from the control's, and the arrival rate of
   confirmed claims for each side in the games (by the forcing read at the 78.48 fuse on a sample), which is what the
   number is meant to move.

No oracle, no human game, no puzzle. The player lives in the measure script, game-free, and is read by no other code.

STATUS: given to a builder agent on 2026-11-15.


78.50 BUILT (branch worktree-agent-a5cde659be768d4f1, 2026-11-15, builder agent; commit e11d4645 and the docs commit after it). A measurement by matches; the wake and every existing player are unchanged; the players live in
catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/subgoal_play_measure.py.
A. The control (the plain search) keeps the FIRST root move of the best value in the search's root order (`v > best` in rust/engine/tactics/src/ledger.rs): no random choice, no other number. Counts: the stage A lines below.
B. Root values: no entry returned them. Added `cs_engine.solve_equals_batch` (rust/engine/py/src/lib.rs, py crate only): the same decision (proof, claims, lemma order, the ledger search, the same `Search`), the ledger deepens within a
   share of the clock (LEDGER_SHARE 0.4, fixed from a 60-position probe before any match) and then each root move is asked "at least the best?" by a null window at the finished depth (`Search::ties`, unchanged), within what is left of
   the same clock. Under the search's pruning only the best root move has an exact value; the null-window question is the sound test of equality; the equal reading is a full pass over the root moves and is cut by the clock in a few
   positions (flagged by `Search::cut`; every player plays the search's own move there). Its time is inside the clock, so the candidate searches shallower than the control (mean ledger depths in the lines below); the match

### 78.50 READ BY THE PARENT (2026-11-15)

Merged to main (fast-forward), the extension rebuilt; tests/test_plan78.py, test_plan78_43_rust_sheet.py,
test_plan78_48_forcing_opportunity.py and test_plan78_50_subgoal_play.py pass on main (158 tests in one call; the one
failure the builder saw was its worktree lacking data). The match lines above are the builder's runs; not rerun by me.
Reading, directional (one run per match):
- Finding the equal moves by a second reading costs the candidate more than half its clock, and a player that pays that
  cost and then plays the search's own move loses clearly to the control. So candidate against control mostly measures
  the shallower search.
- At equal search (candidate against the player that pays the same cost and takes the search's own move) the candidate
  scores above half with its band clear of half, and a random pick among the equals does worse than the search's own
  move. So the choice among equals matters, and this number chooses better than the search's root order does.
- In the candidate's games a confirmed claim arrives for the candidate more often than for the control, and more often
  than in control against control. That is the quantity the number was fitted to move.
- Most positions have many equal root moves. That is where a policy has room, and the plain search fills it by root order.

## 78.51 THE SAME CHOICE AT NO COST: the fitted number as the order of the root moves (SYSTEM_SPEC sections 5, 7, 8)

The search keeps the FIRST root move of the best value. So if the root moves are handed to it in the order of the fitted
number, highest first, its own pick IS the highest-numbered move among the equals, with no second reading.

A. An optional root order for the search's Python entry (a list of root moves, default absent = today's behaviour,
   byte for byte; a test proves the default path is unchanged). Say how the search reorders root moves between its
   deepenings (if it moves the last best move to the front, the pick stays the first-found among equals of the last
   depth; state exactly what the pick then is, and test it against the 78.50 equals entry on positions read whole).
B. The cost: nodes and depth reached at 0.2 s with the number's order against today's order, on the kept games.
   If the number's order costs depth, try the stable variant: today's order, with the number used only to order moves
   inside groups today's order treats alike; state which is used before any match.
C. Matches as in 78.50 (300 opening pairs, both colours, 0.2 s, new seeds from 9000, 8 workers): ordered candidate
   against control; and against the control with a random root order, as the check that order alone is not the effect.
D. The arrival rates as in 78.50 stage D.

The number's weights are the 78.50 file, unchanged. No oracle, no human game, no puzzle. Nothing is switched on in the
wake: the order is passed by the measure script only.

78.51 BUILT (branch worktree-agent-a8fe97cf0e7b5df5f, 2026-11-15, builder agent; stage A in commit e33370e6). Written in stages; the stage B decision below is dated BEFORE any match was played.

A. THE OPTIONAL ROOT ORDER. `cs_engine.solve_batch` and `cs_engine.solve_equals_batch` take `root_orders` (default None: per position None, or a permutation of that position's legal-move indices, first read first; a
   wrong one is an error row, never repaired; `ordering=False` with an order is refused) and `root_order_mode` ("strict" or "ties", default "strict"); also `ledger_depth` (default None = the engine's own cap), added so a
   test can fix the depth. The Rust: `Search::set_root_order` (rust/engine/tactics/src/ledger.rs), `LedgerOp.root_order`, `Params.root_order`; no Cargo file touched. With no order the code path is the one that was.
   What the search does with an order. Between its deepenings it puts the PREVIOUS deepening's best root move first (the table's best), and in a node of the main search reads late quiet moves shallow first (LMR);
   the root is no exception to either. So under today's reading order the pick is sticky: the previous best while it still holds the best value, else the first of the best value in the root's own order.
   - "strict": the given order REPLACES the root's reading order (the previous best is not read first, the lemma / claim orders are not read at the root, and no root move is read shallow first). The move kept
     (`v > best`, the first of the best value) is then exactly: THE FIRST MOVE IN THE GIVEN ORDER AMONG THE MOVES WHOSE VALUE AT THE FINISHED DEPTH EQUALS THE BEST. Tested against `solve_equals_batch` on 40 positions read
     whole, 3 random orders and the identity order, at ledger depth 3, and on 14 positions at depth 4: the pick was that move every time (tests/test_plan78_51_root_order.py). It is "the highest-numbered move among the
     equals" because the order is by number. By reading the code: with the root's late-move reduction left on, a root move equal at full depth could be screened out by its shallow reading, so the statement
     would not be exact; the reduction is therefore off at the root under "strict" (sound: more search, the value unchanged). I did not run the reduced variant to see how often it would have differed.
   - "ties" (the stable variant the plan names): the root's own order stays and the given order breaks ties only inside the groups the root's order treats alike (same previous-best / lemma-claim rank, same gain,
     same killer or history standing; the many quiet moves of no history are one group). The pick is then: the previous deepening's pick while it still holds the best value, else the first, in that reading order, of
     the best value. It is NOT "the highest number among the equals". Tested: the pick is among the equals, the value and depth equal the plain search's.
   An order never changes value or depth of the finished reading (tested: the same depth, value and set of equals with and without an order).
   DEFAULT UNCHANGED: tests/golden_78_51_default_path.json was recorded from the build BEFORE the order existed (the `ledger_depth` knob only), 40 positions, ledger depth fixed at 3, no clock cut: for each the move, proof flag, the
   ledger step's depth, value and nodes of `solve_batch`, and the move, equal indices, depth and value of `solve_equals_batch`. The new build with no order (`root_orders` absent, None, or a list of Nones) reproduces every
   field (test_without_an_order_the_search_is_what_it_was, test_an_absent_order_is_the_same_whichever_way_it_is_absent).
B. THE COST (`--stage b`, 1000 positions drawn at seed 5151 from the 500 kept games, 0.2 s, 8 threads, "today" read twice as the clock's own noise):
