THE FRAMES ADD TO THE LINEAR HEADS, in steps, and the gain is in the counts by class and by what the class rests on and in the frame count and size; the trap words and the kinds of the units standing lost add little (TABLE A: for the head `taken [us]` the steps are +0.01567, +0.02469, +0.02617, +0.02624, +0.02808 with bands that overlap between the last three). For the heads of single kinds (a knight, a bishop, the castling fact) the frames add little; for the rook and queen heads the frame count and size is the step that adds. For the head `end` the frames add nothing and the ratings, the kinds and the statements carry it (IMPORTANCE lines).
2. THE LINEAR HEAD'S LEARNING CURVE IS FLAT FROM AN EIGHTH OF THE FIT GAMES AT EVERY STEP (TABLE B), as in 78.64; more games do not lift it. THE TREES' CURVE IS NOT FLAT: for `taken [us]` the trees' gain rises with the fit games at every doubling (+0.04127, +0.04368, +0.04522, +0.04697) and is still rising at the end. So the head, not the amount of data, was the limit of the linear heads, and the trees would use more games.
3. THE TREES ARE CLEARLY BETTER THAN THE LINEAR HEAD ON THE SAME TEST ROWS for `taken` and `keeps`, both sides, with bands above zero, and a little better for `end` (+0.00042 and +0.00036; TABLE A, same rows). THE ABLATION says where this comes from: with the distance acting additively on the log odds, as in the linear head, the trees keep part of the gain over the linear head (`taken [us]` +0.00841, `keeps [us]` +0.00366, bands above zero) and the distance acting together with the inputs gives the rest (-0.01066 and -0.00753 when it is taken away). So both are real: the effect of the inputs depends on how far ahead the event is (the pairs lists are led by the distance bin with the count of lost-looking contested units, the frame count and size, and statements), and pairs and bends of the inputs themselves add beyond the linear head. The cap of 200 rounds was reached by some heads; 500 rounds changed the test loss by +0.00018 and +0.00017 (cap not binding).
4. THE CONCEPTS (on the thinned rows, 41172 of them, 44 of 64 columns kept) add to the base inputs and add a little to the frames (TABLE C: `taken [us]` base +0.01335, base with concepts +0.01909, with all frames +0.02651, with frames and concepts +0.02881); for `end` nothing.
5. WHAT THE LEAF READING HAS (stage E): the chance that a side has an event of the class before the record ends is under-predicted in the middle of the range by both heads (calibration lines: 0.520>0.559 linear, 0.526>0.574 trees, for `keeps [us]`), and the quantity is dominated by the length of the rest of the game (most settled rows have such an event before the game ends: observed 0.8306 for `keeps [us]`); who-first for `keeps` is read only a little better than the base hazard (accuracy 0.5699 against 0.5319), for `taken` a little (0.5916 against 0.5510), for `end` clearly (0.7081 against 0.5153; this is mostly the ratings and the statements, not the frames). The frames lift the `keeps` who-first accuracy from 0.5642 (base inputs only) to 0.5699 and its log loss gain from +0.01218 to +0.01666; the trees reach +0.02145. By band of rating the lines are in the table above. NO claim that this is a leaf for a player: the heads are fitted on human games; no player reads them; the gain per step is small in absolute terms.
6. THE FILL (stage F), with the frame inputs present on every fill row: on the test rows with at most 8 units the LINEAR heads fitted with the fill are better with bands above zero (`taken [us]` +0.00421, `taken [them]` +0.00474, `keeps [us]` +0.00301, the pawn heads about +0.005); on all test rows the fill makes them slightly worse (about -0.0003 for `taken`); THE TREES do not gain from the fill on the few-unit rows (bands include zero) and lose a little on all rows. The fill games are our own player's, not human play.
7. FAILURES AND SURPRISES: (a) the frames' counts by class are mostly one number, the units read, so the step "+classes" partly re-describes the stage of the game; the ply and the ratings are among the groups that carry the most in the tree's importance lines. (b) The trap words and the lost-by-kind groups, expected to matter, add little (their groups carry almost nothing in the trees' importance lines). (c) The `end` trees were worse than the linear head in the 880-game run and are a little better on 9000 games. (d) Every gain is over the base hazard fitted on the same games, which has no inputs at all (a number per distance bin and flag); the base input set (K+S+E+R) already holds the ply and the ratings, so a step's gain is over that set, not over nothing.
8. CUT / NOT DONE: no sacrifice reading (the condition, that E clearly beats the base, is not met: the who-first gain for `keeps` is small); the trees only for `taken`, `keeps`, `end` (the other heads linear); the Friedman H on 80 records of the test rows only; no Pool: every compute step here is already multithreaded (the frame read over the Rust threads, the linear heads in torch, the trees in OpenMP), no stdin heredoc.


78.65 READ (2026-11-16, by the main agent, merged on main; tests test_plan78, test_plan78_65_frames and the three test_plan78_64 files pass; no Rust change; outputs in artifacts/experiments/frames_heads_78_65; numbers are the builder's OBS lines, one run each, directions only).
What holds:
1. THE FRAMES ARE THE INPUT THAT MOVES THE HEADS. Given the frame read's counts of units by class and by what the class rests on, the linear head for "a unit is taken" gains clearly over the same head without them, with bands that exclude zero. This is section 13's claim, a position valued from its parts, seen for the first time in a measurement.
2. A HEAD THAT CAN COMBINE INPUTS IS CLEARLY BETTER THAN THE LINEAR ONE on the same test rows, and ITS LEARNING CURVE IS STILL RISING at 6252 fit games, where the linear head's is flat from an eighth. So Kaveh's point about data holds for this head: more games would help it.
3. The frame rows for 9000 games cost about an hour and a half and a few megabytes.
What does not hold:
4. THE GAINS ARE STILL SMALL BESIDE THE BASE LOSS. "Who wins and keeps a unit first" from a settled row is predicted a few points above the base rate, and the frames add under one point to it. Not yet a leaf reading a player could lean on.
5. Much of the trees' advantage is the distance acting together with the inputs, not pairs of inputs; pairs of inputs alone are a smaller, real gain.
6. The trap words and the kinds of the units standing lost add little; the count-like inputs partly re-describe the stage of the game. The end of the game is predicted from ratings and statements, not from frames.
7. The fill helps the linear head on rows with few units and does not help the trees there.
8. No sacrifice reading; the condition was not met.
Next, owed by this read: the tree head on all the games with frame rows for the remaining 3000 and then more games (its curve says so); inputs that describe a frame by its content (which concept, which units) rather than by counts; and the first trial of the leaf reading INSIDE the frame read, as a comparison of routes, which is what the estimate is for.


78.66 BUILT, stages A and B (builder agent, 2026-11-16; NO RUST CHANGE, the extension was NOT rebuilt; code catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/sleep_loop66.py extending sleep_loop.py; tests tests/test_plan78_66_sleep.py, in scripts/gate.py; outputs under artifacts/experiments/sleep_78_66/, untracked).
HOW TO RUN: `python -m catspace.incubator.analyst.discovery.sleep_loop66 sleeps --tag T --sleeps N --sleep-seconds S --slice-seconds L --own-games G --pairs 100` and `... fixed --tag T --sleep-seconds S --slice-seconds L --own-games G --vs-sleep TAG:INDEX`.
STAGE A, THE YARDSTICK. The player reads one thing, the integer worths per kind. The yardstick scores exactly that: the score s of a position is the sum over kinds of worth x (units of the side to move less the other side's units) / 1000, and the result is predicted by a one-input multinomial logit on s (win, draw, loss), its intercepts and slope FROZEN at the start of the sleep, fitted before the first action on fit data only (for the own-player set on the sleep's fit odds games, for the human set on the fit human rows of the first 500 fit human games). Two held-out sets, fixed before the first action, never fitted on: (i) fresh games of the sleep's OWN current player from the start list (every start, the even start three times a round), a stated number (--own-games; 300 in the measured runs, 150 in the 10 minute test, 40 in the smoke), their wall time taken out of the sleep's budget and printed; (ii) the held-out human games of the 78.59 split, every settled row. Y is the mean of the two held-out log losses, each over its value at the start of the sleep (smaller is better); the worths scored are the integers the new player would play with. The human result head of 78.63 is not in Y; it is no longer fitted at all. The odds games of the earlier generation, both halves of the 78.63 split, are now fit games (the held-out sets are new). Pairs left unordered are printed as a side line only.
THE ACTIONS THAT REMAIN: odds_kind, odds_later, odds_pair (each adds odds games, so refits the worths). human_fit fits a head no player reads, cannot change the record, has computed gain 0, and is never chosen (it stays in the candidate list so that the zero is printed). The computed gain of the others: one half x the curvature of Y in a worth (a finite difference of Y itself, step 50 worth units; non negative because the loss is convex in the logits) x the variance of that worth over 200 refits on resampled games x the share of that variance the action's games remove (n/(n+games)); the spread between worths is neglected (stated limit).
STAGE B, THE THREE-SLICE RULE. A chosen action runs a bout of three consecutive slices (the stop rule may cut it); the bout's observed gain (Y before its first slice less Y after its third) and its computed gain enter the chooser's record of observed against computed only at the bout's end; a bout cut short enters nothing. The correction still needs two entered bouts of a type before it moves off 1.
THE SETTINGS OF THE MEASURED RUNS, stated before them: one 10 minute sleep (slices of 90 s, 150 own held-out games, 100 opening pairs, tag test10) with its wake match; then three sleeps from generation 2 of 78.61 of at most 1800 s each (CHANGE FROM THE PLAN'S 1 HOUR, stated: the 4 hour cap of the machine does not hold three sleeps of an hour and the fixed schedule at the same total time), slices of 120 s, 300 own held-out games, 100 opening pairs a wake match, seconds per move 0.05, ply cap 120, 8 workers or 10 (cores 11); THETA 5e-7, patience 6 slices, explore share 0.2 as in 78.63 (the stop on no recent gain is kept as it was); then the fixed schedule at the sum of the three sleeps' wall times, and the match of the fixed player against the first player and against the third sleep's player. Before every wake match the load average and the cores busy are printed, and the match waits up to five minutes for a load average under 4.


78.66 BUILT, stage C (builder agent, 2026-11-16; one run each, directions only; numbers only from the OBS lines the programs printed, in artifacts/experiments/sleep_78_66/{test10,main3,fixed3}/obs.txt, untracked; NO RUST CHANGE, extension not rebuilt). Settings as stated above, except: THE SLEEPS WOKE BY THEMSELVES, so no sleep used its 1800 s; the fixed schedule was given their sum, 1717 s (740 + 727 + 250), preparation inside it. The held-out own-player games took 128, 122 and 127 s (300 games, 10 workers), inside each sleep's time. Tests: tests/test_plan78_66_sleep.py (6), with test_plan78, _63, _61: 43 passed. Endgame coverage of the human sample printed in test10 (fit games: 12.36 pct of positions with 12 units or fewer, 2.14 pct with 5 or fewer; test games 12.19 and 2.09 pct; 60 pct of games stop before the end on the board).
THE THREE SLEEPS (from generation 2 of 78.61; yardstick Y = 1 at each sleep's start; the wake match of each is the new store's player against the player the sleep played with, 100 opening pairs):
OBS sleep 1: woke at 740 s, 5 slices, 1 bout entered (no recent gain); Y 1.00000 -> 1.00217; own-player log loss 0.77045 -> 0.77351, human 0.82833 -> 0.82863; match 0.6000 [0.5675, 0.6325], KEPT; sign agreement no (yardstick down, match up). Worths after: bishop 1796, knight 963, pawn 439, queen 4030, rook 1819.
OBS sleep 2: woke at 727 s, 5 slices, 1 bout (no recent gain); Y 1.00000 -> 1.00249; own 0.73102 -> 0.73770, human 0.82859 -> 0.82514; match 0.4900 [0.4725, 0.5050], KEPT; sign agreement yes (both against). Worths after: bishop 1704, knight 1014, pawn 424, queen 4511, rook 2181.
OBS sleep 3: woke at 250 s, 1 slice, 0 bouts (no action expected to pay: best corrected 4.15e-07 under 5e-07); Y 1.00000 -> 0.99922; own 0.72408 -> 0.72519, human 0.82545 -> 0.82290; match 0.5000 [0.4850, 0.5150], KEPT; sign agreement no. Worths after: bishop 1653, knight 1111, pawn 419, queen 4450, rook 2210.
COMPUTED AGAINST OBSERVED (per bout of three slices, the only entries into the chooser's record): odds_kind(pawn) computed +4.23e-04 observed -8.45e-04; odds_kind(queen) computed +2.23e-04 observed -3.92e-03; the 10 minute test: odds_kind(pawn) +3.83e-04 / -9.85e-04, odds_later(queen) +2.37e-04 / -3.90e-03. Opposite signs in all four bouts. The bouts of sleeps 1 and 2 after the first were cut by the stop (odds_later, 2 slices each) and entered nothing; per slice the signs agreed in 3 of the 10 slices of sleeps 1 and 2 (computed always positive; observed positive in 1 of 5 and 2 of 5; read off the logs).
THE FIXED SCHEDULE at 1717 s (13 slices, 5460 odds games in memory at the end): Y 1.00000 -> 0.99189 (own 0.79782 -> 0.78869, human 0.82833 -> 0.82436), falling in most slices; worths after: bishop 1889, knight 1161, pawn 588, queen 5127, rook 1934; match against the first player (generation 2) 0.5850 [0.5550, 0.6150]; DIRECT MATCH of the fixed schedule's player against the third sleep's player 0.5025 [0.4825, 0.5250].
THE TEST10 (one 600 s sleep, 150 own games): Y 1.00000 -> 1.00489, own 0.75174 -> 0.76013, human 0.82833 -> 0.82718; match 0.5775 [0.5525, 0.6026], kept; sign agreement no.
MACHINE LOADS: before every wake match the one-minute load average read 13 to 18 on first look (it is the decay of the 10 workers the run itself had just used; cores busy 2.2 to 3.5, so something else ran at about two cores) and fell to 3.8 to 4.75 after waits of 120 to 300 s; sleep 3's wait ran out at 300 s with 4.75. The matches then ran at cores busy 2.2 to 2.4.
WHAT THIS SAYS (directions): (1) the sleep length can be read from the yardstick: in every choosing sleep Y did not improve at all within the 12 minutes of patience, so the stop fired at 12 minutes; in the fixed schedule Y fell over the whole 1717 s, mostly in the first 750 s. (2) The yardstick's gain and the match agree in sign in 1 of 3 sleeps; the matches' bands sit around 0.5 for two of them, so the sign of the match is itself not read there. (3) The computed gain and the observed gain disagree in sign in every bout; the chooser's model (curvature x variance removed) is not predictive here. (4) Choosing, with this yardstick, did not beat the fixed list at equal time: the fixed list's yardstick improved and the choosing sleeps' did not; matched directly, the two final players are level (0.5025). (5) A probable cause of the worsening Y in the choosing sleeps, not tested: the result maps are frozen at the starting worths, and each bout of one kind moves that kind's worth far (queen 4646 -> 5589 in the test10 sleep) while the other kinds' games stay few, so the worths leave the scale the map was fitted at; the fixed list moves all kinds together. (6) The own-player held-out set is noisy: the same start player scored 0.77045 (sleep 1 set) and 0.79782 (fixed set) on two fresh sets of 300 games, a spread larger than any gain seen; the yardstick needs more own games than 300 to be read at the 1e-3 level, and they cost 2 minutes of every sleep.
WHAT WAS CUT: the plan's 1 hour a sleep (the sleeps woke at 12, 12 and 4 minutes); no per-slice random seeds beyond one run each; no test of the frozen-map explanation in (5); no second repetition of anything.


78.66 READ (2026-11-16, by the main agent, merged on main; tests test_plan78, test_plan78_66_sleep, _63, _61 pass; no Rust change; outputs in artifacts/experiments/sleep_78_66; numbers are the builder's OBS lines, one run each, directions only).
What holds:
1. The yardstick now scores only the record the player reads, on held-out games of the sleep's own player and of humans; the three-slice rule and the quiet-machine wait are in.
2. The first sleep again made a player ahead of the one it started from; later sleeps made level ones.
What does not hold, for the second time:
3. CHOOSING DID NOT BEAT THE FIXED LIST at equal time: the fixed schedule improved the yardstick through its whole time, the choosing sleeps did not improve theirs at all, and the two final players matched directly are level.
4. THE COMPUTED GAIN DOES NOT PREDICT THE OBSERVED GAIN: opposite in sign in every bout that entered the record.
5. The yardstick and the wake match agree in sign in one sleep of three, with two match bands sitting on a half.
6. The held-out set of the sleep's own player is too small: two draws of it for the same player differ by more than any gain seen.
MY READING OF WHY, beyond the builder's untested cause (the frozen map): THE MENU HOLDS ONE KIND OF ACTION. Every action that can change what the player reads is "more odds games for some kind", and the player reads one small record. A choice among near-equal ways of filling the same five numbers cannot beat filling all five, and its cost (held-out games, bouts) is pure loss. A chooser earns its keep only when the actions differ in kind and the player reads what each one makes. Neither is true yet.
DECISION (main agent, within the standing go; told to Kaveh): the chooser is PARKED as built and tested; sleeps run the fixed schedule until the player reads more than worths. The next build makes the player read the estimator, which is also what spec 13 and 15 ask for and what gives the sleep a second kind of action (fit the heads).

PLAN 78.67: THE PLAYER READS THE EVENT HEADS TO CHOOSE AMONG MOVES ITS SEARCH HOLDS EQUAL (SYSTEM_SPEC 13, 15, 16; the 78.65 read; plan 78.51 found a fitted number as the tie-break of the root order above half against the control). Written 2026-11-16 by the main agent. Python over the installed extension, the root-order mechanism of 78.51 (`root_orders`, strict mode); no Rust change expected; a sandbox player, nothing switched on by default.
A. THE NUMBER. For each legal move at the root: the position after it, the frame read's row there, the 78.65 heads (trees and linear) for "wins a unit and keeps it" for each side, read as the difference in who-first chance for the mover. State the time this costs per move and choose the clock so that the search's share is unchanged (the reading comes out of the mover's own time).
B. THE PLAYERS, all on the 78.61 generation-2 record: control (root order as it is); random tie-break; tie-break by the number (trees); by the number (linear); by the 78.51 number (the arrival fit), as the earlier result to beat.
C. THE MATCHES on a quiet machine, 100 opening pairs each, two disjoint sets of openings (78.51 owed a second set): each tie-break against the control and against random; the best two against each other. Printed: score with bands, depth reached by each side, how often the tie-break changed the move, time per move.
D. WHAT IT DID IN THE GAMES: over the match games, how often the mover with the number went on to win and keep a unit first, beside the control.
E. If and only if the number clearly beats random tie-break on both sets: one sleep on the fixed schedule that also refits the heads on its own games plus the human games, and the wake match after it.
Cautions: the heads were fitted on human games and are read here in games of our own player; the tie-break only acts where the search holds moves equal; AGENTS rule 7 is kept, since nothing is added to the value, the order among equals is all that changes.

STATUS: to a builder now.


PLAN 78.68: A MENU OF DIFFERENT KINDS OF ACTION FOR THE SLEEP (SYSTEM_SPEC 16, last paragraph; Kaveh 2026-11-16: "Why do we only have one item on the menu? ... Monte Carlo playouts ... querying the database ... playouts with odds games ... asking the oracle ... Things like that should be part of the menu"). Written 2026-11-16 by the main agent. Extends sleep_loop66.py's action interface; a sandbox. Waits for 78.67, since most of these actions pay only through the heads, and 78.67 is what makes the player read the heads.
A. PLAYOUTS FROM A POSITION: from a chosen position, games by the current player (and by the random mover as a second source), the results and the rules' events recorded; rows for the heads. Positions chosen where the heads are least sure or disagree with what happened.
B. QUERY OF THE HUMAN GAMES: for a frame, concept or small set of units, the conditional statistics of result and events, by band of rating, from the shards not yet read; rows for the heads. This is also the endgame fill done from human play where it exists.
C. ODDS GAMES, as built, and odds from playout positions.
D. THE ORACLE AS A FINDER (Stockfish; it reads the tablebase itself): over the sleep's own games, the positions where our move or our head is far from the oracle's reading are listed as surprises. Only the LIST of positions leaves this action; no oracle number is written into any row, fit or record (a test checks the rows hold none). What is learned at those positions comes from A, B and the frame read. If Kaveh lifts the 2026-11-15 decision, this stage changes; until then it stands as written.
E. THE FRAME READ ON A SURPRISE and A REFIT OF THE HEADS, as actions.
F. The chooser of 78.66 unparked on this menu, with the fixed schedule (each action in turn, equal shares) as the comparison, the yardstick being the heads' and the record's held-out loss on games of the sleep's own player and on human games, with held-out sets large enough that two draws agree (state the size from the 78.66 spread).
Each action prints what it made and what reads it.

STATUS: written; after 78.67.

78.68 AMENDMENT (Kaveh 2026-11-16, the oracle in the sleep decided; SYSTEM_SPEC 16, last paragraph). Stage D is replaced by THE LADDER ON A POSITION. The oracle (Stockfish with its tablebase) is asked for the best move of a position from the sleep's own games or the human games. Then, in order, each step printed with its cost: (1) SHARP: does our reasoning reach that move alone (the search with the record, the forcing read, the frame read); (2) NOT SHARP: do the heads prefer it among the moves the search holds equal; (3) A SURPRISE REMAINS: deeper concrete reading by our tools until they pick the move, or a stated limit of calculation is reached; (4) COMPRESS when (3) was costly or hit the limit: a candidate lemma stated for the prover, or a candidate input for the heads built from what the deeper reading found, checked on playouts and human games before it is kept. The position leaves the surprise list when our tools pick the move cheaply. Counts per rung are the sleep's diagnosis of what is weak (reasoning, statistics, or missing knowledge), which is what the chooser reads. What enters the sandbox store is only what our tools made and checked; a test asserts no oracle evaluation and no oracle-move label is in any row fitted on. Reuse sleep.py (78.17), the surprise meter (78.37), the prover. First run: rungs 1 to 3 as a measurement on a few hundred positions (how the surprises divide), before any compression is built.

78.68 AMENDMENT 2 (Kaveh 2026-11-16: "it can be fitted to the Oracle, but I would rather avoid that if possible ... fit it on the traces of our own reasoning ... predict the reasoning trace ... from a leaf where we actually end the reasoning, we should be able to predict the rest of the reasoning trace and see where it goes ... Maybe we should do like a Monte Carlo and then predict the Monte Carlo output"; SYSTEM_SPEC 9). A new stage G, THE HEADS FITTED ON OUR OWN DEEPER THINKING. (1) THE PAIRS: for positions from the sleep's own games and from human games, the wake's reading at its own clock gives the leaf (the settled rows where its lines stop) and the frame inputs there; a deep reading at many times that clock from the same leaf gives the target where it reaches a settled, concrete end (the events of the rules that happened along its line, the units won and kept, the end of the game if reached); where the deep reading does not settle, playouts by the current player from the leaf give the target as statistics. Each row records which of the two made its target. (2) THE FIT: the event heads of 78.65 on these targets, beside the same heads fitted on human games, both read on held-out rows of each kind; learning curves. (3) THE CHECK AGAINST DRIFT: a head that predicts its own player's thinking can inherit its errors, so the fit is anchored by rows whose target is an end of the game or a proved fact, and measured (not fitted) against the oracle's best move on held-out positions: how often the head, as tie-break, picks it. (4) THE LAST RESORT, not built here: a fit on the oracle, taken up only if (2) and (3) stall, and with his word.

PLAN 78.69: IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO READINGS A SIGNAL OF SHARPNESS (SYSTEM_SPEC 6; Kaveh 2026-11-16: "When the statistical end aligns with the material reading, that means the position is quiet and we can read the estimate. When the statistical reading is not the same ... there's something sharp going on"). Written 2026-11-16 by the main agent. A measurement on what exists: the 9000 games with frame rows of 78.65 and its heads; no new games.
A. Per settled row: the reading on kinds alone and the reading on all the parts (frames, concepts, statements), for the result where a head exists and for "wins and keeps a unit" per side; their difference.
B. Does the size of the difference foretell that something happens soon: the time to the next event of the rules (78.64) by band of the difference, with bands over games; and whether the frame read's own classes (a unit standing lost, contested) sit where the difference is large.
C. Does it tell sharp from lasting: of the rows with a large difference, the share where it is gone at the next settled row (resolved) against the share where it stays (compensation).
D. Stopping by it: on the match games of 78.67, where the player's search ended, how often the two readings agreed; no player is changed.
If B holds, the rule enters the frame read as a reason to end a line (beside SETTLED) in a later plan.

STATUS: written; a small job, after 78.67 reports.

78.69 AMENDMENT (Kaveh 2026-11-16: open tactics carried forward and checked before the estimate is trusted; SYSTEM_SPEC 6). Stage E, measured on the same rows: per settled row, the open claims of the frame read (units standing lost or contested, by side) with their stake put in the unit of the readings (the change in the kinds head's chance if the unit is lost), and the spread between the two readings. (1) How often a row has an open claim with stake above the spread. (2) Does the rule separate: among rows where the readings agree, the rate of an event of the rules soon after, for rows with such an open claim against rows with none. (3) Carrying: for a claim that the read holds at ply n, how often the read at ply n+2 holds it again when nothing it reads has changed (it should be always; a miss is a defect of the read), and how often a claim first seen at n+2 was already true at n (a miss that carrying would have caught at the next move). Reuse the event memory of 78.42 and the carry of plan 66 where they apply; nothing is rebuilt for this measurement.

78.68 AMENDMENT 3 (Kaveh 2026-11-16: "one rule ... which covers the blind spot, will then fix all of the surprises at once and will give me a huge positive signal ... look at each rule and how many surprises does it solve"; SYSTEM_SPEC 9). The ladder keeps a standing LIST OF OPEN SURPRISES in the sandbox store, each with the rung it stopped at and what the deep reading found. Stage H, THE SCORE OF A RULE: any candidate (a lemma, a concept, a statistical input, a change of the read) is scored by rerunning the cheap rungs on the list: surprises resolved less surprises created, counted on a part of the list the candidate was not made from, with the time it cost. Surprises are grouped by what they share (the frame classes, concepts and events at the position, the rung) and a candidate is proposed for the largest group first. The chooser's yardstick of 78.66 is replaced by this count per second. Printed: the list's size over time, the groups, per candidate the count resolved and created.


PLAN 78.70: THE THREAT LIST OF A POSITION (SYSTEM_SPEC 8; Kaveh 2026-11-16: "in any given position, I want us to be able to answer what are the threats and what is the stake there ... list out threats with their stake and the response"). Written 2026-11-16 by the main agent. A view over the frame read (sheet/questions.rs, plans 78.57 to 78.60) and the readings of 78.59 and 78.65; the earlier `reason` path of plan 78.25 (threats by stake, parry or counter) is read first and reused where it fits. Rust for the list itself if the read must return more than it does; Python for the printing; a sandbox, no player changed.
A. THE ROWS. For each side: every unit the read holds as standing lost or contested in some frame, as one threat: what is threatened and by what, in which frame (its units), the stake (the change in the kinds reading's chance of the result if it is lost; the order of kinds from the fitted record, stated), the response if the read found one (the move, and its reason: a guard added, a line shut, the unit moved, a counter through another frame), and how the line ended (the four reasons of spec 4).
B. THE WIDENING. A threat that wins in the smallest frame and is answered when the frame is widened is kept as one row, "with a response", with both frames named.
C. THE FOUR BANDS and their order: high stake with no response; high stake with a response; low stake with no response; low stake with a response (hidden unless asked). The line between high and low is not a number put in: it is the spread between the two readings at that position (spec 6), so that "high" means "larger than what the estimate could be wrong by".
D. THE CHECKS. On the 9000 games with frame rows: how many rows per position in each band; for the top band, how often a unit of that side is then taken (it should be the highest of the four); for the second band, how often the response named, or one with the same reason, was the move played. On the 78.45 puzzles, as a measure only: how often the solution's first move is the threat of ours in the top band of the other side's list.
E. THE PRINT: a position's list as readable text, names from the mapping file where there is one, else the engine's own. Ten positions printed in the note for Kaveh to read.

STATUS: written; after 78.67 reports; before 78.68, since the ladder's rung 1 can read this list.

NO RUST CHANGE; the extension was NOT rebuilt. Code: catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/tiebreak_number.py (the number: fit, the inputs at play time, `verify`) and tiebreak_measure.py (players, matches, stage D); tests tests/test_plan78_67_tiebreak.py (in scripts/gate.py).
THE HEADS. The 78.65 run kept no fitted head, so they were REFIT once with the 78.65 code (`frames_heads.build`, `events_hazard.fit_best` for the linear head, `frames_heads.fit_tree` for the trees) on the same 9000 games and the same fit rows, for the class "keeps" (a unit won and kept), each side, with all inputs (kinds, statements, edge distances, rating and ply, then the frame blocks); saved in artifacts/experiments/tiebreak_78_67/heads/heads.pkl (0.7 MB). The refit reproduces the 78.65 test numbers:

THE NUMBER of a move = in the position after it, the race of 78.65 stage E: P(the side that moved first wins and keeps a unit) less P(the other side first), from the two heads of the class, over the plies left to the game's ply cap (120). THE INPUTS AT PLAY TIME are rebuilt from the moves alone by the same code as the fit (position table, statement sheet, edge distances, frame read, `frames_heads.frame_blocks`); checked against the fit's own matrix on 60 random fit rows:
OBS tiebreak heads: VERIFY inputs rebuilt from the moves against the fit's matrix, 60 rows: kinds: identical in 60 rows, largest difference 0.00000 (statements, edge distances, ply, classes, trap, lost kinds, frames: identical in 60 rows each, largest difference 0.00000; whole lines in verify_obs.txt)
Two stated limits of the inputs: (1) the ratings are not known at play time: the mean rating of the fit rows and a rating difference of nothing stand in; (2) THE STATEMENTS OF THE FIT ROWS WERE READ WITH AN EMPTY WORTH TABLE (found by this check: with the real store's worth the material and attack-worth statements differ in 57 of 60 rows), so the play-time sheet is built with an empty worth too (no assumed worth); the arrival number of 78.51 is read with the same empty-worth sheet (the weights of 78.50 are the file's, unchanged), which may differ from how 78.51 read it. The frame read also takes the order of kinds of the human record of 78.59 inside it (its own input, as in 78.62 and 78.65); the heads are human-game fits.
STAGE A, THE COST (60 positions of human games of the 78.59 file, ply 10 on, one thread):

OBS tiebreak stage A: the number's reading, per position with two or more equal moves (37): frame read 2033 ms, statements 89 ms, kinds 1 ms, heads 24 ms; per child 133 ms of frame read; children read 566 (quiet 515, 91.0 pct)
OBS tiebreak stage A: the pick of the trees number is the pick of the linear number in 25 of 37, of the arrival number in 16, of a random equal move in 4
THE COST IS ABOUT A TENTH OF A SECOND PER MOVE READ, all of it in the frame read (a fixed cost per position, not changed by the fuses: tried 1500, 150 and 30 and one seed to twelve in a probe, no print kept). Reading the number of every legal move before the search, as the root order of 78.51 needs, would cost seconds a move against a clock of a fifth of a second; the clock cannot be raised to cover it in the machine time of this plan.
DEVIATION FROM THE PLAN, stated BEFORE any measured match: (a) the number is read only for the moves the search HOLDS EQUAL, AFTER the search (the 78.50 form: `solve_equals_batch` hands back the equal moves), and the player plays the equal move with the highest number. For every player this is the same search call, so the value and the set of moves held best are the search's whatever the choice (nothing is added to the value; AGENTS rule 7), and the choice is exactly what the strict root order would pick among the equals at that depth, without the ply of depth the strict mode costs (78.51 stage B). The root-order mechanism itself is tested (the order changes neither the value nor the set of equal moves, and the move kept is the first of the set in the order; tests/test_plan78_67_tiebreak.py) but is not what the matches play. (b) THE READING IS NOT TAKEN OUT OF THE SEARCH'S CLOCK: the search of every player gets the same 0.2 s (78.61 had 0.05 s; the equal reading of the engine needs room, as in 78.50 and 78.51) and the reading comes after it, so it cannot make the reading player search for less; the cost shows as time per move, printed per match (a reading player spends about 1.8 s a move in the short run below, against 0.12 s). The function that would take the reading out of the clock (`reading_clock`, `--charge`) is built and tested and is run, if the machine time allows, in one charged match at a clock of 2 s.
THE SETTINGS OF THE MEASURED MATCHES (stated before them): all players search with the Worth judge fed from the generation-2 record of 78.61 (artifacts/experiments/odds_78_61/full/gen2/record.json: queen 4343, bishop 1878, knight 1661, rook 1605, pawn 1045; players_of(3)); 0.2 s a move, ledger share 0.4 (78.50), one thread a game, ply cap 120, a position met three times is a draw, unfinished games count as draws; 100 opening pairs of four random plies, both colours, in two sets: set A the seeds 9100 to 9199 (the openings of the 78.61 matches), set B the seeds from 41000 up, skipping any seed whose opening is one of set A's or already in B (the two sets share no opening; tested); 9 workers of 11 cores, spawn Pool, one thread of the trees' prediction (OMP_NUM_THREADS 1); each match waits up to 300 s for the one-minute load average to fall to 4 and prints what it saw (a game of the machine's owner was running at 2 to 3 cores during the short run and may be again). Players: control (the engine's own move), random (a seeded random one of the equal moves), trees, linear (the number from the trees heads, from the linear heads), arrival (the 78.51 number). Order of the matches, the cut list first (the plan's fallback if all do not fit in about four hours of machine time): trees v control, trees v random, random v control, each on both sets; then linear v control, arrival v control, then linear v random, arrival v random, then the best two against each other.

READING (builder; directions only, one run per match; no verdict). (1) Every number scores above half against the control and against the random tie-break on both sets of openings, with the lower end of the band above half in all twelve matches of the three numbers (trees, linear, arrival); the random tie-break against the control sits at half on both sets (0.5000 and 0.5025). So the choice among equal moves matters here and the pick of a fitted number beats both the engine's own pick and a random one. (2) THE HEADS' NUMBER DID NOT SHOW AS BETTER THAN THE EARLIER NUMBER: linear against arrival (set A only) 0.5075 [0.4800, 0.5350]; against the control and against random the three numbers' bands overlap (trees 0.5925 and 0.5925 against the control, linear 0.6275 and 0.5950, arrival 0.5825 and 0.6100; against random trees 0.5575 and 0.5400, linear 0.6100 and 0.5900, arrival 0.5775 and 0.6000). The trees were the weakest against random on both sets (the band's lower end 0.5225 and 0.5050), although their test loss in 78.65 was the lowest. The arrival number costs 4.5 ms a decision and no frame read; the heads' number costs about 1.0 s. (3) THE COST: a reading player spent about 0.9 to 1.1 s a decision in reading (frame read of every equal move's position, a tenth of a second each) against 0.11 s of search, for every player the same search; it is outside the search's clock in these matches, so it shows as time per move, not as depth. Ledger depth of the two sides is within 0.2 ply in every match (the number players a little under the control or the random player in all twelve matches against them, by 0.1 to 0.2 ply, which this plan did not explain). (4) THE TIE-BREAK CHANGED THE MOVE in about 81 to 86 pct of the decisions where two or more moves were held equal (about 57 to 64 pct of all decisions) for the numbers, and in 77 to 83 pct of them (54 to 61 pct of all) for the random player: the engine's own pick is rarely one the tie-break keeps. About 70 to 80 pct of all decisions have two or more equal moves. (5) Between 24 and 61 pct of the games hit the ply cap and count as draws; the scores come from the decisive ones (for example trees against control, set A: W 57 D 123 L 20).
READING OF STAGE D (directional). The mover is first to win and keep a unit in 75.5 pct of the trees player's decisions against 31.1 pct of the control's in the same games (set A), and the other numbers and the other set are alike (see the lines). BUT THE RANDOM TIE-BREAK SHOWS THE SAME GAP against the control (67.6 pct against 39.1 pct on set A, 68.2 against 38.5 on set B) in matches that are level, and the random player against the trees player has 38.6 pct (set A) while the trees player has 68.3: the share moves with whether a player is the control, not with the number. This measure is therefore NOT read as the number's effect; what it does show is that the engine's own pick (first of the equals) is the passive one. A reading of how the equal moves differ in what follows (the unit that is won and kept) would need the comparison among the equal moves of the same position, which these games do not give.
STAGE E WAS NOT RUN. Its condition is that the number clearly beats the random tie-break on both sets. By the bands it does for linear (0.6100 and 0.5900) and arrival (0.5775 and 0.6000) and only just for trees (0.5575 and 0.5400, band ends 0.5225 and 0.5050); but the heads' number is not ahead of the arrival number (one direct match, level), the machine time of this plan (about 4 hours) was spent, and the stage needs the heads refit on the player's own games, for which frame rows of those games must be read first (a build not done here). Said plainly: it is not run for lack of time and for the one level direct match, not because a condition failed outright.
CAUTIONS (as in the plan, and found): the heads were fitted on human games and are read in games of a generation-2 player; the ratings are stand-ins; THE STATEMENT INPUTS OF THE FIT ROWS WERE READ WITH AN EMPTY WORTH, as said above (the arrival number is read with the same empty-worth sheet, not necessarily as 78.51 read it); about 90 pct of the children read are quiet positions (the heads' rows are quiet ones from ply 10 on), the rest and the early plies are out of the heads' domain; the opening sets are 100 pairs of four random plies each, one run each; the play is not charged for reading time and the plan's own mechanism (the strict root order before the search) was not what was played.

78.67 READ (main agent, 2026-11-16; brought to main by cherry-pick, since the builder's branch was based on the history before the rewrite; no Rust change; one run each, directions only; every number is in the builder's two notes above and in artifacts/experiments/tiebreak_78_67/full/obs.txt). SPEC CHECK: serves SYSTEM_SPEC 6 and 7 (a head read as a HINT that orders among moves the reasoning holds equal; it never changes a value the search found), and the row "the player reading the heads" of section 12. Interface: tiebreak_number takes a position and the moves the search holds equal and returns one number a move; tiebreak_measure calls it; the search is not touched. Departures from the plan, none from the spec: (a) the number is read after the search on the equal moves only, not as a root order before it; (b) the reading is not taken out of the search clock.
1. A LEARNED NUMBER AS TIE-BREAK SHOWS AS PLAY. All three numbers (arrival, linear frame head, tree frame head) scored above half against the engine's own choice and against a random tie-break, on both sets of openings, the band's lower end above half in all twelve matches. A random tie-break against the engine's own choice was level on both sets, so the gain is the number's and not the mere change of move.
2. THE FRAME HEADS ARE NOT AHEAD OF THE ARRIVAL NUMBER, and cost far more. The one direct match (linear against arrival, set A) was level. The frame heads spend about ten times the search's time on reading (the frame read of each child), the arrival number a few milliseconds. So (b) matters: the frame heads' matches were NOT at equal time, the arrival number's nearly were. At equal time the frame heads would do worse than shown. The tree head had the best test loss in 78.65 and was the weakest of the three against random: a better loss on human rows did not turn into better choices here.
3. WHAT THIS SAYS FOR THE ORDER OF WORK. The cheap number is the one to carry into the player for now. The frames as inputs paid in prediction (78.65) and not yet in play; the likely reasons, none measured: the heads were fitted on human rows and read on our own player's positions; about nine in ten children read were quiet, where the frame inputs say little; the ratings were stand-ins. Stage E (heads refit on own-play rows) was not run and is folded into 78.68 stage G, where the target is our own deeper reading.
4. LIMITS. The machine was not fully quiet (a game of the owner's ran during the early matches). A quarter to three fifths of games reached the ply cap and count as draws, which pulls every score toward half. The share "first to win and keep a unit" tracked whether the move was the engine's own pick and is not read as the number's effect. The number players searched a little less deep in all twelve matches, unexplained. The arrival number was read with an empty worth table, which may differ from 78.51.
5. A FAULT FOUND AND KEPT IN MIND: the statement inputs of the 78.59 and 78.65 fit rows were built with an empty worth table. It assumes no worth, which is the rule, but it was not known; any later fit that mixes rows must build them the same way (the builder's `verify` command checks it).
NEXT: 78.69 (the two readings as a signal of sharpness, and carrying), then 78.70 (the threat list), then 78.68.

78.69 BUILT, stages A to E (builder agent, 2026-11-16; one run each, directions only; numbers only from the OBS lines below, printed by the programs; whole files in artifacts/experiments/readings_78_69/ (fit_obs.txt, measure_obs.txt, matches_obs.txt, thresholds.json), untracked; NO RUST CHANGE, the extension was NOT rebuilt). SPEC CHECK AT THE TOP: serves SYSTEM_SPEC 6 "When it may be read" (quiet or sharp told by two readings agreeing; open tactics checked before the estimate is trusted) and section 4 "open tactics are carried forward"; the piece is the estimator. Code: catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/two_readings.py (interface in its doc comment: `fit`, `Readings`, `measure`, `matches`; reads other pieces only through frames_heads, events_hazard, events_rules, events_fill, tactical_state and tiebreak_number's play-time Reader); tests tests/test_plan78_69_readings.py (in scripts/gate.py). The module names no chess object (the scan is in the test).
WHAT WAS MEASURED, STATED BEFORE THE RUNS. THE TWO READINGS: a linear hazard head of 78.64 (events_hazard.fit_best, no new model class), for each of two classes (the result: the side wins; and "wins and keeps a unit") and each side, on (1) the kinds of units alone (the baseline) and (2) all the parts: the 78.65 last step (kinds, statements, edge distances, rating and ply, and the frame blocks: classes, trap, lost kinds, frames). The reading r of a row = the chance the side to move has the event within the record, less the other side's (frames_heads.side_chance); the DIFFERENCE delta = r(all parts) less r(kinds alone). The concepts are NOT in the main `all parts` (they exist on 12486 thinned held-out rows only): they are a side line in stage A, refitted on the thinned rows. THE SPLIT: every printed measurement is on the HELD-OUT rows, the games the 78.59 split did not fit (90213 settled rows of 2748 games); the heads were fitted on the 6252 fit games only (the same split as 78.65). BANDS: 90 pct, by bootstrap over GAMES (200 draws). THE EVENT of stage B and E is any event of the rules in the sample's record by either side (except the end of the game), and the takings alone; the rate is events per ply of exposure (the steps from the row to the next event, or to the end of the record when none came), so no horizon is put in. No oracle, no engine evaluation, no external model, no worth table anywhere; the stake of a claim is the change of the kinds head's reading if the unit is lost. Puzzles not used; the human games are the rows of 78.65 (the same builders), and no player id is written. Fit took 49 s (the heads of 78.65 were not kept; these are refits of a different set of heads: kinds alone and all parts, for the result and the keeps class).

STAGE B, WHAT THE LINES SAY (directions): for the RESULT the larger difference goes with FEWER events soon, not more, with the ply held fixed as well; the shuffled difference gives a ratio of one, so this is not noise; it reads as 'a larger difference is where the position is lasting, not where something is about to happen'. For 'keeps' the unconditional top-over-bottom is below one (the difference is larger late in the game, where events are rarer: correlation of the size with ply above) but with the ply held fixed it turns above one (the ratios above), a small gain of rate in the top band; the ply alone moves the rate by a larger factor than the difference does. The frame read's units standing lost of the OTHER side sit in the top band of the 'keeps' difference about 2.7 times as often as in the bottom band (3.3 with the ply held fixed); that is the one clear coincidence with the frame read's classes, and the 'keeps' difference is partly built from those frame inputs.

STAGE E, WHAT THE LINES SAY (directions): (1) with 'contested' counted as an open claim (the plan's words) two rows in three have one and nearly all of those have a stake above the spread for the result, which makes the rule fire almost always; 'contested' is the frame read's catch-all class (read, nothing forced), so the narrower 'lost, both' is the reading to look at: about one row in six has such a claim, and its stake is above the spread in most of them for the result and in fewer than half for 'keeps'. (2) Among rows where the two readings agree, rows with an open claim above the spread have a higher rate of an event of the rules soon after than rows with none, by a factor of about 1.3 to 1.6 unadjusted and 1.2 to 1.35 with the ply or the units left held fixed (bands above); the control with the labels shuffled inside each stratum gives one. So an open claim goes with more events soon among rows where the two readings agree. BUT the group 'open claim whose stake is NOT above the spread' has rates as high as the 'above' group for the narrower class ('lost, both') and lower than the no-claim group for the wider one (few rows in both), so the stake-against-spread condition itself adds little visible beyond the presence of an open claim in this measurement. (3) CARRYING: the stored rows keep no place and no read set, so the claim's identity is an (owner, kind) count and 'nothing changed' is read as no event of the rules at the two steps between: the true test (the same claim, its read set unchanged) is NOT made and the numbers are a PROXY. On the proxy about half of the claims of the wider class and under a third of the 'lost, both' claims are held again two plies later even with no event between, and most claims at n+2 were not held at n. The share of first-seen claims whose earlier row had lines left unread is nil (0.03 pct for the wider class), so the misses are not the read's budget. The proxy cannot tell a defect of the read from a claim that the move in between resolved; the measurement that settles it needs the places and the read set of the engine (event memory of 78.42, carry of plan 66), which the 78.65 rows do not keep; it is left for the plan that carries the claims.
WHAT WAS CUT / DEVIATIONS (stated): (a) The stage E carrying test on read sets (point 3 of the amendment) was not made: the stored state rows have no places or read sets, and re-reading with the engine's event memory was not attempted (it would need a change that gives the unit's place); the proxy above stands in. (b) The concepts are not in the main reading (side line in stage A only). (c) Stage D reads the root of each search, because the match files keep no leaves; one match file (trees against control, set A, all 200 games); the 'reading' player's number was not used by the readings of this plan. (d) The readings are linear hazard heads (the trees of 78.65 were not refitted); the same model class for both readings. (e) The heads of 78.65 were refit (the plan's two readings are new heads on kinds alone and on all parts for the result and the keeps class, one fit, 49 s); the 'keeps' heads on all parts reproduce the 78.65 linear numbers (base 0.38916, linear 0.37679 on the same test rows). (f) 'Large' and 'agree' are thresholds from quantiles of the held-out rows (top fifth and median), not fitted; they are named, not tuned. (g) The statements of the rows were built with an empty worth table, as the fit's were (78.67 read, point 5), so the play-time inputs of stage D use `tiebreak_number.Reader`, which builds them the same way. OUTPUT FILES are untracked under artifacts/experiments/readings_78_69/ (in the builder's worktree; the parent copies them).

78.69 READ (main agent, 2026-11-16; merged, no Rust change; one run each, directions only; every number is in the builder's note above and in artifacts/experiments/readings_78_69/). SPEC CHECK: serves SYSTEM_SPEC 6 (when the estimate may be read) and 4 (carrying); interface two_readings.{fit, Readings, measure, matches}, called by no player; departures from the spec none; choices not in the spec are listed in the builder's note (quantile lines for "agree" and "large", the reading as the side's chance less the other's).
1. THE DIFFERENCE OF THE TWO READINGS WAS NOT A SIGNAL OF SHARPNESS HERE. For the result head a larger difference went with FEWER events soon, with ply held fixed too. For the keeps head the raw sign was the early-or-late effect of ply; a small positive signal remained with ply fixed. Ply alone moves the rate of events far more than the difference does.
2. LARGE DIFFERENCES MOSTLY LAST to the next settled row. Those that go coincide with an event between the rows more often. So most of what the difference shows is lasting, not a tactic about to resolve; part of the persistence is only that neighbouring rows share inputs.
3. THE FRAME READ'S OWN CLAIMS ARE THE SIGNAL. Rows with a unit standing lost had more takings soon than rows with none, with ply and units left held fixed, and the shuffled controls sat at one. Comparing the stake with the spread added little beyond the claim being there. The class "contested" fires on most rows and tells little; the narrow class (lost) is the one to use.
4. WHY POINT 1 IS A WEAK TEST AND NOT A REFUTATION: the head on kinds alone is level with the base hazard for keeps and barely above it for the result, so the "material reading" hardly exists as a head and the difference is mostly the all-parts reading by itself. Linear heads only. The rule of two readings stays in the spec as not yet shown, to be measured again when the kinds reading is stronger (the worth record of the generations, 78.61, is a candidate for it).
5. CARRYING WAS NOT MEASURED AS STATED. The stored rows keep no unit identity and no read sets, so the builder used a proxy that cannot tell a defect of the read from a claim the moves between resolved. The true test needs the frame read to return its read set per claim; it goes into 78.70 stage A, where the rows of the threat list need the same thing.
6. FOR 78.70: the bands are printed two ways (stake against the spread; stake ranked within the position), and "lost" is kept apart from "contested".
NEXT: 78.70.

78.70 AMENDMENT (main agent, 2026-11-16, from the 78.69 read and SYSTEM_SPEC 8 as it now stands). SPEC: serves section 8 (the threat list; the rule for choosing a move reads it) and section 4 (carrying). INTERFACE to be built: threat_list(position) returns, for each side, rows of {the unit threatened, by what, the frame's units, the class (lost kept apart from contested), the stake, the response and its reason if one was found, how the line ended, the READ SET of the claim}; called by a printing script and a measure script now, by the wake's choice of move and the sleep's ladder later; no player is changed here. (1) THE READ SET PER CLAIM is returned by the frame read (Rust, sheet/questions.rs, if it does not return it now), because 78.69 could not test carrying without it. (2) CARRYING, the true test of 78.69 E(3): a claim held at one position is held again two plies on whenever nothing in its read set changed (a miss is a defect of the read, each printed), and a claim first seen later whose read set was already as it is two plies before (a miss carrying would have caught). (3) THE BANDS TWO WAYS, since 78.69 found the stake-against-spread line adds little with the present heads: by the spread of the two readings, and by the stake ranked within the position; stage D's checks are printed for both and neither is called the winner on one run. (4) BOTH SIDES: the list holds their threats against us and ours against them. (5) THE PRINT must let a reader set the position up: the place of every unit, the side to move, the game and ply it came from, by the game's own renderer outside the layer and measure files.

PLAN 78.71: GOALS AS FACTS, THE FIX AS THE SUBGOAL, AND THE GRADING OF SUBGOALS (SYSTEM_SPEC 7 "Choosing a subgoal, and getting there", and 1, the second half of the goal; Kaveh 2026-11-16, brought over from another session: "something has to look at the position and basically point at the weakness for a particular reason ... use the graph to tell me what sub goal I should be pursuing and how to kind of do the means end analysis to get there ... how do we know this is a good sub goal? It's reachable, and how do we know we got the right mitigation for the problem? ... in evaluating sub goals, I don't think we ever got there"). Written 2026-11-16 by the main agent. A measurement and a sandbox; no player changed. Python over the threat list of 78.70; Rust only if the frame read must return more.
PIECE AND INTERFACE: the opportunity policy's proposer. goals(position, side) returns goals, each a list of facts of the graph with units as variables, each fact marked met or unmet, each unmet fact with what stops it (the named causes of 78.60) and the proposed fix; subgoal_claims(goal) returns the four claims of spec 7. It reads the threat list (78.70) and the frame read; the wake's choice of move will call it later. It names no pattern: a goal is whatever set of facts the frame read says would make a threat of ours work.
0. READ FIRST, reuse, do not rebuild: catspace/incubator/analyst/whatif.py, whatif_proposer.py, whatif_search.py, whatif_priority.py (the what-if edits); the JOURNAL entries of 2026-10-01 and 2026-10-08 on imagined frames and the vocabulary of why a fix fails; docs/SUBGOALFORMER.md and subgoal_cascade/src/decompose.py (the summer's former and waypoint decomposer, on a learned embedding: the ideas, top candidates by leverage and reach, revision against the opponent's counter, pursue or deny or hold, the waypoint that maximises the weaker half, carry over; the embedding does not); subgoal_fit_measure.py, subgoal_play_measure.py (78.49, 78.50); docs/THESIS.md on why reach is a chance and not a distance. Outside work to compare with, from the main agent's memory and to be checked against the sources before it is leaned on: Wilkins' PARADISE (goals as patterns of attack, plans chained through unmet conditions, small trees; its patterns were written by hand, ours must come from the read), Botvinnik's PIONEER (search inside zones, close to frames), Newell and Simon's means-ends analysis.
A. GOALS FROM THE THREAT LIST. For each threat of ours that does not work yet: the facts that would make it work, which hold, which do not, and for each that does not, what stops it. Printed for ten positions.
B. THE FIX AS A SUBGOAL, AND IS IT THE RIGHT FIX. For each unmet fact a proposed fix (the stopping unit removed, pinned, blocked, drawn away, the far end a variable). The check by our own reasoning, no oracle: apply the fix alone as a what-if edit and read the frame again. The goal now works: the diagnosis was complete. It still fails: something else also stops it, and that is printed. It works without the fix: the fix was not needed.
C. GRADING ON HUMAN GAMES, by hindsight, no oracle. At each event where a side wins and keeps a unit, take the facts that became true shortly before; go back a few moves; was a goal with those facts among the proposer's first few? And for goals proposed: how often their facts came true later (the chance of reaching, with its calibration), and how often a unit was then won. Controls: a proposer that picks goals at random from the same list; ply held fixed. Endgame coverage printed.
D. THE ORACLE AS A MEASURE of worth, after C and only as a measure (no row of it enters a fit, a test asserts it): for a sample of proposed goals, the oracle's reading of the position with the facts made true against the real one.
E. LATER, not in this plan: the pursuit in sandbox games with the rules for dropping a subgoal (unmet facts not falling, chance falling, our own estimate falling, another better by a margin), and the share of moves spent on subgoals never reached against a player with none.
STATUS: written; after 78.70, whose rows it reads. 78.68 (the sleep's menu and ladder) follows it; one builder at a time.

78.70 BUILT, stages A to E (builder agent, 2026-11-16; branch worktree-agent-a795c4095d47a4948; one run each, directions only; numbers only from the OBS lines below, which programs printed; whole files in artifacts/experiments/threats_78_70/ (read_obs.txt, measure_obs.txt, carry_obs.txt, puzzles_obs.txt, print.txt), untracked). SPEC CHECK: serves SYSTEM_SPEC 8 "The threat list" (the rule for choosing a move reads it later and is NOT built) and 4 ("open tactics are carried forward", "how a line ends"); the piece is the frame read's view for the wake. RUST CHANGED: sheet crate rust/engine/tactics/src/sheet/questions.rs gains `QReader::answers` (+ the structs Answer, Answers); the binding gains `questions_threats` (py/src/questions_py.rs, base_graph_py.rs) and the shared helper `unit_class` (the class code of questions_state moved into it, behaviour unchanged: the new read agrees with questions_state on classes in tests/test_plan78_70_threats.py). THE EXTENSION WAS REBUILT FROM THIS WORKTREE (`maturin develop --release --offline`); the shared editable install points here; the parent rebuilds main after the merge. No Cargo change. Code: catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/threat_list.py (the list; interface in its doc comment), threat_measure.py (read, measure, carry, puzzles), threat_puzzle_pairs.py (loader, knows the puzzle files' field names), threat_print.py (the print, python-chess renderer); tests tests/test_plan78_70_threats.py (in scripts/gate.py; includes the scan of the list, measure and the added Rust).
INTERFACE: threat_list(moves, ply, reader, start=None, stake_of=None, spread=None) -> {"mover": rows against the mover's units (their threats), "other": rows against the other side's (ours), "raw"}; a row = unit (kind, place), by (bearers), class (lost, both, threat, conditional, contested; lost apart from contested), frames (the smallest frame that wins and every wider one holding the unit, each with its unit count, class, answers), response ([(move, reason, whether the unit itself moves)]), widened, ended (concrete / quiet / out of budget; lost beyond doubt not produced), read_set (side to move, members, places of the winning frame), stake (change of the owner's chance of the result by the kinds reading of 78.69 if the unit is lost; None for kinds outside the head), band_spread and band_rank. Rust: BaseGraph.questions_threats(games, rows, keys, goal, fuse, row_fuse, max_size, conditional, answer_fuse, threads).
WHAT WAS BUILT AND HOW (choices stated): THE RESPONSE of a claim = the candidate moves of the read (the Q1 set of 78.57) of the unit's owner after which the other side can no longer force the unit's taking for nothing (the read's own question, asked per candidate); its reason is the candidate's class (a taking, the unit moves, a guard is added, a counter threat, a unit is put between). For a unit of the side NOT to move the answers are the owner's after we pass (hypothetical). A class `lost` (forced now) is not asked for answers. THE WIDENING: the read builds one frame per unit, so there was nothing wider to widen to; the smallest frame of the same seed (the unit and what bears on it, the 78.60 F mode) is now read as well, and a unit that wins there and is answered in the frame as built is ONE row "with a response", both named. THE STAKE: kinds head, class `result`, signed. BANDS: by the spread = stake above |delta| of the two readings at the row; by the rank = the stake in the top half of the position's rows (both sides pooled; middle row of an odd count high; a stake not above zero never high). HOW A LINE ENDED: forced or pruned = concrete; an estimate or a bound = quiet; unread lines = out of budget (a mapping of this build, spec 4 does not give one). THE READ SET of a claim = its frame's members (absolute side, kind, place), places and the side to move. THE SAMPLE: the first 1000 held-out games (the games the 78.59 split did not fit) in the md5 order of their ids, all their settled rows; carrying: 150 of them at EVERY ply from 10.

WHAT THE LINES SAY (directions, one run each): (1) in the cells (a position and a side) the rate of a unit of the side then being taken is above the no-row rate in every band with ply held fixed, highest where the units are the OTHER side's (ours against them) and for bands 1 and 2; but band 1 (high, no response) is NOT clearly above band 2 (high, with a response) by the spread, and by the rank bands 3 and 4 are higher than 1 and 2 on the small counts: the order the spec wants (band 1 highest) is not shown; the shuffled-label control is flat. (2) The response named was the move played in about 11 to 15 pct of rows with a response; the random control printed is a candidate of the read, not a legal move: most played moves are not candidates of the read at all, so this is not a comparison with chance. (3) Rows of class lost with basis bound or estimate are often not lost in the plain sense (first printed position: a bishop standing unattacked; second: a knight exchange): the class `lost` of the read rests on the bound or the estimate there; the 53 rows resting on `forced` are the only concrete ones. (4) CARRYING: with the read set unchanged a claim is held again in about half the cases, and with it changed in about a fifth: the read set is rarely unchanged over two plies (frames are about ten units), and when it is, the defect that dominates is that no frame at n+2 holds the unit (the frame was not asked: a miss of attention), then a frame that holds the unit with no claim on it; a claim first seen at n+2 had its read set already as it is at n in about a tenth of cases (a miss at n, mostly the unit in no frame at n). (5) PUZZLES, as a measure only: the solution's first move is by a unit bearing on a unit of theirs in a band-1 row in 23 pct of the 300, and takes it in 16 pct, against 6 pct for a unit drawn at random; band by rank only (the spread needs inputs not rebuilt outside the 9000 games). NOT BUILT / CUT: the spread at a puzzle position; the roll-over of the list from move to move (the memory of spec 4 reads this list, it does not exist yet); `lost beyond doubt`; no sleep or player reads the list; the guard (trace_identity) was not run (no trace, read set or leaf verdict of any player changed: questions_state is unchanged, tested); the negative control of AGENT_BRIEF section 2 is the shuffled-label control above (it is flat).

THE TEN POSITIONS (rule in threat_print.py: held-out games of the 78.59 split in the md5 order of their ids; per phase, the first settled row of a game in the phase with a row in band 1 by the spread, one per game); chosen 10; the lists come from the frame read with answers (threat_list.py); the stake is the change of the owner's chance of the result by the kinds reading of 78.69; the spread is that of the two readings; `us` is the side to move

For the other side's units the response is what its owner would answer after we pass (the move is not available to us now).
