### PLAN 78.88: ONE REASON, ONE PURPOSE; AND WEIGHTS BY PART OF THE GAME (2026-11-18, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 symbols as subgoals, the form of the model "a combination, mixture of experts kind of thing")

WHY. In play the reasons act as an opening development rule (78.83). The picks read on the board are sums of twenty to forty small mobility and guard patterns; the same idea appears as several twin reasons; "bears on a unit of theirs" counts a guarded unit like a loose one. And 78.81 fitted ONE set of weights over all parts of the game and never printed agreement by part.
FIRST, a print, no new method: 78.81's agreement with the move played on the CONFIRM positions, by band of unit count (few, mid, many) and by quiet or not, against the search's first move. This tells whether the reasons already fail to agree with humans in the middle game, or agree there and still do not win.
A, TWINS. Group the 136 reasons by how they fire together on the FIND moves (the event columns; a fixed rule for the grouping, stated before looking at the result), one group one feature (true when any member fires for the same side and sign), one weight per group. Print the groups in words and judge whether a group is one idea.
B, THE UNIT BORNE ON. The reasons of the form "a unit of the mover's bears on a unit of theirs" are split by two facts the layer already has: whether that unit of theirs is guarded, and whether the bearing unit is itself borne on by theirs. Game-free words only. No worth enters.
C, WEIGHTS BY PART. The same joint choice fit of 78.81 (controls as there), fitted once per band of unit count on FIND, the band chosen at the position. Three experts, gated by the band. Compared with the single fit on CONFIRM: agreement by band, paired bands.
THEN PLAY, only if agreement in the mid or few band rises with a band clear of zero on CONFIRM: the mid and few window against the control on sets A and B (uncharged, same settings as 78.83), and the full player once.
JUDGE. Thirty decisions, ten per band, picks that differ from the search's first move on CONFIRM positions by a fixed rule, with the top three groups in words, read against the board.
INTERFACE. symbols.py: groups_of(reasons, events) -> groups; split_borne(...) -> reasons; fit_choice gains band=None; Choice by band is a dict band -> Choice; ReasonsReader takes it unchanged through pick. Outputs artifacts/experiments/symbols_78_88/. No Rust change expected. Nothing written to the real store. FIND for every fit and every grouping; CONFIRM only for scores.
READ BEFOREHAND. If agreement by band shows the single fit already agrees with humans in the middle game as well as in the opening, the reasons are not the middle game's problem and the hint must act before the tie (in the search's order), which is the spec's design. If it agrees poorly there and C lifts it, the mixture by part is the next piece of the model.

A, TWINS. THE RULE (written in symbols.py before the run, not tuned): carrier sets on the FIND rows (the tied moves of the human FIND positions, 40323 moves in 3215 positions), Jaccard index, average linkage, merge only reasons of one side, one direction and one sign of weight, stop below 0.5; one group one feature (true when any member fires), one weight. RESULT (OBS groups): 136 reasons in 118 groups; 11 groups hold two or more members (largest 5, then 3, 3, 3, 3, 2 ...), 107 reasons are alone. For information only: at thresholds 0.3, 0.4, 0.6, 0.7 the count would be 90, 106, 126, 128. So the twins are fewer than the plan expected: 78.81's duplicate drop (Jaccard 0.9) had taken the near copies already, and the rest fire together less than half. THE TWENTY LARGEST judged by me in cases.txt PART A (the 11 groups with two or more members, then the nine singletons carried by most moves): of the 11, nine are one idea in the words (own units' mobility rising: five members of group 1; own mobility falling: groups 2 and 7; the other side's mobility falling: group 5; a rook's mobility: group 6; a unit that guards a friend and sees empty ground: group 9; own guards loosening: group 8; an attack on a unit of theirs: groups 4 and 10 with a second member that adds "it may move"; the king sheltered by its own units: group 11); two I doubt: group 3 (a queen's mobility falling carries a positive weight, +0.21 against +0.06 and +0.00 for its kind-free twins: the weight is the queen's, not the idea's) and group 1 (its strongest member +0.29 is "guards a friend that can move", the plain "a unit may move" is +0.035: the OR of the five fires on 9544 moves and its one weight blurs a strong member with weak ones). The merge is mostly of a pattern with its kind-free or lower-level cousin, not of two different purposes. Five in words: (1) group 1, own units gain mobility or a guarded unit that can move; (4) group 4, an attack on a unit of theirs, plain or with a second attack or a possible move; (5) group 5, the other side's units lose a move; (11) group 11, the king guards its pawn and its rook; (8) group 8, own units stop guarding each other. The singletons after them are small mobility and guard patterns; the strong single reasons (0.74 "rook guards king, king guards pawn", 0.57) are alone.

B, THE UNIT BORNE ON. Of the 136 reasons three are of the form "a unit of the mover's bears on a unit of theirs" (bear_form: one atom, size 1): the kind-free one (weight +0.68), the pawn on a bishop (+0.37, kind level) and the not-on-an-edge one (+0.09); the fourth match in the list, "other down", is the other side's and was not split. EXPRESSED how: NOT as patterns. A count of a size-2 pattern (the two bears onto one unit) counts a unit once for each guard, the pattern language has no negation, so "not guarded" and "not borne on" are not patterns, and an instance's two facts cannot be read from counts; the matcher's instances (match_binds) carry the units and the graph's own bear items carry the two facts, so symbols.cell_counts computes four cells in Python from the facts the layer gives (cell = 2 x guarded + borne): the unit of theirs guarded (a unit of its own side bears on it) and the bearing unit borne on (a unit of the other side bears on it). No Rust change; no worth. The totals of the four cells equal the engine's count for the parent on 739 tied moves checked by a throwaway script (not an OBS line of the run) and in the test on real positions. HOW OFTEN EACH FIRES (OBS split, 81945 tied moves of the sample, count of the cell rose / fell): the kind-free pattern: cell 0 (loose, bearer free) 2785 / 720, cell 1 (loose, bearer borne on) 1869 / 615, cell 2 (guarded, bearer free) 10491 / 7127, cell 3 (guarded, bearer borne on) 4107 / 3085; the pawn-on-bishop pattern: cell 1 232 / 160, cell 3 372 / 25, cells 0 and 2 never (a pawn that bears on a bishop is always borne on by it); the not-on-an-edge pattern: 339 / 157, 199 / 72, 1898 / 2243, 1043 / 1143. IN THE FIT (variant ii, OBS report): the kind-free pattern's cells get +0.994 (loose, bearer free), +0.226 (loose, borne on), +0.539 (guarded, bearer free) and no weight (guarded, borne on), against +0.68 for the parent; the pawn-on-bishop cells +0.541 and +0.502; the not-on-an-edge cells +0.458 and +0.310. So the split separates what the one weight blurred: the largest single weight of the model is a bearing on a unit that is loose from a bearer that is not itself borne on; "bears on a unit of theirs" with a guarded target is worth about half. Reading the cases: the king is a unit that is never guarded, so a check is a bearing on a loose unit from a free bearer and lands in the strongest cell: eight of the thirty picks below are checks.

THE RULE (fixed before looking, in the measure's doc): the best variant is the one of i, ii, iii whose events-only pick agrees most with the move played on CONFIRM in the mid and few bands pooled (it is ii); in each band the first ten CONFIRM positions in the sample's order where that pick differs from the search's first move, at most one a game. The pick differs from the first move in 94 of the few band's 132 CONFIRM positions, 276 of 362 mid, 2349 of 2791 many (OBS cases). Printed with ladder_print `--groups88 full` (cases.txt, PART B), each read against the board (which units are attacked, which guarded, printed above each board). MY JUDGEMENT of the pick against the search's first move: few better 0 same 10 worse 0; mid better 0 same 9 worse 1; many better 4 same 6 worse 0; all 4 / 25 / 1. BETTER (many): 4 (Bb4 pinning the knight and clearing the back rank for castling, over a6), 7 (Qe2 over a3), 11 (Bg5 hitting the queen, over a3), 12 (Bg7, over a6): developing moves over a wing-pawn step, as in 78.82. WORSE: 25 (a pawn pushed with check onto a place the king takes it, over a quiet move; the search holds all nine equal, so the position is probably lost anyway). SAME: the rest. In few the pick is often a check or a move of the rook (6, 14, 19, 23, 29: Rc1+, Rb7+, Qe7+, Rd6+, Rg4+) where the search holds two or many moves equal, in positions that are mostly decided; I cannot tell them from the first move in worth and a check is a better practical try than a pawn step in 19 and 23; in 5 (Rg1) and 18 (Re2) the pick is passive or loses a tempo, nothing is lost. The pick equals the move played in 6 of the 30, the first move in 8. IS THE TOP GROUP THE REAL REASON: for the development moves (4, 7, 11, 12) the top groups are guard-and-mobility groups, and in 4 and 12 group 0 "rook guards king, king guards pawn" is the real idea written in other words (the bishop leaves the back rank, the castle is ready); in 11 the group "the other side's unit may move: down" is partly the bishop's attack on the queen. For the checks (6, 14, 16, 19, 23, 24, 29) the top group is the split's cell 0 (+0.994): a bearing on a unit of theirs that is loose, from a unit not borne on: the king is the unit that is never guarded, so every check carries the model's largest weight; that is "the attacked unit is loose", true of a check and of 20 (Rc7 attacks the loose pawn on c6), but not the reason a player gives for a check. In 1, 5, 9, 10 the top group is incidental (a discovered bearing, a rook beside its king, a queen's bearing on a guarded pawn). In 25 the top group is the pawn that bears on the king and is borne on by it: the split's cell for a loose unit and a borne bearer carries +0.226, the pick's weight comes from the other groups. In 30 the first move carries no group at all (silence) and the pick has one, the king guarding a pawn; the loose pawn on h6 is the issue and it is in no group.

STILL WRONG. (a) The twins are few at the fixed threshold (11 groups of two or more): the grouping did not make the reasons "one reason one purpose"; most mobility and guard patterns remain alone, and a group is mostly a pattern with its kind-free cousin. (b) The split is of three reasons only (the rule of the plan, the mover's own bearing); it moves the model by about a point overall and in no band by a band clear of zero. (c) The bands are thin: the few fit is the controls only and the mid fit four groups, so "weights by part" was not tested fairly; more human endings are needed, not engine continuation. (d) The one-standard-error rule is hard on thin data. (e) One run each; directions. (f) The pick still does not see a unit that can be taken or lost: none of the groups is "my unit is loose" for the mover's own units; the cases 18 and 25 show it. (g) The judgement of 30 boards is mine and one reading, five of them quickly.

DEVIATIONS: none from the plan. The split covers the three reasons whose event side is the mover (the plan's "a unit of the mover's"); the fourth of the form (side other, down) was left. The "play" stage is not built (the condition was not met). Choice gained an optional field `units` (default None): 78.81's builders of Choice are unchanged.

By band of unit count on unseen positions, 78.81's pick agrees with the move played about equally often in every band (about a third), but the search's own first move agrees more as units come off, so the pick's edge is clear only in the many band and, in the mid band, only where no tied move takes a unit. Where a tied move takes a unit the pick is worse than the first move in every band.
A CORRECTION OF MY OWN WORDS in the 78.82 and 78.83 READs and to Kaveh. I called the many band "the opening" and the reasons "an opening development rule". The many band is seventeen units or more, which is the opening AND most of the middle game; the mid band, nine to sixteen, is a late middle game and early ending. What made it look like an opening rule is that the decisions read in 78.82 and for the many band of 78.83 were by rule the first of each game. Nothing measured so far separates the opening from the middle game. That is the next measurement.
A, B, C DID LITTLE. Few twins were left after 78.81's duplicate drop (136 reasons to 118 groups). Weights by part could not be tested: the human sample holds few positions with few or middling units, so those fits fall back to the controls. No play was run, by the plan's own condition.
THE JUDGED DECISIONS (the builder's, one reading, not reread by me): better 4, same 25, worse 1 of thirty; with few and middling units nearly every pick is the same in worth as the first move, many of them a move that gives a threat to the goal unit, which the largest weight favours because that unit is never guarded.
STILL MISSING IN THE REASONS: no reason for "a unit of mine is loose"; the pick for a taking.

WHY. See the correction above. Two things are not known: where inside the many band the hint earns its score, and whether the weak result with fewer units is the reasons or the thin sample (FIND holds few positions there).
PART ONE, prints and two matches, no new method. (a) 78.81's agreement on CONFIRM by a finer scale: by ply (four equal-count bins of the many band) and by unit count in steps (the many band cut in three), quiet and not, paired against the search's first move. (c) Thirty decisions from the LOWER part and the mid band, picks that differ, by a fixed rule that does not take the first decision of a game, judged against the board.
PART TWO, the sample. A second human sample drawn to cover the later game: from the same held-out games (less the ladder's games and the games of the first sample's CONFIRM part), positions taken evenly over unit-count bins instead of at most five a game early, until each bin of unit count from few to the lower many holds at least as many tie positions as the upper many bin of the first sample, or the games run out; print the coverage per bin and how far the few band falls short. Where it falls short, fill with generated games as section 10 says (our own self-play games of 78.58, the result known, never an engine continuation of a human game), marked as generated, used for FIND only. Same split by game into FIND and CONFIRM. Then: the single fit of 78.81 refitted on the wider FIND (reasons as they are, variant ii of 78.88), and the fit by band; agreement on the new CONFIRM by band against the search's first move and against the old weights.
PLAY after part two only if agreement in a band with fewer units rises with a paired band clear of zero.
INTERFACE. symbols_measure sample gains a stratified mode; nothing else new. No Rust change. Nothing written to the real store. No player ids anywhere.
READ BEFOREHAND. If the lower many part scores above half in play, the hint is a middle-game hint as well and the earlier wording was simply wrong. If only the upper part does, it is an opening hint. If the wider sample lifts agreement with fewer units, the thin sample was the cause; if not, the reasons do not hold what matters there.

### PLAN 78.90: THE MOVER'S OWN LOOSE UNIT, AND ONE FIT ON BOTH SAMPLES (2026-11-18, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 symbols as subgoals, 9 the score)

WHY. Three plans in a row name the same missing item: no reason sees that a unit of the mover's is left borne on and unguarded (78.88 the judged cases, 78.89 decisions 13, 26, 27, 29). And each sample alone is lopsided: the first holds the early game, the second the later game, and the refit on the second lost the lower many part.
A, THE REASONS. The cells of 78.88 (guarded or not, the bearing unit borne on or not) are built for the mover's own units as well: "a unit of theirs bears on a unit of the mover's", split by whether that unit of the mover's is guarded and whether the bearing unit is itself borne on. Made true and made false by the move, as every reason. Game-free words only, no worth, computed where 78.88's split is computed.
B, ONE FIT ON BOTH. FIND is the union of the two samples' FIND parts; the same joint choice fit of 78.81 (controls as there), once with the reasons as they are with variant ii, once with A added. Scored on both CONFIRM parts by band and by quiet or not, against the search's first move and against the old weights, paired bands.
C, A COUNT, no new method. On the tie positions of both CONFIRM parts: in how many tie sets does at least one tied move leave a unit of the mover's borne on and unguarded that was not so before, by band; and how often the old pick, the new pick and the search's first move is such a move.
PLAY, only if A lifts agreement over B without A in a band with the paired band clear of zero: the full player with the new fit against the control and against 78.82's player, sets A and B, uncharged, same settings.
JUDGE. Thirty decisions where the new pick differs from the old pick, ten per band, by a fixed rule, read against the board.
INTERFACE. symbols.py: split_borne gains side="theirs" (default, as now) or "own"; nothing else new. Outputs artifacts/experiments/symbols_78_90/. No Rust change expected. Nothing written to the real store. No player ids anywhere. FIND for every fit; CONFIRM only for scores.
READ BEFOREHAND. If A's weights come out as a player would expect (leaving an own unit loose strongly negative) and the worse cases go, the reasons were missing a word. If the count in C shows the search often holds such a move equal, that is the fast equal reading's fault again (78.84, 78.85) and belongs to the reasoner, not to the hint.

FOUR ON THE BOARD: 20 (a bishop of the mover's is attacked and unguarded; the old pick takes a knight with a check and leaves the bishop to be taken; the new pick takes the knight with the bishop, saving it): better, and the top reason (the bearing on the mover's loose unit made false) is the real idea. 6 (a pawn of the mover's is attacked and unguarded; the old pick pushes another pawn onto an attacked square and leaves both loose; the new pick steps the king next to the pawn, guarding it): better, the top reason real. 11 (the old pick takes a free pawn; the new pick moves a rook to an edge square to hit a guarded pawn and leaves the free pawn): worse, the top reason ("bears on a guarded unit of theirs") is not the idea. 28 (the old pick takes a knight, which will be traded back at once; the new pick retreats a knight from the attack): worse, and here the very reason that was added misfires: the negative weight on "leaves a unit of mine borne on and unguarded" is read on an exchange and on a forcing move (also 29, a rook check that leaves the rook attacked but wins through a promotion; the new pick is a quiet queen move). ### 78.90 READ (main agent, 2026-11-19; one run each, directions only; numbers from artifacts/experiments/symbols_78_90/full/obs.txt)

MERGED. Tests of the touched files passed at merge (test_plan78_90_own 11, test_plan78_88_groups 11, test_plan78_89_sample 12, test_plan78_81_reasons 14, test_plan78_82_play 12, test_plan78 17). No Rust change. The full engine gate is still owed.
THE NEW REASON. The cells for "a unit of theirs bears on a unit of the mover's" took the weights a player would expect: leaving an unguarded unit borne on is negative, ending such a bearing is among the largest positive weights. In agreement it helps with few units on the later-game sample, band clear of zero, and is level elsewhere; in the lower many part the fit on both samples is still under the old weights. Against the control the new player scored above half and a little above 78.82's player's score; head to head against 78.82's player it did not score above half. Not shown better in play.
THE COUNT, AND A LIMIT ON WHAT IT SAYS. The search's first move leaves a unit of the mover's borne on and unguarded about twice as often as the move the human played, in the many band. The builder reads this as the equal reading's fault. I do not accept that as stated: the count flags a unit that is taken back in an exchange as loose (decision 28, where the human played the flagged move), so it mixes exchanges with real losses. It is a direction to check, not a fault shown.
MY OWN READING of two decisions. Decision 28: the old pick takes a unit and the taking unit is then unguarded, but the line is an even exchange; the new reason reads it as a loss and the pick retreats instead; worse, as the builder says. Decision 20: the builder says better; I read both takings as coming to the same end (either way two units are taken for one), and call it the same. The other twenty-eight I take from the builder (better 10, same 14, worse 6 by its count; all five worse cases of the many band).
WHERE THIS LINE OF WORK STANDS. Three plans (78.88, 78.89, 78.90) have each moved agreement by about a point or two in one part and nothing in play beyond 78.82. The same two limits return each time: the pick is under the search's first move wherever a tied move takes a unit, and a pattern of one position cannot tell a unit that is lost from a unit that is exchanged; that question belongs to the line reading, which the reasoner already has. More cells will not close it. The spec's design is that the hint acts through the search's order, before the tie, and that is not yet measured.

### PLAN 78.91: THE HINT IN THE SEARCH'S ORDER (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 "subgoals enter through the prior", 5 the search's reading order)

WHY. So far the hint only chooses among moves the search already holds equal. The spec's place for it is the order in which moves are read. Whether the reasons order moves better than the search's own order of quiet moves is not known. A root order can already be given to the search (plan 78.51, set_root_order, modes strict and ties), so the first two parts need no Rust.
PART ONE, a print, no new method. On positions of both CONFIRM parts (a fixed number per band, the same for every order): the search's own best move at a long clock (ten times the play clock) is the reference; no outside engine. For each order of the legal moves, the place of that reference move: (i) the search's static order before any reading (takings by gain, then the rest as generated); (ii) the same with the quiet moves ordered by the reasons' score (78.81's weights, and 78.90's fit A); (iii) the order left by a short reading (the play clock). Print mean place, first place and first three, among quiet moves only and over all moves, by band. Also print the hint's cost per position beside the play clock.
PART TWO, only if (ii) is better than (i) among quiet moves with a paired band clear of zero in some band: the search at fixed depth with the root order given by (ii) in the mode that only breaks the search's own ties of order, against no root order: nodes to the same depth, and whether the chosen move and value are the same. Then play against the control on sets A and B, uncharged and charged, same settings as 78.89.
PART THREE is NOT built here: the order at inner nodes needs the reasons' count in Rust at well under a millisecond. Part one's cost print and part two's node count say whether that build is worth making; print where the pick's time goes (pattern count, replay, binding) so that the port can be sized.
JUDGE. Twenty positions where the reasons' order puts the reference move first and the static order does not, and ten of the opposite, by a fixed rule, read against the board.
INTERFACE. Nothing new in the layer: a measure script calling the reasons reader for a score per move and the existing root order argument. Outputs artifacts/experiments/order_78_91/. No Rust change. Nothing written to the real store.
READ BEFOREHAND. If the reasons order quiet moves no better than the static order against the search's own deeper choice, the hint has no place in the order and stays a tie-break, and the work goes to the reasoner's debts. If they do, the Rust port of the count is the next build.

Rust tests of cs_tactics and cs_decision passed, the extension in main was rebuilt, seven touched Python test files passed (test_plan78_92_choice 12, test_plan78_85_debts 9, test_plan78 17, test_plan78_50_subgoal_play 15, test_plan78_67_tiebreak 8, test_plan78_82_play 12, test_plan78_91_order 15). The switch verify_choice is off in every default; I checked the defaults in the diff.
THE DEBT IS REAL AND LARGER THAN THE EQUAL READING'S. At the depth the matches reach, the move the search plays is under the best of the same search without its two prunings, at the same depth, in roughly one position in seven; the share is not smaller at a deeper setting. The cause is the late-move reduction alone; the null move does nothing either way, in the count or in play. Two plies deeper the reference still holds most of these, against a baseline in which a deeper search changes its mind in about a tenth of positions anyway.
WHAT THE SHORTFALLS ARE. About a fifth are a game's end the reference sees. Of the rest, most are smaller than the smallest worth in the judge's table: differences between unequal worths in an exchange, which a player may call level. So the share that a player would call a mistake is well under the headline share. The builder's reading of twenty boards (with aids of its own outside the engine, one of them a count with assumed worths, which is allowed for a judge and for nothing else): eight confirmed worse, two a slower win, three an artifact of the table, seven beyond its aid, none where the reference is wrong in the judge's own units. I did not reread them.
78.90's COUNT IS ANSWERED. Of the first moves flagged as leaving a unit loose, about one in seven is a real loss by the reference and the rest are exchanges or harmless. My doubt in the 78.90 READ was right in the main, and the builder's "the reasoner's fault" was right for the smaller part.
THE LATE REDUCTION buys about two plies and a score that one run does not separate from a half. That is a surprise worth a second run: the usual belief is that it buys strength.
THE REPAIR. verify_choice asks the chosen move again without the prunings and, when it fails, takes the first move of the search's own equal reading that holds. Offline it removes about a third of the under-best cases and adds none; it cannot see the larger part, where the chosen move holds its value and a better move exists. In play the verifying player scored above the player without it, with the band clear of a half, at about a quarter of the move's clock, taken from the equal reading's slot. ONE RUN, and the condition that let it be built was met by a hair. It stays off until a second run on other openings says the same, and turning it on in play is Kaveh's decision (section 13).
A LATENT FAULT named by the builder, not fixed: best_move(verify_ties=True) goes through a path that builds its own parameters and ignores the switch (since 78.85). No measurement of 78.85 used that path (they used the batch entry); it is fixed in the next plan.
DEVIATIONS accepted: null_move and late_reduce as keywords of the batch entry and fields of Params (default as the search is); the batch row grown from twelve to fifteen with the first twelve unchanged; two node settings; the control row; three matches run on the extension built before the switch (same prunings).
SPEC CHECK of the builder: section 5 named, interfaces listed, no departure. Three silent choices (what replaces a failed choice, where the verification's time comes from, how the reference's depth is made fair) are written into section 13.

### PLAN 78.94: GOALS AS DOUBLE THREATS, IMAGINED FOR BOTH SIDES; THE FIRST MEASUREMENT (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 the future imagination layer, decided 2026-11-19; 8 the threat list; 5 the line reading)

WHY. Kaveh's decision of 2026-11-19 (section 7): a goal is a position where two threats are made at once that no one reply meets; the stake orders goals; the budget is questions, not length; both sides are imagined; among equal moves the choice is by progress toward the goals. Nothing of this is built. Before a build, a measurement says whether such goals are found at all in quiet positions and whether human moves go toward them.
INTERFACE FIRST (one module, game-free; Rust where a reading is hot, the existing bindings otherwise):
  imagine(state, side, budget) -> list of Goal. A run of side's own moves with the other side standing still (the game's pass; a state where passing is not allowed gives no goals), searched best-first, each node costing one question: "does the threat list of this position hold two threats of side's that no one reply meets, by the line reading?"
  Goal = { first: the first move of the run, run: the moves, threats: the two or more threats, stake: what the line reading says is won after the best reply (the judge's own worths, nothing assumed), questions: how many were asked }.
  The budget is N questions; past N the search goes on only inside a frame it is reading that still makes progress (an exchange in progress, a joined frame), and stops when that frame is ruled out or succeeds. N is a parameter; measured at several values.
  veto(state, goal) -> { holds | broken by: move, questions }. Layer two: with the other side moving in the gaps of the run, does the goal still come true; read by the search on the real line, not by counting.
  choose(state, equal_moves) -> move or none: imagine for both sides; if a goal of theirs survives our best run, the equal move that breaks it or meets it comes first; else the equal move that is the first move of our highest-stake goal that holds; else none (the caller falls back).
PART ONE, counts, no play. On quiet positions of both CONFIRM parts (no confirmed tactic for either side by the threat list; a fixed number per band): how often imagine finds a goal for the mover and for the other side, at several N; the length of the runs; the stakes; how many survive veto; questions and milliseconds per position.
PART TWO, the test on human moves. Where a goal of the mover's holds and its first move is among the equal moves: how often the move played is that first move, against the search's first move and against the pattern pick, paired bands. The same where the choice is a reply to their goal.
PART THREE, only if part two is clear of zero in some band: choose() as the chooser among equal moves in play against the control and against 78.82's player, sets A and B, uncharged and charged.
JUDGE. Thirty positions through ladder_print: the goal in words (which two threats, on what, the stake), the run, their best spoiling move if any; read against the board: is it a goal a player would name.
NOT IN THIS PLAN: breaking a goal that is too far into a closer one (the proposer of section 7 does part of it; left for the next plan); a learned distance; the opening prior of Kaveh's second direction (waits on section 13 item 12).
READ BEFOREHAND. If goals are rarely found within a budget the play clock can pay, the layer needs the learned shortcut before it can play, and the counts say how far off it is. If they are found and human moves do not go toward them, the definition of a goal is too narrow (two threats at once only) and the stakes or the threat list are the next thing to look at.


### PLAN 78.94 REVISED: THE FUTURE JUDGE IN THREE STEPS (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 the future imagination layer, "how it is built"; this replaces the order of PLAN 78.94 above, whose interface for a Goal is kept)

WHY. Kaveh, 2026-11-19: first a future judge trained on human game trajectories, then the winning points found in human games, then the prediction from here to those points. The plan above started with an explicit run of own moves; that run is now only the check.
THE ORACLE: not in any fit here (section 13 item 12 is open). It measures the labels, behind the ladder's wall, on a sample.
STEP TWO FIRST IN TIME, because step one needs its targets. LABELS. Over the games of both human samples and further held-out games of the month file (split by game into FIND and CONFIRM; coverage per band of unit count printed; no player ids): every position gets, for each side, whether a goal holds there (two or more threats of that side by the threat list that no one reply meets, by the line reading), its kind in game-free words (which fact patterns the two threats are, on what kind of unit by the judge's worth order), its stake, and what followed in the game within a fixed number of plies (the stake was won, part of it, nothing) and the game's result. Print how often goals occur, by band and ply, the chance each kind pays, and how the chance of winning the game moves when one occurs, beyond what the count of units already says. Oracle as a measure on a sample of some hundreds: is the goal real by its best move.
STEP ONE. THE FUTURE JUDGE. A model over the fact graph (the encoder the estimator's heads already use; one more head, nothing new invented): from a position and a side, the chance that a goal of that side holds within k plies later in the same game, for a few k, and of which kind; trained on FIND trajectories, positives and negatives from the games themselves. Also the pairwise form he asked for: given the present position and a target description in facts, the chance it comes true later; negatives are targets taken from other games and from the same game's past. Scored on CONFIRM games: calibration, ranking against the base rate by band, and against two plain baselines (the count of units and the pattern reasons of 78.81).
THE CHECK. On a sample of CONFIRM positions the explicit run of own moves of the plan above (imagine, veto) says whether a goal can be reached at all; print how the judge's chance agrees with it.
STEP THREE. From a position, the judge's chance for the mover's goals and for the other side's goals after each equal move; the equal move that most raises ours less theirs is the pick. Test on human moves as before (the move played against the search's first move and the pattern pick, paired bands, by band, quiet or not). Play only if clear of zero in some band: against the control and against 78.82's player, sets A and B, uncharged and charged.
JUDGE. Thirty positions through ladder_print: the judge's top goal in words, its chance, what happened in the game; read against the board.
INTERFACE. goals_of(state) -> per side list of Goal (as defined in the plan above); label_games(games) -> rows; FutureJudge.fit(rows), .chance(state, side, k) and .chance_of(state, target); choose(state, equal_moves) -> move or none. No decision-path crate depends on cs_learn: the judge is called from the Python side of the measure and the match player, as the reasons reader is. Outputs artifacts/experiments/future_78_94/. Nothing written to the real store.
READ BEFOREHAND. If goals are rare in human games or do not pay, the definition (two threats at once only) is too narrow and the labels say what else precedes a gain. If the judge does not beat the unit count and the patterns on CONFIRM, the encoder or the target is wrong and nothing is played.


### PLAN 78.94 REVISED, AMENDMENT (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 9 "the oracle labels positions and frames in sleep, for the prior", decided by Kaveh the same day)

The line "THE ORACLE: not in any fit here" of the revised plan is withdrawn. STEP TWO's labels are made in sleep with the oracle: for every sampled position of the human games, whether it is winning, losing or neither for the side to move (the oracle's verdict at a fixed setting, kept as a class with the setting printed, the raw number stored beside it for the record only), and at the positions where the class changes or a goal holds, the frame: the oracle's best move and line, read by our own threat list and line reading into graph facts (which threats, on which kind of unit, the stake), so that each label is a frame in our own words and not a number. Labels are made for FIND and CONFIRM games alike; the judge is fitted on FIND only.
A goal as defined (two threats no one reply meets) is one kind of frame among those found; the labels also say which frames precede a win that are NOT of that kind, which answers whether the definition is too narrow.
STEP ONE's future judge predicts those frames and the winning and losing points from earlier positions of the same game. It is a prior: it orders and chooses among equal moves and never scores a leaf. The wake calls the judge, never the oracle.
THE CHECK against the labels is our own reasoner: for a sample, does our line reading confirm the frame the oracle's line shows; print the share it cannot see, by band. That share is the reasoner's gap, a result of its own.
Kept as it was: the split by game, coverage per band, no player ids, the test on human moves, the conditions for play, the thirty judged positions, the interfaces. One disk-heavy job at a time; the oracle run is checkpointed per game and uses all cores.

INTERFACE (written before the bodies, in each module's doc): future_goals.goals_of_list / goals_of (a Goal = two or more confirmed threats of one side on different units whose sets of kept replies have nothing in common; kind "open" when one has no reply, "fork" otherwise; stake = the line reading's net); future_labels (universe, choose_games, plies_of, class_of, Labeller.label, run; the only caller of the oracle, through ladder_oracle.analyse); future_judge (rows_from_labels, Inputs, side_matrix, FutureJudge.fit / chance / fit_pair / chance_of); future_imagine (Imaginer.imagine, .veto); future_choose (Chooser.scores / choose); future_measure (stages counts, fit, score, explicit, human, cases); ladder_print --future94.

THE ORACLE: Stockfish 18 at /opt/homebrew/bin/stockfish through the existing wrapper (audit_oracle._init, the repo's tablebase path): depth 16, one line, one thread, default hash, one process a worker, 10 workers. Class: winning when it gives a forced end or scores at least 200 on its own scale, losing the same the other way, else neither (a stated choice). The raw score is stored beside the class and no fit reads it (a test perturbs it and the rows do not change). At a winning point (867): a unit is taken along the line, no threat read 41.9 pct; one threat, no goal 24.5 pct; nothing our reading names 22.6 pct; a forced end 9.8 pct; a goal (open or fork) 1.3 pct. So 856 of the 867 frames that precede a win are not two threats at once: the definition as built is too narrow for what precedes wins by a wide margin. THE REASONER'S GAP: of 3532 oracle frames our concrete list holds a threat whose first move is the oracle's first move (or a forced end) in 400; it cannot see 3132 (88.7 pct); by band few 91.5, mid 86.5, many 89.0 pct; of the frames whose line reading names nothing, 99.0 pct are unseen. (Caveat: seeing is the strict test of a taking or the quiet first move of a threat in two moves; a position whose oracle best move our search would also pick is not a gap in play.)

Direction: the judge reads the tension of a position (what stands loose and what moves) better than the unit count and the 78.81 patterns do; it was asked on rows where no goal holds yet, and what it mostly predicts is that threats are already there.

THE EXPLICIT RUN (imagine, veto; 120 quiet CONFIRM positions, 40 a band, both sides; budgets 8 and 32 questions): a goal after at least one own move was found for the mover in 3.3 pct (8 questions) and 7.5 pct (32), for the other side in 5.0 and 10.8 pct, none in the few band; 2.4 s and 8.8 s of one thread a position for the mover. PLAY (stage five): the condition (a band clear of zero against the first move) is met in the many band, not against the pattern pick as a whole; the matches were NOT played here (time; the machine was held by the labels, the pass-by-pass match player was not built). Left for the next plan.

THIRTY POSITIONS read against the board (cases.txt). Goal positions: 1 (two loose pawns, the king takes them: a player names it; the oracle prefers a queenside break), 3 (Qxg5+ wins the bishop with check: right), 4 (queen takes the bishop with check, then the loose pawn: right, the judge's 0.715 for a goal or winning point within 8 plies is sensible), 6 (two loose pawns in a race that ends drawn: the goal is real, its worth is not), 5 and 7 (mate in two and in four: the pawn goal the reading prints is not what a player names, the forced end is); 8 and 10 (the other side's two pawns about to promote: the reading says a goal of stake 4343 / 7641 and a forced end, the judge 0.69 for them: a player would say 'promotion', not 'two pawns'). Frames not two threats: 11 (the oracle's quiet Bg3, no threat read, a player sees a developing-versus-structure choice), 12 (king-and-pawns ending, oracle winning, humans drew: nothing named), 14 and 15 (one threat after three plies, plausible). Judge-high positions 21 to 30 are sharp middle-games (loose and attacked units on both sides); the judge's 0.3 to 0.45 for either within 8 plies looks sensible, five of the ten saw a winning point within eight plies; frame None there because no class change or goal made one. Four on the board: 4 (black queen c7, white bishop c5 and pawn a5 loose, queen takes with check: a clean won-material goal), 5 (white to move, the goal printed is on bishop c8 and pawn f7, the real frame is the check on d3 and the rook mate: the reading misses that the forced end is the frame), 9 (white loses the queen or the bishop a3 on the diagonal; a player names 'the queen and bishop are both loose', a real double threat, though the oracle's class is only -309), 12 (two connected pawn pairs: the oracle says won at 20000, a tablebase verdict; the humans drew; the judge's 0.23 is low-ish but not wrong for a position where humans do draw it).

WHAT IS STILL WRONG. (a) Goals as defined are rare (under 1 pct) and the one-threat and quiet frames dwarf them: the definition does not cover what precedes wins. (b) The goal reading's replies are the frame read's and the sweep's; a goal can stand when a counter-threat meets both. (c) The 'seen' test of the gap is strict. (d) One run on 900 games; the goal heads have 123 to 377 CONFIRM positives; the match was not played. (e) The veto is one line, the search's. (f) Win and losing heads are mirrors; only win is fitted. (g) Classes at depth 16 flip two plies later in 3411 of 3532 frame positions: the class threshold is noisy near its edge. (h) The sample's tie positions are mostly opening-to-middle, where the judge's edge is largest in the many band. (i) A frame is read at 1, 3 and 5 plies of the oracle's line only.

DEVIATIONS from the plans: stage five not run; the goal head's population excludes rows where a goal already holds; the imagine run's order uses the quiet first moves of threats in two moves and takings first, and a named fuse of 8 questions past the budget; statements read in a worth are left out of the judge's inputs; L heads not fitted; the pairwise targets are descriptions of goals only (frames are not targets); judge.pkl and the label files are in the untracked folder.

### 78.94 READ (main agent, 2026-11-19; one run each, directions only; numbers from artifacts/experiments/future_78_94/full/obs.txt)

MERGED. Tests of the touched files passed at merge (test_plan78_94_future 15, test_plan78 17, test_plan78_68_ladder 10). No Rust change. Stages one to four were built; the match play of stage five was not run.
WHAT A GOAL IS, MEASURED. A goal as decided (two confirmed threats that no one reply meets) is rare in human games: well under one position in a hundred. Where one holds it pays: in most cases units are won within a few plies, against about one case in five without one, and it goes with winning the game well beyond what the count of units says. So the definition picks out something real.
BUT IT IS NOT WHAT PRECEDES MOST WINS IN THESE GAMES. Of the oracle's frames at a point where a side becomes winning, almost none are two threats at once. The largest groups are a unit simply taken with no threat read before it, one threat alone, and a line our reading names nothing for. In human games at this level a win mostly starts when the other side leaves something to be taken or fails to meet ONE threat. This fits Kaveh's own words of the same day (chances of frame outcomes as played, not best play): against a player who errs, one threat has a chance of paying, and that chance is what the prior should carry. It is a finding to put to him, not a change I make to his definition.
THE FUTURE JUDGE (the estimator's inputs, linear and tree heads, FIND only) predicts a goal some plies ahead clearly better than the count of units and better than the pattern counts; it predicts a winning point only a little better than either. The pairwise form (position, target) did not beat the target's own frequency. As a chooser among equal moves it agrees with the move played a little more than the search's first move overall, much more with many units, less with few; against the pattern pick it is level overall, much better where a tied move takes a unit and worse on quiet positions with many units. The two picks are good in different places.
THE EXPLICIT RUN of own moves finds a goal in a small share of quiet positions and the search's reply spoiled every one of them. A goal that is some own moves away is, as built, never reached against a replying side.
THREE THINGS I DO NOT ACCEPT AS STATED.
(1) "Our reasoner cannot see about nine oracle frames in ten." The test asks that our list of confirmed threats holds a threat whose first move is the oracle's first move. A quiet best move or a plain retaking fails that test without the reasoner being blind. It says our THREAT LIST does not name most of what the oracle plays, which matters for building frames from it, not that the search misses it.
(2) The goal test has false alarms. I read position 9 against the board: the other side is said to hold a goal on two units, and the mover has one move that takes one unit out of the threat and guards the other with it, which is also the oracle's move. The set of replies the test tries is not complete. The counts of goals are therefore an upper count.
(3) The oracle's class at a fixed edge is unstable from ply to ply by the builder's own count, so "a winning point" is a noisy label near the edge.
I read position 9 only; the other twenty-nine judgements are the builder's.
DEVIATIONS accepted: no play; the judge on the estimator's inputs and not a new network; statements that read a worth left out of the inputs; the legal-prefix cut of an oracle line the kernel refused.
SPEC CHECK of the builder: sections and interfaces named, no departure. Its silent choices are written into section 13.


### PLAN 78.95: WHAT PRECEDES A WIN, COUNTED FAIRLY; ONE THREAT AND ITS CHANCE; THE TWO PICKS TOGETHER IN PLAY (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 the future imagination layer and "the prior learns the tactical situations ... probabilistic outcomes of frames", 9 the oracle in sleep)

WHY. 78.94 left three doubts of measurement and one finding: most wins in human games start from one threat or a unit left to be taken, not from two threats at once.
PART ONE, the measurements made fair (no new method; the labels of 78.94 are reused, no new oracle run unless a count needs it).
(a) The goal test's replies: every legal reply is tried, not a kept list; a reply meets a threat when after it the line reading no longer confirms that threat. Recount the goals and what follows them; print how many of 78.94's goals fall.
(b) The reasoner against the oracle's frames, three questions kept apart: does our search at the play clock play or hold equal the oracle's first move; given the oracle's first move, does our line reading confirm the gain; does our threat list name it. By band and by kind of frame.
(c) The label's edge: a winning point counts only if the class holds at the next position of the same side as well; print how many points remain and redo the frame kinds on them.
PART TWO, one threat and its chance. For each kind of frame that precedes a stable winning point (a unit left to be taken; one threat; two threats; a forced end; none named), from FIND games: how often the side that could do it did it, and how often the other side met it when it could, by band. These are the chances of frame outcomes as played. A head of the future judge per kind: the chance that such a frame holds for the mover within k plies, and for the other side.
PART THREE, the chooser. Among equal moves, each move is scored by what it changes in those chances (ours less theirs), weighted by the stake in the judge's own worths and by the chance the frame pays as played; settings chosen on FIND. The test on human moves as in 78.94, against the search's first move, the pattern pick and 78.94's judge.
PART FOUR, play, with the early stop: the chooser of part three, and the plain joining of the two picks of 78.94 (the judge where a tied move takes a unit, the patterns otherwise), each against the control and against 78.82's player, sets A and B, 0.2 s, uncharged; charged only for a player that is ahead uncharged. The match player calls the judge, never the oracle.
JUDGE. Thirty positions: ten goals that fall under (a), ten frames of one threat with the chance they pay, ten picks of the chooser that differ from both other picks; read against the board.
INTERFACE. future_goals.goals_of gains complete=True; future_labels gains stable points; FutureJudge gains heads by kind; Chooser gains the weighted form; a match player in a new module calling them. No Rust change expected. Outputs artifacts/experiments/future_78_95/. Nothing written to the real store.
READ BEFOREHAND. If the fair counts leave the picture as it is, the prior's target is "a frame that pays as played", of which two threats at once is the rare strong case, and that is put to Kaveh as a change to the definition. If play shows the joined pick ahead of 78.82's player, that is the first gain in play since 78.82.

Position 26 (black to move, a2 pawn and f8 rook attacked, Qf3+ available): Kg8 chosen by the chooser lets white take the a2 pawn... a strong player prefers the check Qf3+ the human played; the weights give the pick a reading of +0.3 on every kind for the king move against +0.1 to +0.2 for the checking queen move, and no kind of frame names the check. Position 29 (black with a pawn capture dxc4 available among 19 equal moves, Ng4 chosen): every reading is +0.0; the chooser is silent in effect and picks a knight move to the edge.

WHAT IS STILL WRONG. (a) One run each; the sample of games is the one of 78.94 (900 games). (b) The complete test tries replies by the line reading's confirmation of the taking where the unit stands: a castling reply moves a second unit that this does not follow, and a reply that meets a threat by losing more elsewhere still counts as meeting it. (c) Complete goals are computed only at the 148 positions that had a kept goal; that no goal was missed is shown there (scope all) and by the containment of the kept replies, not at all positions. (d) The kind of a frame comes from the oracle's stored line cut at the first move the engine refuses and read after 1 and 3 plies (the winning side X) or 2 and 4 plies (Y): a longer line may hold a threat the reading did not reach; two threats has 39 stable winning points and 54 and 103 positives on CONFIRM. (e) The chances as played condition on the oracle's first move being played, which makes the class hold by construction; "pays" is not independent of "did". (f) The stake of a kind is the material of the stored line in the record's worths (negative for none named); no worth is assumed, but none named has a stake of 0 by the floor. (g) The chooser's per-kind readings are small outside the endings; the weights equal the chance that a frame pays, which is almost the same for every kind, so the chooser behaves like one sum over the five heads. (h) The matches were played with other work on the machine only before the waits (loads 2.3 to 3.9 at each start), and two stopped early. (i) The charged chooser loses about a ply, which the 200 ms per tie decision explains.

DEVIATIONS from the plan: part one (a) tries the complete replies only where the kept test already finds a goal (reason in the module doc and in item (c) above); the frames are read at every winning or losing position from the stored line, not only at class changes; the chances "as played" are defined by the oracle line's first and second moves (written in cmd_chances before the counts); the weights of the chooser use the record's worths of the stored line's material; the ten goals of the judge group are from CONFIRM games; labels.jsonl and inputs.npz of 78.94 were copied into the new folder; scripts/future95_matches.sh and future95_charged.sh run the matches.
TESTS: tests/test_plan78_95_frames.py 15 passed; tests/test_plan78_94_future.py 15 passed; tests/test_plan78.py 17 passed; tests/test_plan78_68_ladder.py 9 passed. No full gate. No Rust change; the editable install was not moved.


### 78.95 READ (main agent, 2026-11-19; one run each, directions only; numbers from artifacts/experiments/future_78_95/full/obs.txt)

MERGED. Tests of the touched files passed at merge (test_plan78_95_frames 15, test_plan78_94_future 15, test_plan78 17). No Rust change. All four parts were built and the matches played with the early stop.
THE PICTURE OF 78.94 STANDS. With every legal reply tried, about half of 78.94's goals fall and none new appear, so two threats at once are rarer still. At the positions the oracle calls winning and that stay winning, the frame is mostly a unit left to be taken, one threat, or nothing our reading names; two threats at once are well under one in a hundred. Note that this count is over every winning position that holds, not only the points where a side becomes winning as in 78.94; it is a different and larger set, and the two are not to be compared row by row.
THE COMPLETE REPLY TEST OVERCORRECTS. I read position 3 against the board. The test says the pair of threats falls because of an in-between move that gives up the strongest unit for nothing, and a second reply that still loses a unit two plies later. Neither meets the threats in a player's sense. The builder's own note says the same of the rule (a reply that meets a threat by losing more elsewhere still counts), and its reading of that position as "a player agrees" is not accepted. So the count by kept replies is an upper count and the count by every reply a lower count; the truth is between them. Both are far under one position in a hundred, which is what matters here.
THE REASONER AGAINST THE ORACLE, asked fairly. At the winning points that hold, the search at the play clock plays the oracle's first move or holds it equal with its own in about three cases in four; the line reading confirms the gain in about two in five; the threat list names it in one in five. So 78.94's "nine in ten unseen" was the third question only, as I said then. Two things follow. In about one case in four the search prefers another move outright. And in about one case in three the oracle's move is among the equal moves but is not the one played, which is exactly the room a choice among equal moves has.
CHANCES AS PLAYED. The line's first move is played by the humans in about half the cases for a unit left to be taken and less for the other kinds. That the class "holds when the move was played" is close to true by construction and is not a chance of paying; the builder says so. The weights built from it are therefore weak.
HEADS BY KIND predict each kind of frame some plies ahead better than the count of units, and better than the patterns for a unit left to be taken and for one threat. As a CHOOSER the kind-weighted form is no gain: level with the search's first move in agreement, below the pattern pick and below 78.94's judge. Its readings are near zero outside the endings, so its picks there are noise (the builder's judged positions 21 to 30 say the same).
THE PLAIN JOINING of the two picks (the judge where a tied move takes a unit, the patterns otherwise) agrees with the human's move more than either pick alone.
PLAY. Both players are ahead of the control uncharged. Neither is ahead of 78.82's player: both pooled bands hold a half. Charged, only the joined pick stays above a half against the control. The condition written beforehand (the joined pick ahead of 78.82's player) is NOT met. The machine's load was high at the end of every match, as before, and two matches stopped early.
WHAT THIS ADDS UP TO. Three different choosers among equal moves (the patterns of 78.82, the judge of 78.94, the joining) all land at about the same score against the control and level with each other. Agreement with the human's move went up and play did not. Either the choice among equal moves is worth about this much and no more, or agreement with humans is the wrong target for it. The measurement that tells the two apart is the oracle's class of each equal move: how often is there a move among the equals that keeps the class while another loses it, and how often does each chooser take it.
DEVIATIONS accepted: the complete test only where the kept test finds a goal (containment shown); frames read at every winning or losing position; the definitions of met, stable, kind, chance and stake, which the spec does not give and which go to section 13. One `rm -f` on a file of its own, against the brief; no harm.
SPEC CHECK of the builder: sections and interfaces named, no departure.


### PLAN 78.96: WHERE THE CLASS IS LOST, THE SEARCH OR THE CHOICE; A PRIOR FITTED ON WHICH EQUAL MOVE KEEPS IT (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 the prior and the future imagination layer, 9 "the oracle labels positions and frames in sleep, for the prior")

WHY. Three choosers among equal moves score the same in play. Before a fourth is built, measure the room: at how many positions do the equal moves differ in the oracle's class, and who takes the right one. Kaveh's words of 2026-11-19 are that the oracle names winning and losing positions in sleep and the prior is trained on them; this is that, applied to the positions each equal move leads to.
PART ONE, the room (sleep; the oracle as a labeller). A sample by game from the labelled games of 78.94, all three classes of the side to move, spread over the bands, FIND and CONFIRM kept apart. At each position: the search at the play clock, its set of equal moves, its own first move. The oracle, at the setting of 78.94, gives the class of the position after each equal move, and after the oracle's own best move. Print by band and by class of the position: the share where the equal moves differ in class (the room of a choice); the share where no equal move keeps the class though the oracle's move does (the search's part); the share where each of the search's first move, the pattern pick, the judge of 78.94, the joined pick and a random pick keeps the class. A short run on a few hundred positions first, with the count of oracle calls and the time printed, then the full sample sized to about an hour.
PART TWO, the prior. Fitted on FIND positions where the equal moves differ in class: which equal move keeps the class. Inputs are what the two existing picks already read (the change in fact patterns the move makes, and the estimator's inputs after the move); no new facts, no number of the oracle among the inputs, the class of the moves is the target only. One linear and one tree head, chosen on FIND. On CONFIRM: the share of positions where its pick keeps the class, against every pick of part one, with bands by game, by band of units.
PART THREE, play, only if part two is ahead of the pattern pick on CONFIRM by a clear band: the new pick against the control and against 78.82's player, sets A and B, 0.2 s, uncharged, with the early stop; charged only if ahead uncharged. The match player calls the fitted prior, never the oracle; the wall test of 78.95 is repeated for the new module.
JUDGE. Twenty positions where the equal moves differ in class: ten where the new pick keeps it and the pattern pick does not, ten the other way; read against the board, saying whether a player would call the moves equal at all.
INTERFACE. A new module for the labelled equal moves (takes positions and a search setting, returns for each the equal moves and the class after each; called by the measure only); a fitted pick with the same call as the existing Chooser (takes a position and its equal moves, returns one); a match player as in future_play. No Rust change expected. Outputs artifacts/experiments/prior_78_96/. Nothing written to the real store.
READ BEFOREHAND. If the equal moves seldom differ in class, the choice among equals has little room and the next work is the search's part (the quarter of winning points where it prefers another move, and the line reading that confirms only two gains in five). If they often differ and no pick takes the right one much more than random, the facts the picks read do not carry it. If the fitted prior takes it and play follows, that is the first prior trained on the oracle's labels that gains in play.

THE ROOM IS REAL AND MOSTLY UNTAKEN. In the sample (stratified by class and band, so shares of the sample, not of games) the equal moves differ in the class kept at about one position in eight, more with many units and most where the position is neither winning nor losing. Some equal move keeps the class nearly always. In play it is ahead of the control, charged as well, and LEVEL with 78.82's player. Its scores against the control come from matches stopped early after few games, which reads high; the full matches against 78.82's player are the ones to trust.
SO FOUR CHOOSERS ARE LEVEL IN PLAY, and now there is a reason in numbers: in the room they differ from each other by a few points while the distance to what is there is some thirty points. The inputs they read (the change in fact patterns, the estimator's inputs after the move) do not carry most of what separates a move that keeps the class from one that loses it.
WHAT THE BOARD SAYS. I read position 1: the search holds giving up the stronger unit for a weaker one equal with five quiet moves that keep the win, and plays it first. The builder read seven and found the same kind of thing in most: the sets called equal hold moves a player would never call equal. So a good part of the room is not a choice among good moves; it is the equal reading at the play clock letting a losing move in. That is the reasoner's business more than the prior's.

### PLAN 78.97: WHY A LOSING MOVE IS HELD EQUAL, AND WHAT THE VERIFIED CHOICE TAKES OF THE ROOM (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 5 the tactical reasoner's equal reading and the verified choice, 9 the oracle as a measure and labeller in sleep)

WHY. The room of 78.96 is large and no chooser takes much of it, and on the board many of the losing moves in it are not equal to a player. Before any further prior, find what would tell them apart. This also pays a debt of 78.93: why the verified choice moves the score while replacing so few choices.
THE DATA. The labelled equal moves of 78.96 (artifacts/experiments/prior_78_96/full), room positions only, FIND and CONFIRM. No new oracle run is needed for parts one and two.
PART ONE, what our own reading says with more of it. For every equal move of a room position, our own search's value of that move: at the play clock, at five times it and at twenty-five times it, and at the play clock with the prunings off. Print, by band and class, the share of class-losing equal moves that leave the equal set under each, and the share of class-keeping moves that leave it (the price). This says how much of the room is depth, how much is the prunings, and how much our reading does not see at any clock tried.
PART TWO, the verified choice. With verify_choice on, for the search's first move, the pattern pick and the prior of 78.96: the share of room positions where the move finally played keeps the class, against the same with it off; how often the verification replaced the choice; and of the replacements, how many went from losing the class to keeping it and how many the other way. One line that answers the debt of 78.93.
PART THREE, what kind of loss it is. For the class-losing equal moves that stay equal at every clock of part one: from the oracle's stored line after the move, whether units are lost within six plies (a tactic our reading misses) or not (a slow loss, the value's business). By band. For the tactical ones, which statement of the line reading or threat list is absent or wrong at the position after the move, as a count by kind.
JUDGE. Twenty class-losing equal moves that stay equal at the longest clock, ten of each kind of part three, read against the board: what a player sees that our reading does not.
INTERFACE. A measure module only, calling the search through its existing bindings (best_move, solve_equals_batch, move_value) and reading 78.96's labels; nothing in the decision path changes and no switch is turned on in play. No Rust change expected. Outputs artifacts/experiments/room_78_97/. No matches.
READ BEFOREHAND. If a longer clock or the prunings off empties most of the room, the lever is how the reasoner spends its time on the equal moves, and the verified choice is the first form of it. If most of the room stays at every clock and is tactical, the lever is a missing reading. If it stays and is slow, the lever is the value, and the prior cannot stand in for it.

DEFINITIONS made here (not in the spec; to section 13): THE ROOM is 78.96's positions where some equal moves keep the class and some do not (2594: FIND 1332, CONFIRM 1262). A move LEAVES a set when it is in 78.96's set and not in the set a setting holds; a run cut by the clock or failed has no answer and is left out. The settings: r1 (the play clock again, the noise control), 5 times and 25 times the clock, the play clock with the late reduction and the null move off, and `on` (verify_choice, mode slot). STUCK = a class-losing move that stays at 5 times, 25 times and prunings off. TACTICAL = after the longest even number of plies (at most six) of the oracle's line after the move the mover has lost more than the other side in the measured worths (future_frames.material_net), or the oracle gives a forced end against the mover inside it; otherwise SLOW. The kind of the missing statement for a tactical move, the first that applies: absent (the threat list does not name the other side's first reply), unconfirmed (named, the line reading does not say CONFIRMED), unheld (the search at the play clock does not hold the reply), all present. For part two the "off" arm is r1 and the "on" arm is the run with verify_choice; a pick is made on the set its run handed back (the verification touches the search's own move only; there is no call that asks a named move the verified question and none was added).

### 78.98 READ (main agent, 2026-11-19; one run, directions only; numbers from artifacts/experiments/equal_78_98/full/obs.txt)

MERGED. Tests of the touched files passed on main (test_plan78_98_equal 8, test_plan78 17, test_plan78_68_ladder 10). Part one only, as the plan says for cause (a): no mend, no Rust change, no match.
THE RULE, as the code has it: a root move is equal when its answer at the finished depth is at least the position's value, with no margin, in the judge's integers; and the judge in the equal reading is the measured record of worths summed over the takings of the line. The estimator is not in it.
THE CAUSE. Of the stuck moves whose replies our reading states in full, about five in six are held equal because the judge's value of the two lines really is the same, at the play depth and two plies on, in every band. A small part is the pruned search's value being too low (the debt of 78.84, small here) and a small part is a loss two plies past the depth.
WHY THE VALUES ARE THE SAME. The record the search plays with (the odds record of 78.61) orders the kinds with the unit a player holds second strongest BELOW the two a player holds weaker, and its stated half widths are several times the gaps between those three. So giving that unit for one of the others reads as a small gain. 78.61's own READ said the order below the top was not settled; the search has played with that unsettled order since. The two other measured records (self-play results, human results) order the kinds as a player does, with narrow half widths. Reading the same positions under either takes about a third of the stuck moves out of the equal sets, at a price of about a ninth of the class-keeping ones, which is what twenty-five times the clock bought in 78.97 at no cost in time.
ALSO IN THE COUNT, and not a matter of the record: in about half of the cases the class-keeping move reaches the very same exchange a move later, so the judge sees no difference between taking now and keeping the choice; and many stuck lines give a unit of the weakest kind for nothing while the position's value already has the mover losing a unit whatever it plays. These are the leaf's business (what is the position worth beyond the takings), not the record's.
AGAINST 78.76. I read then that the record is not the main cause of the open surprises on the ladder, and that still stands for the ladder's puzzles. In play, on the choice among equal moves, it is the clearest single cause found. The two readings are of different things.
NOT ACCEPTED AS STATED: nothing. The builder's extra stage (the same reading under the other records) was not in the plan and is the most useful thing in it; accepted.
THE DECISION IS KAVEH'S: which measured record judges. All three are fitted on results and none is put in by hand, so no rule is touched by a change; but it is the judge of every reading, so I do not change the default. Section 13 item 18. What I can do without his word is measure it in play.
SPEC CHECK of the builder: sections named (it corrects my plan's section numbers: the equal reading is section 4, the value 5), no departure.

WHY. What is left in the room is mostly moves the unit count cannot tell apart, and a good part of the room's labels sit on the class edge. From 79.00's labelled equal moves: a move FIRMLY loses when the oracle's class after it is lower than before, the second asking agrees, and the oracle's number is away from the class edge by a margin chosen on FIND; FIRMLY keeps likewise. For each equal move of a firm-room position: the line the search's value comes from (79.00's trace gives it for the losing moves; the same trace for the keeping ones), the position at its end, and the estimator's chance for the mover there. FIND and CONFIRM by game, by band. Short run first.
PART THREE, the debt (measure only). For the cause-(b) moves of 79.00 in the firm room: does asking the equal question of each candidate with the prunings off, at the same depth, inside the time the verified choice now spends, put them out, and at what price in keeping moves.
NOT IN THIS PLAN: any engine change, any match. If part two is clearly ahead on CONFIRM, the next plan puts the estimator under the record as a second key at the leaf, behind a switch that is off, and plays it.

### PLAN 79.02: WHAT THE EQUAL SET HOLDS WHEN THE READING IS CUT OR PRUNED, AND THE MEND (2026-11-19, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 4 the equal reading and the verified choice, 12 the debt of plan 78.84)

WHY. Moves whose own line, read at the same depth, is worth far less than the first move sit in the equal set (79.01 positions 2, 3, 5; cause (b) of 79.00, about a quarter of the losing equal moves). The equal reading is cut by the clock in more than a fifth of decisions. A set called equal must hold only moves the reasoner has asked and held; a move not asked, or held by a pruned answer that the same search would overturn, is not known to be equal.
SEARCH FIRST. The code of the equal reading (ledger.rs, Search::ties; the binding's EqualsLedger) and plans 78.84, 78.85, 78.92, 78.97, 78.98 for what is done on a cut and with which bounds a move is held. State it in plain words before measuring.
PART ONE, the count (no engine change). On the firm room of 79.01 at the play clock under the human-result record: for each equal move, was it asked before the cut or not; was its answer from a reduced or null-move line; the share of firmly losing and of firmly keeping equal moves in each case, by band. And the same for all sampled positions of 79.00, not only the room, so the price is seen.
PART TWO, the mend, only what part one supports, behind a switch that is off by default in Params with a Rust test, the binding row's first elements unchanged. Candidates, each generic: (i) a move not asked before the cut is not in the set (the first move always is); (ii) the order of asking follows the deepening's own order of moves, so the cut drops the least likely; (iii) a move held only by a reduced line is asked once more unreduced while the slot lasts, the pick's or first move's rivals first. No new time: inside the equal reading's present slot.
PART THREE, the measure. Firm room, FIND to choose and CONFIRM to report: firmly losing moves put out, firmly keeping moves put out, the first move and the pick firmly keeping the class, the size of the set, depth. Then play only if CONFIRM is clearly better: the stack's player with the mend against without, with the pick on both sides, human-result record, sets A and B, 0.2 s, min_pairs=60, sanity first.
JUDGE. Positions 2, 3, 5 of 79.01 and twelve more where a firmly losing move leaves the set: is it gone for the reason the count says, and what is played.
INTERFACE. Part one a measure module over the bindings (reuse leaf_firm, leaf_debt, equal_trace). The mend in rust/engine in the reasoner, switch off by default. Outputs artifacts/experiments/cut_79_02/. Nothing in play changes by default; nothing written to the real store.
READ BEFOREHAND. If unasked or reduced holds carry a good part of the firmly losing moves, the mend is a repair of the reasoner and the debt of 78.84 closes. If they carry little, the equal reading is sound as it is at this clock and what is left is the value's inputs, which waits for Kaveh's word on the estimator's heads (section 13).



### 79.02 BUILT (builder agent, 2026-11-19 02:10, branch worktree-agent-a665e721df6138462; serves SYSTEM_SPEC 4 the equal reading and the verified choice, 12 the debt of plan 78.84; piece: tactical reasoning, the equal reading; part one and the measure of the mend are MEASURE modules, the mend is an engine change behind a switch `reask` OFF by default; one run each, directions only; every number is an OBS line of artifacts/experiments/cut_79_02/full/obs.txt (and full5x, short), untracked; no oracle call was made, the wall test is kept; no match was played because the rule written beforehand was not met)

WHAT THE CODE DOES ON A CUT, stated before any number (cut_count.STATEMENT, first line of obs.txt). The equal reading (ledger.rs `Search::ties`, `probes`; the binding's `EqualsLedger`/`equals_one`) asks the root moves one after the other in a fixed order (the moves that gain first, best gain first, then the rest by their number in the game's list: `ordered`, NOT the deepening's own order), each "at least v at the depth D the deepening finished?" by a null window on the table the deepening left warm, with the late-move reduction and the null move on. A move is equal iff the answer is v or more. When the slot's clock stops it, `probes` stops: the answers given stay, the move being asked and every later move are dropped. So a move not asked before the cut is NOT in the set (the set is too small, not unsound): candidate (i) of the plan is already how the code behaves. The one exception is the move the search plays, which the binding adds to the set whatever the reading did. A move is held by ONE kind of answer: the pruned null-window answer, a bound that may be a reduced one (the late-move reduction reads a late quiet reply two plies shallower, the null move reads a pass shallow) and that the table stores as a full one; the played move is held by the deepening's own value, and by one unpruned asking when the verified choice is on.
INTERFACE. cut_out (output folder, OBS lines; no oracle), cut_count (pure: hold_kind, first_state, dropped, equal_moves; CutTracer over the engine's audit; run, count), cut_mend (pure: labels_of, put_out, pick_state, put_out_reasons, conditions; Mend: the stack's search with the switch as a parameter; run, rule, count, cases), cut_play (the match: the two sides differ in the switch alone), ladder_print --cut02. ### 79.02 READ (main agent, 2026-11-19; one run, directions only; numbers from artifacts/experiments/cut_79_02/full/obs.txt)

The switch reask is in the reasoner and OFF by default; nothing in play changed.
MY GUESS ABOUT THE CUT WAS WRONG. On a cut the code drops the move being asked and every later one, so a cut makes the equal set smaller and never lets an unasked move in. The one exception is the played move, which is always in. The set is not unsound for lack of asking.
REDUCED HOLDS ARE A PART, NOT THE MAIN PART. A move held only by a reduced reading (mostly the late-move reduction) is far more often a losing one, but such moves are about one firmly losing equal move in nine in the firm room. About four in five firmly losing moves are held by the plain answer too.
THE MEND WORKS AS BUILT AND DOES NOT MOVE THE CHOICE. With the switch on, more firmly losing moves leave than the clock's own noise removes, at a small price in keeping moves, inside the clock; but the second asking reaches about two of twelve held moves a position, and the pick keeps the class no more often. The rule written before CONFIRM was not met, so no match was played. Five times the clock did not make it reach further. The switch stays off; whether it is ever worth turning on is not shown.
SO THE DEBT OF 78.84 IS NOW SIZED: it is real, it is the reductions, and it is a small part of what is left. Most of what is left is plain holds: the judge's value cannot tell the moves apart. That is the value's inputs.
ONE NEW THING, counted late and labelled so by the builder: in about one firm-room position in seventeen some root move's full value at the finished depth is ABOVE the value the search reports for the position. Position 2 of 79.01 is one: a move that wins the strongest unit is there at that depth and the search's value says nothing is won. That is not about equal moves at all; it is the search not playing the best move it could read at its own depth. It has only been counted in the firm room, where it is not the common case of play.
