### PLAN 79.17: CAN WE MATE? THE MEASURE OF PROGRESS BROUGHT INTO THE NEW ENGINE, MINED FROM GOOD AND BAD GAMES, HELD BY THE WAKE AS A GOAL BEYOND THE HORIZON (2026-11-20, main agent, at Kaveh's go; SYSTEM_SPEC 7 the last two blocks before section 8, 8 the rule for choosing a move and the wall, 9 sleep, 4 memory, 11; pieces: opportunity policy, sleep, wake)

LEDGER ROWS MOVED: 35 (a measure of progress), 23 (the chain of goals ends inside the horizon), 13 (a subgoal held across moves and dropped for a stated cause), 24 (a subgoal reached is counted as an event to train on), 25 (subgoals mined from good and bad games). WHY THESE FIRST: Kaveh's direction of 2026-11-20 names them, and they are one mechanism: the far goal is the end of the game, the subgoal inside the horizon is "the measure one step lower", the reaching of it is the event, the holding of it is the memory. Rows 5, 17, 26 wait: the small endings have no line's end to estimate that the measure does not already say, and no human data is read here.
WHY. Six plans left the whole level with the bare search because every goal made lies inside the search's horizon. The endings of a few units against a lone unit are the smallest case where the goal lies far beyond it. October's system solved one of them with a mined measure; nothing of that is in rust/engine.
SEARCH FIRST (print the table before code). `technique_miner.py`, `technique_measures.py`, `technique_sample.py`, `technique_question.py`, `technique_corpus.py` (plans 73.5, 73.5b, 73.6: the atoms, the compositions, the criterion "a drop within d of our moves against every reply, or the floor", the lesson that the table's own moves are a poor teacher); Lean `Ideas/Core/ForcedByMeasure.lean` and `Ideas/Generated/Measures.lean` (cite, change nothing); `rust/engine/tactics/src/toward.rs` (the AND-OR search with a leaf oracle: the question "can the measure be made lower against every reply" is that search with the leaf "the measure is below the held value"); `sheet/base_graph.rs` (places, steps, edge distance, bearing: what the atoms are built from); `carry.rs` (what is kept from move to move); `goals.rs`, `rule.rs`, `wall.rs` (where a held goal orders and chooses); `goal_reach.py` (the count of goals reached). Reuse, duplicate none.
PART A, THE TEST BEFORE ANYTHING (a measure, Python harness, no engine change). Two classes: two of the long-moving units and the lone leader against a lone leader; one such unit and the leader against a lone leader. Starting positions drawn at random from the class's won positions, the stronger side to move, both colours. The defender is the table's reply that holds longest; a second defender is the old player. The attackers: the wake as on main, and the old player, at 0.2 s and 2.0 s a move. Printed for each cell: games, wins inside the game's own rule on quiet plies, mean plies to the end, games ended by repetition or by the quiet-ply rule, and the table's distance at the start by bins. The table is read only by the harness (the defender, the label of a start as won); the attacker never sees it. A short run of ten games a cell first. If the wake already wins every game of the two-unit class at 0.2 s, say so: that class is then inside the horizon and the one-unit class is the test.
PART B, THE MEASURE AS A PIECE, Rust, game-free, unit tests first. Interface first, in the module's doc comment: a TERM is a composition (one atom; the sum or product of two; a tuple compared in order) of ATOMS read from the base graph with the units of the two sides as variables and no name of the game: the count of places a unit can walk to by its own steps over places the other side does not bear on, the area that set spans along the board's lines, a unit's distance in its own steps to the nearest place of fewest steps and to the nearest edge, the distance in steps between two units, per line-direction distances between two units and to an edge, whose turn. `measure::value(term, graph, state, side)` returns the tuple of numbers; it is a pure function of the position. Tests: against October's Python readings on a fixed set of positions (the test file may use the game's renderer; the crate may not); one negative control.
PART C, THE MINER, in sleep (a Python driver over part B; all cores). For each class two sets of games and a third kept apart: GOOD, games that reached the end by steady play (the attackers of part A that won, and generated games in which the stronger side wins); BAD, games that kept the win by the table's label and did not reach the end (the attackers of part A that drew, and a generated attacker that moves at random among the moves the table still calls won); TABLE, the table's own shortest lines, used only to test October's lesson, never as the teacher. Two tests on every term of the library, cheapest first: (1) it falls along the GOOD games and does not along the BAD ones, printed as the share of our moves after which it is lower, by set; (2) October's criterion on a sample of the class's won positions: at every position the search of toward.rs finds a line of at most d of our moves, against every reply, after which the term is lower, or the game's end is found; d from 1 to 3. A term passes with no failing position; the simplest passing term is the class's measure. Printed: the passing terms, the best failing terms with their failing positions, how the TABLE set scores on test (1). Written to a file under artifacts/experiments only, never into the store. Printed endgame coverage for every sample (positions by the table's distance, both colours).
PART D, THE WAKE HOLDS THE GOAL, Rust in cs_decision, unit tests first. `WakeInputs` gains a held goal: the term, its value when it was last lowered, the plies since. Each decision: the value now; if lower than held, a subgoal reached is logged (the event of ledger row 24, with the position's key) and the held value moves; then the search of toward.rs asks for a line within d of our moves after which the term is lower against every reply, inside a share of the clock the steps already have. The first move of such a line is named to the search first, and among the moves the calculation holds equal it is the move played, with the reason said in the log ("toward the held goal: the measure falls from x to y in k moves"). The wall stands: a move the calculation holds worse is never played for the measure, and the measure never enters a line's value (subgoals enter through the order and the choice, never the value). The goal is dropped only for a stated cause that is logged: the class changed (a unit was taken), no line lowers the term within d, or the game's end is found by the search, which then plays it. The goal is carried by carry.rs from move to move. With no goal given the wake is as on main (test: logged decisions equal).
PART E, THE TEST AGAIN AND THE WHOLE, in this order: Rust unit tests; integration tests (a decision with a held goal on five positions of each class, the log read against the board); part A's cells again with the goal held, same starts, same defenders, same clocks; then the measure's fall along each game printed (drops a game, longest run of our moves with no drop, goals dropped and why). Twenty decisions from twenty games judged against the board by the builder. The 300 puzzles and one match of 100 games at 0.2 s against the old player with no goal given, to show ordinary play did not move. If a measure passed for both classes, the miner alone (parts B and C, no play) is also run on two of the long-moving units against one, and what it finds is printed.
STOP POINTS. After part A, report in the BUILT block and go on. If part C finds no passing term for the one-unit class, stop there: print the best terms and their failing positions and build no part D on a term that failed.
NOT IN THIS PLAN: any table or oracle read by the wake or by anything it reads at play; any term, atom or number put in by hand for one class (the library is the same for every class and names no unit of the game); any write to the real store; any human game; any new fit; a change to the old player; a piece turned off.
LIMITS THAT STAND: as plan 79.16 (the scan of tests/test_plan78.py; no AI trailers; protected files; `--offline`; one disk-heavy job at a time; matches on a quiet machine through `run_games` with the early stop; Pool from a script file; numbers only from OBS lines, one run each, directions).
READ BEFOREHAND. If the wake with the held goal ends the one-unit class inside the quiet-ply rule where the wake without it repeats, rows 35, 23 and 13 are in for a goal beyond the horizon, and the next step is the same mechanism where the measure is not handed a class: mined subgoals in whole games (row 25) and the event as a training signal (row 24). If the miner finds no term, the library of atoms is what is short and that is the finding. If the term passes the miner and the wake still does not win, the fault is in how the goal enters the choice, and the logs of part E say where.

WHAT EXISTS (search first, print the table before code). `cs_memory`: `lemma` (a restricted Datalog over the game's fact vocabulary, with variables: the placeholders are here already), `matcher` (the one join that binds a body to facts), `snapshot` (an immutable, content-addressed store), `claim` (a position's class and its reader), `op`, `cards`. `cs_decision`: `carry.rs` (open tactics and the held goal carried a game), `goal_table.rs`, `lemma_prior.rs`, `claim_op.rs`, the chance table and reasons of `WakeInputs`, the worth record. `cs_tactics::measure` (terms), the mined measures in artifacts/experiments/whole_79_17. Python: `lemma_store.py` and its statuses (proved, conjecture), the October event loop's read sets. The base graph and `Board::key_hashes`. Reuse; no second form of anything that exists.
THE INTERFACE, written first in the crate's doc comment and in the BUILT block, before any body:
- A STATEMENT: a pattern over the graph's facts with placeholders (the lemma language as it is, extended only where a test shows a need), what it says of the pattern (a relation holds; a move is proposed; a number; a term to lower), its STANDING (fact of the rules at a position; proved, with the name of the Lean theorem; conjecture, with the sample it held on; belief, with a probability and its count), its HOLDER (ours; ours about the other side), and what it READ (the facts or keys it depends on), so that it falls when one of them changes.
- THE LONG-TERM MEMORY: belongs to the game as such. Read in the wake through one reader; never written in the wake. A trained model or a table is an entry with its own interface (what it takes, what it returns, its standing as a belief) and is reached only through it.
- THE MEMORY OF THE GAME AT HAND: belongs to one game. Written by the wake, emptied at the game's end; it can hand what surprised it to sleep.
- THE WAY TO CHANGE THEM (Kaveh: "some sort of a mutation API on our representation layer"): add, replace, retract, and fall-by-change (given what a move changed, every statement that read it is dropped and listed). On the long-term memory a change makes a new content-addressed snapshot with its parent, and is open only to sleep. On the game's memory a change is in place and logged.
- SCRATCH that a layer does not want kept (the search's own table for one decision) stays inside that layer and is not part of this.
PART A, THE STATEMENT AND ITS TESTS, Rust in cs_memory, unit tests first. The test of this layer being done, as Kaveh gave it and as extended: (1) a position is encoded and recreated exactly over a large sample of positions from generated games (the game's own state and the base graph's part); (2) every statement of every standing and holder is written, read back and found identical; (3) a statement falls when, and only when, something it read changes (with a negative control); (4) a pattern with placeholders binds on a position exactly where a slow plain reference says it does.
PART B, THE TWO MEMORIES AND THE CHANGES, Rust in cs_memory, unit tests first: the reader, the four changes, the snapshot with its parent, the game's memory with its log.
PART C, WHAT EXISTS IS MOVED IN, NOT COPIED. Into the long-term memory, each behind its interface: the goal table, the chance table and reasons, the worth record, the lemmas of a snapshot, the mined measures (as conjectures, with their sample). Into the game's memory: the open tactics and the held goal of carry.rs, and the record of the game. The wake reads them only through the two memories; `WakeInputs` loses the fields that are replaced. THE GUARD: with the same inputs the wake's logged decisions are equal to main before the move, on the logged positions of 79.16 and 79.17 (decisions may not change in this plan; any difference is listed and is a fault to mend, not to accept).
PART D, THE COST. The hot path stays fast: nodes a second of the search and the wall of a decision before and after, printed; a statement read in the wake costs no allocation where the old field cost none.
NOT IN THIS PLAN: any new atom, pattern, lemma or learned thing; filling the opponent's side (the holder is sayable and tested, nothing is put in it); the layers above 1; any change to the old player; any write to the real store (the long-term memory is built from the files the wake reads today and written under artifacts/experiments only).

AMENDMENT TO PLAN 79.19 (2026-11-20, Kaveh: "When I say two memories, one for long term for chess, I mean for any game that we learn. So basically keyed by the game, the specific variant of that game ... regular chess, anti-chess ... checkers, all of that would be here. Properly namespaced, partitioned"). The long-term memory is ONE store for every game the system learns, partitioned by the game and its variant: the key is what the game itself reports (its name and the content address of its rules), never a word written in a layer crate. A reader is opened for one game and sees that game's partition only; the changes of part B name the partition they change; nothing learned in one game is read in another unless it was checked again in that other game and written into its partition with its own standing. THE INTERFACE (also in cs_memory's crate doc comment, committed before any body in c39c61dd):
 STATEMENT `Statement { id, pattern: Vec<Lit>, says: Says, standing: Standing, holder: Holder, also: Vec<String> }`. pattern = the lemma language as it is (variables, negation); says = Holds | Proposes(Response) | Number(f64) | Lower { term, within }; standing = Fact | Proved(theorem) | Conjecture(sample) | Belief { probability, count }; holder = Ours | OursAboutOther. `reads()` (each literal as Read::Facts, `also` as Read::Key), `bindings(&FactIndex, limit, &mut steps)` (the existing matcher), `falls_by(&Change)`, `to_json/from_json`, `validate`, `from_lemma`. `Change { added, removed, keys }`, `Change::between(before, after)`. `encode_facts/decode_facts` (a position's canonical text). Called by: the memories below, the unit tests, the wake's reader.
 LONG-TERM MEMORY `LongTerm` (one store for every game; partitioned by `GameKey { name, rules }` = the game's name() and the content address of its rules, `GameKey::of(name, rules_text)`); `Partition` (immutable, content-addressed, with its parent; statements and named entries; `write(root)` to `<root>/<name>__<rules>/<id>.json`; `load(path, &Decoders)` refuses a file that does not hash to its name); `Reader` (opened for ONE game by `LongTerm::reader(&key)`; `statement`, `statements`, `entry`, `get::<T>(name)`, `bound`, `id`, `parent`, no way to change); `LongTerm::sleep() -> Sleep` the only door: `add`, `replace`, `retract`, `fall_by_change`, `add_entry`, `replace_entry`, each naming its partition and returning the id of the NEW snapshot (the old stays as its parent). `Kept` (trait) and `Decoders` for a trained model or table behind its own interface.
 GAME'S MEMORY `GameMemory` (statements and typed slots; written by the wake; `add`, `replace`, `retract`, `fall_by_change`, `put_slot`, each logged with a reason; `end()` empties it and hands back what surprised it, the statements that fell, and the log).

PART A, THE INTERFACE, written before any body. The question to layer 4 carries a goal. A goal is one type with three cases: a statement in layer 1's form (a pattern with placeholders over the facts of the graph, for a side, that the side wants to hold), the game's end in the side's favour, and a gain by the judge. The last two are what the entry does today and stay as they are in substance. The answer says, for the goal: REACHED by force (the line, the bindings where it holds, and what the judge says the line cost or won, read after the goal holds so that a goal reached by giving a unit away is said as such), OUT OF REACH within the depth read in full (every line read, the goal held in none: a statement about that depth only, never beyond it), or NOT SETTLED (the budget cut it; a cut is a gap, never a verdict). The value judges the line's end; the goal decides when a line ends and, later, which moves are read. A goal never changes a value (AGENTS rule 7).
PART B, THE BODY. First sound, then narrow. (1) Every move is read: an and-or search to the goal on the budget of nodes, deepened a ply at a time, positions met again by layer 1's history, the pattern matched on the live graph with make and undo and not on a graph built anew at each node. (2) Only then the narrowing: an order of moves (those that add a fact of the pattern or take away what blocks one come first) and, if the builder can state it soundly, a cut of moves that cannot serve the goal nor answer the other side. An unsound cut is not kept; if no sound cut is found say so and keep the order only. Every narrowing is measured against (1) on the same questions: same answers, fewer nodes.

ONE TREE SERVES THE LIST: at a position the patterns of all goals still open are matched together over one set of rows; the search returns for every open goal the plies to reach it; a child is read for the goals still open only (an or-node stops asking for a goal once a child reaches it, an and-node stops asking once a reply leaves it out of reach). (2) THE NARROWING, measured against (1): (a) a table of answers by position and goal across the deepening ("reached within n", "out of reach within n"; never stored for an answer that rests on the line) and the matching of a position kept by position; (b) an order of moves by the first open goal (arriving on a place the pattern names, leaving one, taking a unit, a kind it names). NO CUT OF MOVES WAS KEPT: the one sound cut, at the last ply (a move that changes no row of the pattern cannot make it bind), can be known only from the position the move makes, so it saves matching and not nodes, and the table's rows already stand for it; a cut at an earlier ply is unsound (a move that changes no row may still open a later move). ### PLAN 79.28: A GOAL IS REACHED ONLY IF IT OUTLASTS THE REPLY (2026-11-22, main agent, at Kaveh's "ok" to the proposal of the 79.27 report; SYSTEM_SPEC 11 the block "Reached means the goal outlasts the reply", 7 goals; piece: tactical reasoner)

LEDGER ROWS MOVED: 36 (layer 4's answer), 14 (the language of a goal). No other row.
WHY. In 79.27 a goal counts as reached when its pattern binds at any position of the line, for one ply or more. A thing the other side undoes at once is not reached.
SEARCH FIRST and print: reach.rs (where a pattern's binding ends a line), the reference in layer4_goals.rs, cs_rep's matcher and lemma forms for any literal that already says two placeholders differ, the Lean index for the same.
PART A, THE MEANING, interface before body. REACHED: on every reply of the other side the pattern binds at a position where the asking side is to move, or where the game is over. So a pattern that binds after our move counts only if it binds after each reply too; one that binds at the root with us to move is reached at nought plies. TOUCHED: the pattern binds after a move of ours and some reply unbinds it, and the goal is not reached within the depth; said apart, with the line and that reply, and never counted as reached. The other two answers stand. The answer of a reached goal says the plies and the bindings at the position where it is held.
PART B, THE BODY, in the one tree of 79.27, with the table and the order kept; the reference in the test is rewritten apart to the same meaning and stays slow and plain. The pairs: one line reaches two goals only if both are reached in this meaning.
PART C, TWO DIFFERENT UNITS. If layer 1's pattern language has no way to say that two placeholders differ, add one (a literal of the language, in cs_rep, written and read back, with its test in layer 1's tests against the slow plain matcher); if it has one, use it. Then the fixture's kind "two units bear on one" is written with it, and the fixture is remade so that no kind is reached by the reference in fewer than ten cases of its eighty; if a kind cannot be made so, say why.
PART D, THE TEST as 79.27's, on the new meaning: never reached where the reference does not reach, never out of reach where it reaches, touched only where the reference says touched; every reached line replayed by the rules, the pattern binding at its end and after every legal reply before it where the meaning asks; floors at three budgets; the old goals unchanged (120 of 120); the guards unchanged. Print how many of 79.27's reached answers are now touched.
PART E, LINES FOR A READER. A printing script (its name ends in _print.py) that writes, for twelve reached and six touched answers chosen by a fixed rule across the kinds, the position, the goal in plain words, the line, and the position at its end, as text a person can read against a board. The main agent reads them before the piece is called done.
IF IT IS SLOWER OR WORSE: diagnose and mend, do not set aside. Print where the nodes go.
NOT IN THIS PLAN: moving any caller; the two copies of the deepening; choosing goals.
LIMITS THAT STAND: as plan 79.27.

TOUCHED: not reached, and the side can force the pattern to bind right after a move of its own (the other side to move, the game not over, at least one ply in) in such a way that, whatever the other side does, a position is met where the goal is held or is so touched; the reply that unbinds it is read, so a touched line is at most the depth less one. WHAT IS BUILT. A crate `cs_base` (rust/engine/base), a member of the workspace, depending on no crate of ours. It names no game and no thing of a world (no board, no place of a game, no unit, no side to move). Six modules, the interface of each written before its body:
1. `logic`. The fact, the argument, the literal, "differ", the check of a body, the index of facts and the matcher MOVE here from cs_rep (fact.rs's Fact; lemma.rs's Arg, Lit, DIFFER, validate_body; matcher.rs). cs_rep hands them on under their old paths, so no caller changes and the wake decides as before. New: a formula over the literals with and, or, not, some, every (over a finite set), at least so many; read against the same index of facts; on a body of literals alone it must give the bindings the matcher gives.
2. `sets`. A finite set, membership, a kind as a set, how many, with union, meet and part-of.
3. `number`. Whole and real numbers in one type with one total order (a value that is not a number is refused when made), arithmetic that says when it overflows.
4. `structure`. Three forms. A graph: nodes, links with a label, neighbours, a path, distance in steps. A sequence: items in order, before and after, the difference of two neighbours. Geometry: a point, distance, direction, a region with "inside" (at least a half plane, a box, a disc, a many-sided figure, and the union and the meet of two), between. One interface of distance that both the graph and the plane give. Read cs_rep's graph.rs first: if a pure core of it can be lifted here with cs_rep using it and nothing slower, do that; if not, say why with what you measured and do not make a second graph that copies it.
5. `chance`. A finite spread of outcomes with their chances (they sum to one, each between nought and one), the expectation, the product of two that do not depend on each other, the spread given a condition.
6. `choice`. A finite tree whose nodes are: a result; a choice in turn by one chooser; a choice at once by two choosers (a table); a choice by chance (a spread over trees). An order of preference over results for each chooser. Two readings: whether a chooser can force a property of the result against every counter-choice (with chance on the way: the least chance with which it can), and the value when the two choosers want opposite things. For a choice at once only pure choices: the lower and the upper value; mixed choices are NOT built and the interface says so. The search of layer 4 is NOT moved or changed; this is the meaning it must agree with, and a comparison with it is not in this plan.

PART A, CHOOSERS AND WANTS (the fault Kaveh found: the value reading assumes opposite wants). A chooser is an identity, any number of them, not one of two. A node in turn is by one chooser. A node at once is between two parties, each a set of choosers that pick as one. Each chooser has an order of its own over results. Defined, not assumed: two choosers are OPPOSED when one order is the reverse of the other on the results of the tree, ALLIED when the orders agree. Readings: (i) a SET of choosers can force a property against every counter-choice of the rest (the reading of 79.30 with one chooser is the case of a set of one); (ii) what a set of allied choosers can make sure of in their order whatever the rest want; (iii) for two opposed parties the lower and the upper value as before. The old two-chooser calls stay as thin cases of these, so the tests of 79.30 hold.
PART B, THE MIXED CHOICE. For a choice at once between two opposed parties: the best spread over one's own options and the one value, exact, by a small linear program written here over exact numbers (see part D); in a tree the value of a cell is the value of its subtree. Tests: the value lies between the lower and the upper; the two parties' guarantees meet; a table with a pure answer gives it with chance one; known small tables by hand. Lean: the law that the guarantees meet, proved if it can be by reasoning (search Mathlib first), else left OPEN and said; the bounds law proved.
PART C, THE BELIEF. A belief is a spread over suppositions. Its change by what is seen: each supposition says how likely it made what was seen; the new spread weighs by that (refused when nothing supposed could have made it). A choice against a belief: the expectation of each option under the belief and the best option (a single option, by the law that against a fixed belief no mixing gains; state and prove it in Lean). Layer 0 gives the form only; nothing here says what is believed of anyone.
PART D, EXACT NUMBERS. Num gains exact fractions; whole and fraction arithmetic is exact and says overflow; a real is used only when asked for. The chances of a spread are Num; a spread of fractions sums to exactly one, the tolerance is used only where reals enter. The expectation, the product, the given spread and force with chance are exact on fractions. Tests of 79.30 that used the tolerance on exact inputs now ask equality.

(3) `value_between` refuses a tree where a table's party has members on both sides (`SplitParty`) and a chooser on neither side (`NotCovered`). (4) `Chooser::other()` removed. `Tree::Table` gained two fields, `Tree::chance` and `Spread::new` take `Num` chances (`Spread::from_reals` keeps reals with the tolerance), `Spread::product` returns a `Result`, `Spread::total`, `chance_of` return `Result`s. (5) A real stays a real (its operations go through f64); a real equal to a fraction compares equal and hashes alike, but its arithmetic is not exact. (6) The simplex is over `i64` fractions, so a large table can say `Overflow` where a wider integer would not; it was kept to the one number type of the layer. (7) The JSON trait is `cs_rep::lemma::LitJson` (not a new module). (8) choice is a folder (mod.rs, lp.rs). (9) Part F reads depth three at most because the tree is made in full, and takes its facts the way layer4_goals.rs's reference does (copied, a test cannot share another test file). (10) The belief's likelihood must be in [0, 1]; the belief over reals keeps the tolerance. (11) The Lean coalition tree `GTree` identifies choosers by a natural number.

### PLAN 79.35: LAYER 2 SAYS FOUR MORE GAMES ON THE SAME LAYER 1: TWO WITH ANOTHER START (CHESS960, HORDE) AND TWO WITH OTHER RULES OF MOVING AND ENDING (ATOMIC, ANTICHESS) (2026-11-23, main agent; at Kaveh's word "sure lets do these variants. also atomic chess and antichess"; SYSTEM_SPEC 11 "The cut of layers 1 and 2 is carried into the code" and its last block; pieces: rules, representation)

LEDGER ROWS MOVED: 41 (new: layer 2 says variants with another start and with other rules, layer 1 unchanged), 40 (its open point: no variant with another start is tested). Said plainly: this plan changes no decision of the engine at chess; it is made at Kaveh's word, as a named exception to row 38. The measure of the whole (row 39) is made at its READ and must not move.
WHY. The start was put in layer 2 so that a variant may start differently. Today only chess, king of the hill and three-check are tested and they start alike. A game counts as said by layer 2 when it has all four: its description (rules/chess.gdl with a delta under rules/variants), the kernel's mode, a certificate that the two agree by co-play, and a fixture written from an outside library that shares no code with the engine.
THE FOUR GAMES. Chess960: the same kinds, board and counts, another arrangement, one of 960, and the leader's two-unit move from wherever the two units start. Horde: another arrangement AND other counts, one side with no leader and 36 of the smallest kind; that side loses when none of its units is left. Atomic: the start of chess; a taking removes the taker, the taken and the units around the place except the smallest kind; a leader may not take; a leader removed ends the game; the two leaders side by side change what an attack on a leader means. Antichess: the start of chess; a taking is compulsory when one is there; the leader is an ordinary unit; no two-unit move of the leader; the smallest kind may become a leader at the last row; the side with no unit or no move wins.
PART A, THE INVENTORY, printed before any code and put in the BUILT block: for each of the four games, what exists today (kernel mode, description, certificate, fixture, any test), and every place in rust/engine/game/src outside kernel.rs and gdl_game.rs that assumes the start of chess, one leader a side, or that a move leaving the leader attacked is the only refused move.
PART B, THE INTERFACE, written and committed before any body and shown in the report: how layer 2 is asked for a game whose start is a parameter (the 960 starts) and what it returns; how a description gives another start (a delta that takes away the start's clauses and gives others, or the description read with a start given); what bearing on a place and may move to a place mean in a game where a taking is compulsory or a taking removes more than one unit, and how the test states it. PART B, THE INTERFACE AS BUILT. `starts::Starts: Game` (`start_count`, `with_start(n)`), implemented for the kernel in outside.rs (960 for the game named chess960, 1 for every other) and delegated by `Ruled`. `rules::restart_delta(text, start_facts) -> delta`: `(retract (init <fact>))` for each initial fact of `text`, `(init <fact>)` for each fact of the start; composed by `cs_gdl::compose`. `Ruled::open_variant(game, name, root, declaration, delta, start)`: the base of the declaration, the delta file composed, the start delta composed when facts are given; the rules' address is that of base plus delta WITHOUT the start (two starts of one game are one game: tested). `bear` is the geometry of the kind on the board as it stands; `may_move` the places stepped onto by the kind's step and the game's rule of what may be taken; compulsion, what a taking removes besides the unit taken, the leader left struck, the two-unit move, the taking in passing and the two-row step are not read by either. THE CHOICE FOR CHESS960: the start is a parameter of the kernel and, for the description, a generated delta of initial facts (restart_delta of the facts the kernel gives); the delta file rules/variants/chess960.gdl holds the RULES and reads the files of the leader and of the rooks from the initial facts, side by side (a side's rook of a wing is the outermost first-row rook of that side on that side of the leader), so one description serves all 960 starts and any position shown. Said plainly: this plan changes no decision of the engine and puts nothing on the engine's path; it produces numbers from which the translator's plan is written. The measure of the whole (row 39) is made at its READ and must not move.
THE QUESTIONS THIS PLAN ANSWERS, each by a printed number. (1) What share of a decision's wall time does the engine spend inside the rules today (the kernel's allowed moves, next state, end, and the placed questions)? (2) How fast is a plain translation of the description to Rust, in positions a second, beside the evaluator and beside the outside library, on the same positions? (3) Which pieces of the translated code take the time? (4) Does the translated code give the same answers as the evaluator on every position tried?
PART A, THE SHARE OF THE RULES IN A DECISION. A printing script (scripts/rules_share_print.py) on the wake as it plays at 0.2 s a move over a fixed set of positions: the wall time inside each rules call of layer 2 and the whole decision's wall time, by a profile that does not change the code on the engine's path (a sampling profiler already on the machine, or counters in a private build of the binding in the scratchpad; never the shared module). Printed: the share by call, the number of calls a decision.
PART B, THE INTERFACE, written and committed before any body and shown in the report. The translator (catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/gdl_to_rust.py, beside the translator to Lean that exists) takes a composed description (the base and a delta) and writes one Rust source file. It knows no game: no name of a relation of chess appears in the translator, only the fixed words of the description language (role, init, true, does, legal, next, terminal, goal, distinct, not). What it writes: one Rust function for each relation of the description (a PIECE), the state as the set of true facts, and the five questions (the side to move, the allowed moves, the next state, whether it is the end, the outcome) built from the pieces. State plainly how symbols, facts and the state are held, and how a relation that does not read the state is told from one that does.
PART C, THE FIRST TRANSLATION, plain and correct before fast: no pass for speed except what is free (symbols as numbers, relations that do not read the state computed once and kept). The written file for chess goes under rust/engine/game/tests/generated/ and is compiled only into a test and a timing program of cs_game; it is NOT part of the crate's sources and nothing on the engine's path uses it. The generated file is committed with the hash of the description and of the translator at its head, and a test fails when either hash differs from the file's.
PART D, THE SAME ANSWERS. On every position of the chess fixture and on positions of seeded random play (the corpus of the chess certificate): the allowed moves, the next state as facts, the end and the outcome of the translated code equal the evaluator's, and the counts after a few plies from the start equal the fixture's. And by piece: for each relation that does not read the state, the translated function equals the evaluator on its WHOLE domain (every tuple), printed as a count per relation; for each relation that reads the state, on the states above. Any disagreement stops the plan and is reported with the relation and the smallest case.
PART E, THE TIMES, single thread, three runs each, the machine's load printed: positions a second for allowed moves plus next state, over the same list of positions, for the evaluator, the translated code and the kernel over the outside library; and for the translated code the time by piece (the ten pieces that take most, with their share and their number of calls). If the translator needed a change for the variant, say what and why.
PART G, THE GATE. tests/test_plan79_37.py: the translator's source holds no relation name of any description under rules/ (a scan against the names the descriptions define); the generated files' hashes match; nothing under rust/engine/*/src includes or names the generated files; the test is in the gate after 79.36.

No source under rust/engine/*/src, no Cargo.toml and no Cargo.lock changed; kernel.rs, gdl_game.rs, gdl/src/lib.rs and ledger.rs are the files of 2153532f (tests/test_plan79_37.py compares them with that commit).
THE INTERFACE AS BUILT (also the module text of catspace/incubator/analyst/discovery/gdl_to_rust.py). `translate(text, module) -> str`: a composed description in, one Rust source out, `pub mod <module>` with the same public items for every game (a test is written once, through a small trait in tests/translated_common). It reads the description with the reader that exists (discovery/gdl.py: `parse`, `clauses`, `Program` with its strata and each rule's join order); a second reader was not written, and scripts/gdl_to_lean.py was not reused (it makes Lean text, not a join order). Symbols: every constant of the description (every symbol of a clause or a sort, and `noop`) is a `u32`, numbered in the order of the names; a compound term (the moves) is a `u32` made at run time by one table that gives the same number to the same compound, numbering from where the constants end. Facts: a relation of n arguments is `Rel<n>`: rows in the order made, a hash set of them, and for each set of argument places the joins ask by, an index from the numbers at those places to the rows (the places are read from the join orders and fixed in the file). The state: the set of true facts as one sorted list of rows for each fluent (`State`); the relations of one evaluation live in `Dy`, the ones that do not read the state in `St`. THE TWO KINDS OF RELATION are told apart by the dependency graph as the evaluator does: a relation reads the state when it is a `true` fluent, `does` or `record`, or depends on one through a positive or a negated literal; the others are evaluated once in `Game::new` into `St`. Each strongly connected set of relations is one function (a piece); a recursive set runs the semi-naive rule; each clause is one function of nested loops in the reader's join order. The five questions (`mover`, `moves`, `next`, `terminal`, `outcome`) are `GdlGame`'s in the same words on numbers (a question loads the state and runs only the pieces its answer depends on). The two files: tests/generated/chess.rs 278,785 bytes, 6,017 lines (99 pieces, 368 clauses) and tests/generated/atomic.rs 341,792 bytes, 7,473 lines (129 pieces, 414 clauses), each headed by the sha256 of its description and of the translator.
WHAT THE TRANSLATOR COULD NOT TRANSLATE PLAINLY: nothing was left out and no relation is named in it (tests/test_plan79_37.py scans its source against the 213 names the descriptions under rules/ define: 0 in both, after the first version held 8 plain words that are also relation or sort names and was reworded). Forms and how they went: `or` and `not`/`distinct` are the reader's (an `or` is expanded into clauses by the reader); a compound term in a body literal is matched by a lookup in the term table and in a head or a key is built by it; the sort and signature declarations are not read by the translator (the code has no types, only numbers; the tests read them for the whole-domain check); `record` is an input relation that no state gives rows (the evaluator's run does the same), so the repetition rule is not exercised by either; a relation used with two numbers of arguments, a description with no `role`, are refused with a message that names them (tested). `noop`, the move that passes, is a word of the language the translator knows by that name, as `GdlGame` does.

Direction: about four fifths of a decision's wall is inside layer 2 and the library under it, and nearly all of that is the library generating the legal moves (the kernel's `mover` and `outcome` ask whether the game is over). WHAT THE NEXT PLAN SHOULD READ FROM THIS. The gap: the plain translation answers a position in about 0.4 ms (chess), the kernel in about 0.3 microseconds; no general pass in the plan's list is likely to close a factor of 1,000 at once, so the target should be set by the share: at 79 per cent of a decision in rules, a translated engine 1,000 times slower than the library would make a decision 1,000 times slower unless the wake asks the rules far less often (it asks `outcome` 1.25 million times and `moves` 43 thousand times in 0.2 s). For each hot piece, the general pass that would speed it (none built): king_ray and slide (recursive rays over the board, 5.9 and 3.8 million rows visited): a relation over a small fixed set of places kept as a set of bits (one word of 64 places) with the rays as tables, a pure function of line and occupancy; after, stays, after_occupied (the board after each candidate move, 1.7 million rows for 1,920 positions): keeping what a move did not change (the board once, a candidate as a change of it); exposed (3.6 million rows visited for 4 thousand made): an order of joining that starts from the king's rays and stops at the first witness (a relation read only for whether it has a row); attack_by and attacked: bits again; three_nonking (atomic, 153 million rows visited for 1,620 made): an order of joining or an existence test that stops at the third row, since the description asks "at least three" by a join of three. WHAT IN THE DESCRIPTION MAKES TRANSLATION SLOW: legality is written as the board after each candidate move (`vacates`, `fills`, `stays`, `after`, `after_occupied`, `king_after`, `king_ray`, `exposed` are relations of the candidate and every cell, about 870 `after` rows a position), the rays (`slide`, `king_ray`) are relations of five and seven arguments rather than a function of a line and the occupied places, and `three_nonking` counts by a triple join; nothing in the description is wrong, it is written to be read, and a translator that keeps it plain is slow by that. CRATES THAT DO THIS JOB, named from memory as options only (no network, not read, not added): `ascent` and `crepe` compile Datalog written in a Rust macro at build time (`ascent` is the one cs_gdl's header names as unusable for a description read at run time), `datafrog` (the Datalog engine under rustc's borrow checker) is a library of joins; none reads GDL.

Four of them walk lines over a small fixed set of places through hash indexes; three write the whole state again for every candidate move; one is read only for being non-empty.
PART A, THE PLAIN TRANSLATION BECOMES THE REFERENCE OF EVERY PIECE. `translate` takes the list of passes to apply; with none it gives today's file, byte for byte. A test harness (test files only) runs a piece of the plain module and the same piece of a module with passes on the same input rows and compares the rows made, for every piece, on every state of the fixtures and of the seeded games, and for pieces that do not read the state on their whole extension. A piece a pass removes or merges is compared at the first relation that survives it, and the report lists such pieces. The tests of 79.37 against the evaluator stay and are run on the module with passes too.
PART B, THE PASSES, each general (it reads only the shape of the clauses, the sorts and the signatures; it names no relation; the scan of 79.37 holds), each its own commit, each measured alone and together (positions a second, three runs, load printed; the time by piece again):
  (1) A SMALL FIXED SORT AS NUMBERS FROM NOUGHT: a relation whose every place is of a small declared sort is held as a dense table (and, where it has one or two places, as words of bits), asked by position, with no hash.
  (2) A RELATION ASKED ONLY WITH PLACES BOUND IS ANSWERED ON DEMAND: where every use of a relation binds some places (a negated literal, a test for one row), it is not made in full; it is answered for the asked key and stops at the first witness where only being non-empty is read.
  (3) WHAT A TURN DOES NOT CHANGE IS NOT WRITTEN AGAIN: where the next state's clauses copy a fluent's rows that a turn leaves alone, the copy is kept as the old rows and a change. The builder states the general condition on the clauses under which this is sound, tests it, and refuses the pass where the condition does not hold.
  A pass that makes a piece slower or gives a different row is diagnosed and mended, not set aside; one that cannot be made sound in general is reported with the clause that defeats it, and left out.
PART C, THE SECOND GAME. The same translator with the same passes writes the second game's file; its tests pass; its times are printed. A pass that helps one game and not the other is said.
PART D, THE REPORT'S NUMBERS: positions a second for the kernel, the plain translation, each pass alone and all together, both games; the ratio to the kernel; the ten hottest pieces after the passes with what would speed each next; the count of piece-by-piece comparisons and of disagreements.
PART E, THE GATE. tests/test_plan79_38.py: the translation with no pass is the committed plain file; the scan of names holds for the translator with its passes; the files with passes carry the hashes and the list of passes; a fresh translation is the same file under two hash seeds of the process; nothing under rust/engine/*/src names any of it; no source of the engine differs from the commit before the plan.
LIMITS THAT STAND. As plan 79.37. No hand-written piece for one game in this plan. No change of any description. The reader may be mended where a fault is found, and then the certificates are made again and counted.
NOT IN THIS PLAN: putting translated code on the engine's path; certificates for it; the placed questions; the two faults of 79.36; the cost of asking whose turn it is in the layers above (named in the 79.37 READ; it waits for Kaveh's word because its plain mend is in a protected file and changes the speed of the old player too).

The interface of the first three was committed before any body; the fourth pass (below) is not in the plan and its interface text was written with its body.
THE INTERFACE AS BUILT is the module text of discovery/gdl_to_rust.py: `translate(text, module, passes=())`, `PASSES = ("dense", "demand", "copy", "delta")`; with no pass the file is the plain one, byte for byte but for the translator hash line (the head hash changed because the translator's source changed: the two plain files were made again by scripts/gdl_to_rust_make.py, and tests/test_plan79_38.py holds them to differ from the files of 12f17e26 in that one line). With passes the head holds `// passes: <names>`, and the module has `PASSES`, `COPIED`, `Game::demanded()` and `Game::ask_many(...)`. Files: generated/{chess,atomic}.rs (plain) and {chess,atomic}_{dense,demand,copy,delta,fast}.rs (`fast` = all four).
THE PASSES. (1) dense: a relation whose every place is of a declared sort of constants, with at most 2^22 tuples and at most 2^16 keys for any index asked by, is a bit table with bucket-array indexes (no hash) and is cleared by its own rows, the `Dy` being kept between questions. (2) demand: a relation that reads the state, is not recursive and is not read by a question, whose uses all bind a place or only ask existence, is not made; each use is answered for its key by its own clauses joined from the key (stopping at the first row for an existence test); a relation read whole, or whose answer from its key is a loop over a whole relation of the state, stays in full (the clause that defeats it is kept in `Plan.refused`); the rules that are made in full are joined by the translator's own `JoinRule` (the reader's order, but a demanded relation no bound variable reaches goes last; pinned to the reader's on every clause with nothing avoided: 0 differ). (3) copy: a next clause whose head is the row of its one positive literal (the fluent's own `true`) and whose other literals are `distinct` or negated tests over that row alone is run as a filter of the old rows in `next`, the other clauses adding the changes. THE SOUNDNESS CONDITION (stated and tested): the clause is a function of one old row alone; the pass refuses a clause with a second positive literal, a repeated head variable, another fluent's rows, or a compound term in a negated literal (tests/test_plan79_38.py, four refusals). (4) delta (NOT IN THE PLAN, added from the first profile): each rule of a recursive set is joined once for each of its literals of the set with that literal first, read from the rows new in the last round, borrowed; the reader's order started from a table of steps and scanned the new rows once for each of its 420 rows (the rays, 5.9 million rows visited for 1,920 positions). Sound because a conjunction does not depend on the order of its literals and the semi-naive rule is unchanged.
PART A, THE HARNESS (translated_common/pieces.rs, translated_pieces.rs). The plain module is the reference; for each game and each of the five modules, at every position of the fixture and every move it records and every state of the certificate's 20 seeded games (relations at the first 6 games, the questions at all), the harness compares as text: the five questions and the next state; every relation the module makes in full against the plain module's rows (a relation the plain module makes and the other neither makes nor answers on demand fails the test as a lost piece: it caught `capture`, an unused demanded relation, in the first run); every way a demanded relation is asked (rows or existence) with keys made from the plain rows and from rows with one place taken from another row, and the whole relation; and every relation that does not read the state, whole.

### PLAN 79.40: A RELATION OVER A SMALL SORT IS BITS, AND A JOIN OVER IT IS WORD OPERATIONS (2026-11-23, main agent; SYSTEM_SPEC 11 "The crux of layer 2 is a translator from the description to Rust, made fast piece by piece under tests"; piece: rules)

FROM THE 79.38 READ: four passes over rows in hash sets bought about two and a half times; five hundred remain. The form of the data is the cost.
PART A, THE FORM, written as interface before any body. A new pass, general as the others. (1) A tuple of small declared sorts is numbered densely (two sorts of eight make one sort of sixty-four when relations use them together; the translator finds such products from the signatures, it is told none). (2) A relation whose places are such sorts is held as sets of bits: for each value of its bound places, one word (or a few) for the free place. A fluent of the state is held the same way, so a state is a fixed array of words, with no rows allocated. (3) A clause over such relations is compiled to word operations: a positive literal is an and, a negated one an and-not, a join through a relation with a fixed table is a loop over the set bits with a table lookup, existence is a test against nought. (4) A recursive relation that walks along a fixed step relation until a test fails is compiled as that loop over words; the pass states the shape it recognises and refuses others, which stay as today.
PART B, PINNED PIECE BY PIECE to the plain module with the harness of 79.38, on every state of the fixtures and the seeded games and on whole extensions; the tests against the evaluator pass on the new module; a wrong pass made on purpose is caught.
PART C, THE ORDER OF JOINING from the sizes of the relations where they are known at translation (the static ones), measured alone.
PART D, NO ALLOCATION IN A QUESTION: where the profile shows making and freeing memory, the evaluation's working memory is kept between questions; measured alone.
PART E, BOTH GAMES by the same translator; the times as in 79.38 (kernel beside each, three runs, loads printed); the ratio to the kernel; the hot pieces after; what each pass bought alone and together.
PART F, THE GATE tests/test_plan79_40.py as that of 79.38. The generated files of single passes are NOT committed any more: only the plain file and the file with all passes for each game are kept in the repository; the others are made in the test run (the builder moves the tests of 79.38 to that, and says what it changed).
LIMITS THAT STAND as plan 79.38. One commit for each pass. A pass that makes anything slower or different is diagnosed and mended, not set aside.
